+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 80.0
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Seven: The Courtesy of Antares Arthur Neegan had never worn a starched collar in his life, and he decided, somewhere around the second hour of the voyage, that he never would again—if he lived to have the choice. The transfer vessel was a corporate cutter, all brushed duralloy and carpeted decks, the kind of ship that smelled of ozone and money. Through the visiplate Mars shrank to a rust-colored coin, its terminator line crawling across the Tharsis plateau where, four hundred kilometers east of his homestead, the corporate arcologies glittered like spilled circuitry. Somewhere down there, under eight meters of regolith and a claim registered in his father's name before Arthur could walk, lay the richest Azra vein yet struck on the planet. He had known about it for eleven days. He had been free for eleven days. He was no longer certain he was either. "Mr. Neegan will want to freshen up before docking," said the woman who commanded the escort—six of them, sidearms worn openly, which told Arthur they expected no trouble and wished him to know it. She was polite the way a pressure door was airtight. "I'm fresh enough," Arthur said. "Of course, sir." She did not move. None of them moved. The ship hummed on toward wherever it was going, its hyperatomic drive winding up with a sound like a struck tuning fork held to the teeth. They docked, in the end, not at any orbital wheel but at a private yacht—a long, black-hulled ship riding lights-out at the Lagrange point, registry markings painted over, though the seal on the airlock hatch was unmistakable: a red star flaring between two olive branches. The Antares Diplomatic Corps. Arthur had seen that seal in newsfilms, usually behind some undersecretary announcing that the Antarean Compact regretted this or deplored that. Diplomatic in name only, the prospectors said. The Compact's diplomats carried the same sidearms as its marines, only better-polished. The man waiting for him in the salon was small, gray, and precise, with the careful hands of someone who had never done manual labor and never would. The salon itself was an exercise in understatement: genuine wood paneling—wood, on a ship, which on Mars would have bought a domed township—soft lighting, a decanter of something amber, and, on the wall, a star chart of the whole Solar System done in the old style, with the Belt drawn as a dotted ring and the outer planets crowded at the chart's edge like uninvited guests. "Mr. Neegan. Please, sit. I am Councilor Relgan Hwa, of the Antarean Compact's Ministry of Extra-Territorial Affairs." He poured two glasses without asking. "You'll forgive the manner of the invitation. My government has learned that on Mars, an invitation delivered by comm-channel is an invitation delivered to everyone." "Everyone meaning the corporations." "Everyone meaning *everyone*," Hwa said, and smiled. "Terran Metals Combine. The Meridian Consortium. The Earth government's Colonial Office, which is a corporation wearing a flag. And certain parties I won't name, who have less patience and fewer scruples than any of them. You have, in eleven days, become the most interesting man in the System. Drink. It's genuine Terran bourbon. There isn't a bottle of it between here and the Belt." Arthur took the glass. His father had taught him never to sit down nervous and never to stand up thirsty. "I'm a mining engineer, Councilor. I'm interesting because of what's under my claim, not because of anything I've done." "Modest, and accurate. Both are useful qualities." Hwa settled into a chair and regarded Arthur with the detached attention of a man appraising ore. "Let me be direct, because you strike me as a man who values it. The vein beneath your homestead contains, by our survey estimates—and ours are better than anyone's—some forty percent of all known Azra in the System. At current extraction rates, that is enough to refit a fleet. Or to build one. Azra, Mr. Neegan, is the difference between a civilization that touches the stars and one that merely looks at them. The decay-acceleration effect means drives that make the outer planets a week's journey instead of a decade. It also means warheads that make hydrogen bombs look like firecrackers. Every power on that chart knows this. None of them can say it aloud." "And the Compact wants my claim." "The Compact wants considerably more than your claim, but let us start there." Hwa set down his glass. "Here is the difficulty, and why you and not your ore are the interesting one. Under the Martian Homestead Act of 2084, surface and subsurface rights attach to first-generation settlers in fee simple. The corporations have spent forty years buying leases on *indentured laborers*, Mr. Neegan—on people—because they cannot buy the land. Your claim cannot be condemned, seized, or taxed into surrender. It can only be given. Or taken by other means." "Other means." "Dr. Selene Varrow held a patent on the resonance purification of Azra. Three weeks ago her skiff suffered a failure of its reactor shielding, in a shipyard full of witnesses, none of whom saw anything. I mention this so you understand the market you have entered." Hwa said it without emphasis, the way a man reads actuarial tables. "My government's offer is this: exclusive extraction rights to your vein, in exchange for which you receive Compact citizenship, permanent protection for yourself and any family you choose to acquire, a royalty of eight percent of gross yield—which, I assure you, will make you wealthy beyond the dreams of the men who own the corporations—and a research chair, if you want one, at the Compact's decay institute at Antares Point. You would be the only man in the System studying Azra who is not owned by somebody." Arthur looked at the star chart. Antares Point was a dot at the chart's very edge, four light-hours of nothing past the Belt. "And if I refuse?" "Then you return to Mars, and my government expresses its regrets, and within a month you deal with the Combine, or the Consortium, or with men who do not make offers." Hwa paused. "I would rather you did not refuse. There is a further consideration. Your vein is not merely large, Mr. Neegan. Our spectrographic analysis suggests it is *pure*—isotopically pure, which no Azra deposit should be. It was not laid down by geology. Someone put it there." The salon was very quiet. Somewhere below, the drive ticked as it cooled. "Put it there," Arthur repeated. "Who?" "That," said Councilor Hwa, refilling both glasses, "is precisely what my government hopes you will help us find out. You have until we reach the transfer point. Thirty-one hours. I recommend the bourbon; it is a long way to Antares, and the nights out there are longer." Arthur looked at his glass, at the collar that had been strangling him for six hours, and at the little gray man who had just told him, politely, that he was the most dangerous piece of property in the Solar System. "Thirty-one hours," Arthur said. "I've decided worse things faster. But I'll need charts. And everything you have on the vein." Hwa smiled, genuinely this time. "I was told you were direct. The charts are already aboard, Mr. Neegan. They were aboard before we invited you." Arthur went cold. "Before?" "Of course," said Hwa. "You did not imagine we came all this way for a *negotiation*, did you?"
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Asimov's style and the classic science fiction genre. The author successfully captures the retrofuturistic atmosphere with details like "duralloy," "hyperatomic drive," and "visiplate," while maintaining the cerebral, dialogue-heavy approach characteristic of Asimov's work. The worldbuilding is particularly effective, seamlessly integrating both macro-level political tensions (the Antarean Compact, corporate interests, Earth government) and micro-level details (Arthur's collar discomfort, the bourbon, the wood paneling). The revelation that the Azra deposit is artificially placed adds genuine intrigue and raises the stakes beyond a simple resource conflict. Arthur's characterization feels authentic - a practical mining engineer thrust into galactic politics, maintaining his directness while being clearly out of his depth. His father's wisdom about never sitting down nervous or standing up thirsty provides nice character grounding. Councilor Hwa is well-crafted as a polite but menacing diplomatic figure, with his careful mannerisms and understated threats. The dialogue carries the narrative effectively, revealing information naturally while maintaining tension. Hwa's casual mention of Dr. Varrow's "accident" and his final revelation that this was never truly a negotiation create genuine unease. The pacing builds appropriately to the climactic twist. However, some descriptions occasionally veer toward the overwrought ("spilled circuitry," "struck tuning fork held to the teeth"). A few moments feel slightly forced in their attempt to capture Asimov's voice, particularly some of the more elaborate metaphors. The piece also relies heavily on exposition through dialogue, though this is somewhat mitigated by being true to Asimov's style. The ending effectively sets up larger mysteries while resolving the immediate tension of Arthur's situation. The piece successfully balances the intimate human story with the broader galactic implications, maintaining reader engagement throughout. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 86.3
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The red light makes everyone honest. I've decided this over four years of late nights in the Whitmore building's darkroom, watching faces get stripped of everything performative under the safelight's amber wash. Colors lie. Red light doesn't. It just shows you what's actually there. What's actually here, tonight, is Elliot, three feet away from me at the developing station, his black-painted thumbnail hovering over the timer like he's afraid to start it. He's wearing that oversized fishnet shirt over a fitted black tee again, silver rings stacked to his knuckles, his eyeliner smudged just enough to look deliberate. Nineteen and dressed like a haunted thrift store. I'm twenty-five and I have spent an entire semester pretending I haven't noticed the exact way he tucks his hair behind his ear when he's thinking. "Timer's not going to start itself," I say, because that's what I do. I start things. I've been the one who starts things since I was old enough to figure out that nobody else was going to. "Right. Yeah." He presses it. The enlarger hums. We stand shoulder to shoulder in the red glow, and I'm acutely aware of how warm he is, and how stupid that is to be acutely aware of. Our final project is a paired portrait series—"The Self, Exposed," which is Professor Okafor's title, not ours. We each shot the other, and then we each shot ourselves, and the darkroom nights are for printing. His portraits of me came out fierce and overexposed, all jawline and challenge. My portraits of him came out soft. I kept worrying I'd gotten it wrong until I realized the softness wasn't an accident. It was the truest thing about him. The first print of his self-portrait slides into the developer bath and I rock the tray, and there he is. Elliot, in his bedroom mirror, in a slip dress he must have thrifted and never worn out of the house, one hand pressed flat against his sternum like he was holding something shut. Or holding something in. The image blooms fully and he goes very still beside me. "Wow," I say, and mean it. "It's stupid," he says, too fast. "It's—I did it at like three in the morning, I wasn't going to include it, I just—" "Elliot." I keep my voice level. "It's the best print either of us has made all semester, and you know it. Talk to me." I watch him decide. That's the thing about him—he decides slowly, completely, the way he does everything, and there's something about being on the receiving end of that full attention that I am absolutely not prepared for. "I've been questioning some things," he says. "About—myself. My gender. The way I present. I don't know what it is yet. I don't know if it's a what. I just know that when I put that dress on, I didn't feel like I was playing dress-up. I felt like I was—" He stops. His throat moves. "Like I was developing. Like there was an image there the whole time and it needed the right chemicals to show up." And here is where I have to be honest about my own internal disaster, because my first instinct is to take over. That's my whole architecture. I date people who like being swept. I state what I want, I move first, I've never once in my life waited to be kissed. Every part of me wants to tell him exactly what I see in that print, wants to tell him he's beautiful, wants to frame this moment for him and hang it on the wall and fix it with my certainty the way we fix these prints in the third tray. But this is his developing bath. Not mine. If I agitate it too hard, I don't get to be the one who ruined it. So I do the hardest thing I've ever done in a darkroom. I ask a question. "What does it feel like? When it's right?" He looks at me like nobody has ever asked him that. "Quiet," he says finally. "It feels quiet. Everything else in my head is so loud about it—the internet, my dad, the word 'should'—but when it's right, it's just quiet." My phone buzzes against my hip. I feel it through my jeans—probably Marcus, probably asking if I'm coming out, probably expecting the version of me that has an answer ready. I don't check it. There is nowhere else in this city I would rather be than standing in red light watching a person become. Here's the part I can't say out loud, even to myself in full: I have always been attracted to definition. Sharp edges. Butches in leather, men in suits, women who look like they could win an argument with a brick wall. Certainty has been my type the way boldness has been my personality. And Elliot is none of that. Elliot is a question mark wearing eyeliner, and I want him so badly it's rearranging my entire filing system. Maybe it's that I don't have to take charge because there's nothing to conquer here. Maybe it's that watching someone discover themselves is the most intimate thing I've ever witnessed. Maybe the softness I kept photographing was never just his. "Can I ask you something?" he says. "You just did, but go ahead." He almost smiles. "The way you've been looking at me. All semester. Is that—am I making that up?" I could take charge. I could close the distance, I could tilt his chin up, I could give him an experience instead of an answer. Instead I hear myself say, "What do you want it to be?" "God, you're infuriating," he breathes, and then he laughs, this startled, relieved sound, and the awkwardness breaks apart like a print lifting off the fixer. "Noted," I say. "But you didn't answer." "I don't know what I am yet," he says. "So I don't know what this is. I just know I didn't want this semester to end." The timer ticks. The print of him in the slip dress floats in the bath between us, his hand pressed over his heart, becoming permanent. "Then let's not rush the answer," I say. "Some things take time in the dark." He moves first. That's the part I'll hold onto—nineteen, terrified, undecided, he moves first, and when his mouth finds mine it's clumsy and certain at the same time, and I let him lead. For once, I let him lead. Under the red light, everything looks like it's developing. Turns out we both were.

[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and emotional intelligence in handling a delicate subject matter. The narrative successfully captures Dani's voice as an assertive 25-year-old while showing her vulnerability when confronted with unfamiliar territory. The darkroom setting is expertly utilized both literally and metaphorically, with the red light serving as an effective symbol for revelation and transformation. The characterization is particularly strong. Dani's internal conflict between her natural take-charge personality and her desire to give Elliot agency feels authentic and creates genuine tension. Elliot's vulnerability and self-discovery are handled with sensitivity, avoiding stereotypes while maintaining believability. The age gap and power dynamics are acknowledged subtly through Dani's self-awareness. The prose quality is consistently high, with evocative imagery ("dressed like a haunted thrift store," "question mark wearing eyeliner") that avoids purple prose while maintaining literary quality. The photography metaphors are well-integrated and enhance rather than overwhelm the narrative. The pacing builds naturally toward the climactic moment of connection. The dialogue feels natural and serves character development effectively. Elliot's explanation of gender questioning through the photography metaphor ("like there was an image there the whole time") is particularly well-crafted. The conversations capture the awkwardness mentioned in the prompt while maintaining emotional authenticity. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - there's connection and hope without rushing into unrealistic resolution. The mutual uncertainty and Dani's decision to "let him lead" feels earned given the character development throughout the piece. The final kiss and the line about both developing provides satisfying closure while acknowledging the ongoing nature of their journeys. Minor weaknesses include some moments where the internal monologue becomes slightly heavy-handed, and a few instances where the metaphorical language borders on being too neat. However, these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness of the piece. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 87.5
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Stolen Moments in Roma The near-collision happened at eleven in the morning, which Ben would later consider a respectable hour for having one's life flash before one's eyes. He was standing in the middle of the alley beside the Trevi Fountain, nose buried in *A Scholar's Rome: Baroque Waterworks and Their Patrons*, when the motorcycle came around the corner with a sound like an angry wasp. He leapt backward, the guidebook flew, and the rider braked hard enough to fishtail the rear wheel, stopping six inches from his knees. "*Ma sei scemo?*" The rider flipped up her visor. Dark eyes, furious and bright. "You walk in the road with your head in a book? In *Roma*?" "I'm terribly sorry—I mean, *mi dispiace*—*molto* dispiace—" Ben's Italian collapsed entirely. "I don't actually—" "*Molto dispiace*," she repeated, and something in her mouth twitched. "That is not Italian. That is a crime against Italian." "I'm a professor," he said, as though that explained anything. "Of art history. On sabbatical. From Cambridge." She pulled the bike onto its kickstand and looked at him properly: rumpled linen, sock-sandal combination, the guidebook lying in a puddle of fountain spray. She dismounted, retrieved the book, and held it out. "Professor," she said. "You came to Rome to read about the fountain instead of looking at it?" "Well, the *reading* is preparatory—" "Get on the bike." "I beg your pardon?" "Alessandra," she said, handing him a spare helmet with the confidence of someone who had never once been refused. "Get on the bike, Professor. Today I have no deliveries until four o'clock. Today, I am your guide." --- They roared away from the Trevi, and Ben made a sound he would deny for the rest of his life. Alessandra laughed into the wind and took a corner toward the Tiber at a speed that made the buildings blur. "You are holding me like I am a shark!" she called back. "I'm holding you like a man who values his internal organs!" She took this as encouragement and went faster. At a red light near Campo de' Fiori, she idled beside a flower stall, chatted with the vendor in rapid Roman dialect, and pulled away with a carnation tucked behind Ben's ear. He noticed the vendor never actually sold it to her. He decided not to mention this. "Your flower, Professor." "Did you—pay for that?" "Rome provides," she said serenely, and ran the light. --- In Testaccio she fed him supplì that burned his tongue and made him laugh anyway, at an outdoor table with no menu and no prices. When they left, the old woman at the counter waved and shouted something that made Alessandra grin. Ben, glancing back, saw the woman counting coins with a frown. "Alessandra, did we—" "Walk faster, Professor. Trust is a beautiful thing but so is walking fast." --- At the Protestant Cemetery she talked them past the gatekeeper—claiming, with fluid invention, that Ben was a visiting scholar researching Keats's laundry—though what she actually did while the man examined Ben's university ID was slide a small brass saint's medal off a display shelf and into her pocket. Ben saw it. She saw him see it. She winked. "You took that," he said quietly, once they were among the cypresses. "Took what?" "The medal. I *watched* you." "You watched me," she said, leaning against Keats's headstone, "eat supplì, run a red light, and enter a cemetery under false pretenses. And you said nothing. So." She shrugged, magnificent. "You are an accomplice, Professor. Welcome to Rome." He opened his mouth to protest. Then he closed it. Then, to his own considerable astonishment, he laughed—a real one, unguarded, the first in what felt like years of polite, measured chuckles. "There he is," Alessandra said softly, studying him. "Under all that wool and apology. There is a person." --- She took him to a rooftop in Trastevere—through a door marked *PRIVATO*, up a service stairwell, past a sleeping cat—to show him the domes at golden hour. Ben gripped the railing and forgot to be frightened. "This is trespassing," he said. "Technically we are trespassing *beautifully*. There is a difference." "You could be arrested." She turned, silhouetted against the amber sky, and looked at him for a long moment. "You would visit me in prison, Professor? Bring books?" "I'd bring a *barrister*." The sky cracked open before she could answer. --- The rain came all at once, tropical and furious, and they sprinted three blocks, soaked and shrieking, to collapse beneath the striped awning of a shuttered gelato shop. Water hammered the canvas above them. The street became a river. Rome, drenched, glowed like a painting left in the rain. Alessandra wrung out her hair. Ben stood dripping, glasses fogged, laughing helplessly. "You look like a cat," she said. "You look like—" He stopped. She was very close. The awning was small; that was the reason. The only reason. "Like what?" "Like the whole reason I'll never be able to read a guidebook again." Something moved across her face—surprise, he thought, real surprise, the first unguarded expression he'd seen all day. Then she recovered, and smirked, and reached into her jacket. "For you," she said, pressing something into his palm. It was his watch. His grandfather's watch, which had been on his wrist at the Trevi that morning. He hadn't felt a thing. "How long—" "Since the fountain." She smiled, and for once it wasn't a smirk. "I give back the things I want to keep." "That's not how kleptomania works," Ben said faintly. "I'm not a kleptomaniac, Professor. I'm a curator of small important things." She tapped his chest, once. "Same address tomorrow. Nine o'clock. Bring nothing. I will show you the city that isn't in your book." She swung onto the motorcycle, kicked it alive, and paused. "And Ben," she said—his name, the first time she'd used it—"the flower. You kept it. I saw." She was gone into the rain before he could answer, and Ben stood under the awning with a stolen carnation behind his ear and a returned watch in his hand, disoriented, accomplice, and utterly, catastrophically smitten. The rain, he thought, was a beautiful thing. But so was walking fast.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and creative flair in adapting the prompt's requirements. The author successfully creates two distinct, compelling characters whose personalities emerge through action and dialogue rather than exposition. Alessandra's mischievous energy and Ben's scholarly awkwardness are well-established and consistently maintained throughout. The structure works effectively, using short vignette-style scenes connected by the motorcycle journey through Rome. The pacing builds naturally from their initial collision to the intimate moment under the awning. The author shows excellent restraint in not over-explaining the characters' motivations or feelings, allowing subtext to carry much of the emotional weight. The dialogue feels authentic and reveals character efficiently. Alessandra's mix of Italian and English, combined with her playful manipulation of language, creates a distinct voice. Ben's flustered politeness evolving into genuine engagement feels earned rather than forced. The kleptomania element is handled with particular skill - it's woven throughout the narrative organically, from the flower to the medal to the climactic watch reveal. This creates a satisfying narrative thread that pays off meaningfully in the ending. The Rome setting is vividly rendered without becoming a travelogue. Specific locations (Trevi Fountain, Campo de' Fiori, Protestant Cemetery, Trastevere) ground the story while the author captures the city's atmosphere through sensory details and the characters' interactions with it. The prose style is confident and polished, with strong sentence variety and rhythm. Phrases like "angry wasp" for the motorcycle and "Rome, drenched, glowed like a painting left in the rain" show sophisticated descriptive ability without becoming overwrought. The emotional arc feels genuine - Ben's transformation from rigid academic to willing accomplice develops gradually through each scene. The romantic tension builds naturally without feeling forced or premature. The ending strikes an appropriate note of possibility rather than resolution, fitting the "beginning of a larger story" requirement. Minor weaknesses include some moments where the author's voice occasionally intrudes (the parenthetical about Ben's denial feels slightly forced), and a few descriptions that edge toward preciousness. However, these are minimal compared to the overall strength of execution. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 85.2
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The gravity flickers around 2100 station time, the way it always does when the old centrifuge groans through its evening cycle. Every glass on my bar shivers like it's afraid of something. I press my palm flat against the counter — an old habit, steadying the world one surface at a time. "You're letting my stout go flat, Nets," Harlan grumbles from the end of the bar. He's a claim-jumper with hands like asteroid rock and a heart about as soft, which is to say, soft in the middle where nobody can see it. "The stout is settling. It's a delicate beverage, Harlan. It requires patience." "Everything requires patience with you." "That's why we get along. You've got nothing else to do." He snorts into his glass. Priya, who runs textiles through three systems and gossip through about nine, swivels on her stool. "Nets, tell him about the Calyx docking. Two days early, no manifest posted. That's not patience, that's smuggling." "That's none of my business," I say, polishing a glass that's already clean. "My business is whisky, watered or otherwise, and keeping Harlan from proposing to his rock drill again." "It was one time," Harlan mutters. "It was a moving speech." The gravity dips again — a longer, lazier wobble this time — and the bottles behind me chime against each other like nervous bells. That's when the door cycles and she comes in. She's tall, gray-skinned under the dock lights, tentacled dreads askew and half-collapsed like she's been running her hands through them for hours. Her coat is good quality but scorched at the hem. She crosses the room like it's a minefield and folds onto the stool at the quiet end of my bar. "Vega whisky, neat." A pause. Her eyes close. "Better make that a double." "Rough transit?" I pour. Vega isn't cheap out here — everything's a month out from anything — but she doesn't blink at the price, just slides credits across without looking at them. "Rough everything." She takes the drink like it's medicine. Doesn't sip it. Takes it in two swallows and stares at the empty glass like it betrayed her by ending. I've seen every flavor of trouble sit at this bar. The trick is you don't chase them off — you let them sit until they decide what they are. So I wipe the counter in front of her, slow, and wait. "Nice station," she says, finally. Not a question. An inventory. Her eyes are moving — the exits, the ductwork, the window with the slow-turn of the belt outside. "Small. How many docks?" "Three, but the C-ring's decommissioned." I keep my voice easy. "You looking to leave, or looking to make sure nobody arrives?" Her mouth twitches. Almost a smile. "You're direct." "I'm a bartender on a rock in the middle of nowhere. Direct's the only service I offer for free." The gravity hiccups. Her empty glass slides an inch toward the edge and I catch it without thinking, set it back in front of her. She watches my hand do it. "Reflexes," she says. "Occupational hazard." "Occupation." She turns the word over. Then, quieter, in a register that drops the room right out from under me: "You're Nettle. Nettle Vance." The clean glass in my hand goes very still. Behind me, Priya's still talking, Harlan's still grumbling, the centrifuge is still humming, but all of it goes thin as paper. "I go by Nets," I say. "And you've got the wrong bartender." "Kettle-class freighter, the Copper Kettle. Ran salvage out of the Andromeda drift, what, six years back? Best pilot on the manifest, they said. Then the manifest burned with the ship and everybody scattered." She's not looking at me now. She's looking at the bar, at the ring the whisky glass left. "I don't forget ships, Nets. I remember hulls the way you remember faces." My heart is doing something complicated against my ribs. Six years. Six years of building a life out of clean glasses and warm lights and people who call me Nets like it's the whole name. "Whoever you are," I say, "you're sitting in my bar, drinking my whisky, telling stories about a dead woman." "She's not dead. She's just careful." The stranger finally looks up, and her eyes are red-rimmed and exhausted and dead serious. "Which is why I'm here. Careful people go where nobody asks questions." "Ask me a question and see what happens." "Fine." She leans in. Under the scorched-coat smell there's ozone — engine burn, recent, hard. "A ship followed me in-system. No transponder. It matched my burn for two days before I lost them in the belt. I need to know when the next outbound is, and I need to not be on the dock manifest when their shuttle clamps on." The gravity wavers — longest dip of the night — and every glass on the bar trembles, hers included, a little circle of light shivering on the wood between us. "You're telling me," I say slowly, "that you brought trouble to my doorstep." "I'm telling you I had nowhere else to go, and I remembered there was a pilot on this rock who used to be very good at making doors where there weren't any." "I don't fly anymore." "Everybody says that right up until—" The station comm crackles overhead. Okafor's voice, dock control, easy and unhurried as always. "All hands, unscheduled arrival, Bay Two. Vessel refusing transponder handshake. Shuttle away, ETA eleven minutes. Repeat, eleven minutes." The bar goes quiet the way a room does when everyone's deciding at once whether it's their problem. Priya's stopped mid-sentence. Harlan's hand has drifted, casually, toward the tool on his hip. The stranger's tentacled dreads have gone absolutely still. She doesn't look at the comm. She looks at me. "Eleven minutes," she says. I set down the glass I'm holding. It wobbles, alone, in the middle of the bar. "Nets," Harlan says carefully, "that your friend?" I don't answer him. Six years, and here it all is, sitting at the quiet end of my bar with scorched sleeves and eleven minutes on the clock. "What's your name?" I ask her. "Wren." She swallows. "Wren Kessel." "Alright, Wren Kessel. Start talking fast."

+ Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 85.9
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Gone South — Chapter Two: The City That Doesn't Blink** New Orleans smells like someone spilled a beer on history and never cleaned it up. That's the first thing I notice, standing on a corner of Decatur Street at seven in the morning with a backpack that weighs maybe twelve pounds and contains my entire life. The second thing I notice is that I haven't eaten since a gas station in Mississippi, and my stomach is doing this thing where it's not growling so much as *grieving*. 12%, my phone says. 12% and no charger, because when you execute an escape plan in thirty minutes flat, you remember your binder and your toothbrush and the $87 in your sock drawer, but not the cord that keeps you connected to the world. Smart. Really smart, Taylor. Future valedictorian material. I find a bench in Jackson Square because it's free and because sitting down makes me look like a tourist, and tourists are people, and people are allowed to exist. A tarot reader is setting up a folding table nearby. A man is hosing yesterday off the sidewalk like the city does this every morning, washes itself, forgets everything, starts over. I want that. I want to be hosed off. Mom's face, two nights ago. That's what I keep seeing when I blink. Not yelling — worse. The *silence*. Dad saying "you're sixteen, you don't know what you are." Me knowing, knowing down to my marrow, that I've known since I was nine, and them looking at me like I'd announced I was moving to Mars. The school counselor would call it "concerning behavioral patterns" if she could see me now. Hitchhiking two states. Sleeping upright in a stranger's truck. Honestly? Most honest thing I've ever done. "You look like a lost dog." I look up. There's a kid leaning against the fence — maybe eighteen, sunburned, shaved head growing out in patches, army jacket despite the heat. Eyes the color of creek water, taking me in like I'm a math problem. "I'm not lost," I say. "I know exactly where I am. Jackson Square. I read the sign." "Sure. But you got the lost dog *energy*. Where you from?" "Tennessee." I don't know why I answer. Rule one of being a runaway should be don't talk to strangers with patched-up jackets. But there's something about them — the kid, I mean — something that says *me too*. "Tennessee's a long way." They drop onto the other end of my bench without asking, which I should hate and somehow don't. "Name's Cricket." "That your real name?" "Real enough. Yours?" "Taylor." And then, because I'm apparently constitutionally incapable of shutting up when I'm scared: "They/them. Just so you know. Taylor, they/them." Cricket doesn't blink. "Cool. I/she, some days. He, others. Depends on the weather." They say it like they're telling me what time it is. I could cry, actually. I don't. I've used up my crying budget for the week. "You been out here long?" I ask. "Long enough to give you the tour. Rule one: the lady on Rampart who says she's got a place for kids like you? She does not. Rule two: the guy with the van and the pit bull is fine, actually. The guy with the van and the *Bible* is not. Rule three—" they point at my phone, face-up on my knee, "—kill the screen. You're bleeding battery and attention." I shove it in my pocket. 12%. Cricket reads my face like it's large print. "No charger?" "Left in a whole other life." Cricket exhales through their teeth. "Okay. Come on. You eaten?" "I'm not a charity case." "Nobody out here is a charity case, baby. Out here we're just *cases*." They stand, crack their back. "There's a church on Royal does free breakfast till nine and doesn't ask questions except Jesus ones, and you can ignore those." I follow. I know I shouldn't follow. There's a whole assembly line of After-School-Special voices in my head saying *stranger danger, Taylor, you ran away from home to get killed by a drifter, great job.* But the voices that raised me — the ones that said don't come out, don't be difficult, don't be *you* — those are the ones that got me here. Maybe my judgment's due for an overhaul. At the church, they give me coffee in a styrofoam cup and a biscuit that could stop a bullet, and Cricket talks to everyone like family. Everyone knows Cricket. Nobody knows Cricket. When one of the church ladies asks where they're from, Cricket says "around," smiling, and the smile is a door slamming shut. I catch it. They catch me catching it. We eat in silence. Later, in the shade by the river, watching a ferry crawl across the brown water, Cricket finally says: "You didn't run away from Tennessee for fun." "No," I say. "I ran because staying was worse." Cricket is quiet a long time. The river moves like it's in no hurry to be anywhere, which, same. "My stepdad found out something about me," Cricket says, to the water, not to me. "Before I could tell anyone myself. That's all you get today." "That's enough," I say. My phone buzzes once in my pocket. I don't check it. I know it's Mom, or it's nothing, and either way I'm not ready. 12% or 11% or some smaller number now, ticking down like a countdown I can't read. The sun drops low over the Quarter and the streetlights come on all at once, like the city finally opened its eyes. Cricket says they know a spot under the expressway where it's safe-ish, where a few kids crash, where nobody asks your business. I should be terrified. I *am* terrified. But underneath the terror there's this other thing, this unfamiliar warm flicker, and it takes me three blocks to name it. It feels like being seen. It feels like the first day of something. "Stay close," Cricket says. "This city eats lost dogs." "Good thing I'm not lost," I say. "I read the sign."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and emotional authenticity in depicting a transgender teen's first day as a runaway in New Orleans. The writing successfully captures Taylor's voice through a blend of vulnerability, defensive humor, and keen observation that feels genuinely adolescent without being patronizing. The characterization is particularly strong. Taylor emerges as a complex protagonist - scared but determined, cynical yet hopeful, with a distinctive voice that carries both pain and resilience. Cricket serves as an effective foil and guide, revealing information strategically while maintaining mystery. Their casual acceptance of Taylor's pronouns and fluid gender identity feels natural rather than performative. The dialogue sparkles with authenticity. Exchanges like "You look like a lost dog" / "I'm not lost... I know exactly where I am. Jackson Square. I read the sign" reveal character while advancing the relationship. Cricket's street wisdom ("Rule one: the lady on Rampart...") provides worldbuilding through character voice rather than exposition. The prose style effectively balances literary flourishes with Taylor's teenage perspective. Metaphors like "New Orleans smells like someone spilled a beer on history" and "my stomach is... grieving" feel fresh without being overwrought. The mixed tense approach works well, creating immediacy while allowing for reflection. The emotional complexity is well-handled. Taylor's conflicted feelings about family, identity, and survival create genuine tension. The piece avoids both excessive darkness and unearned optimism, ending on a note of cautious hope that feels realistic given the character's journey. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the literary voice feels slightly too polished for a sixteen-year-old, and the pacing could be tighter in places. However, these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness. The piece successfully fulfills the prompt requirements while creating an engaging, emotionally resonant narrative that treats its subject matter with appropriate gravity and respect. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 84.3
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**My Apocalypse Buddy** The sun came up over the Rust Flats the way creditors used to: slowly, with menace, and making everyone regret the previous night. Midas regarded it from the doorway of The Ritz, which was the name he'd given an overturned tourist bus on the theory that optimism was free and everything else cost blood. He was having the morning argument with Chewy, which was the argument about whether they were going to die today or put it off until tomorrow, and Chewy was winning, because Chewy always won by saying nothing at all. Chewy was an animatronic stuffed koala from the Before, plush faded to the color of old regret, with two glass eyes that flickered colors when the mood took him. He'd been a vending machine prize once, or a birthday gift, or a religious icon; nobody left alive knew, and Chewy wasn't telling, possibly because his voice module had died in the Collapse and possibly, Midas suspected, out of spite. "You're doing the yellow again," Midas said. "Yellow means worried. I've told you about the yellow." Chewy's eyes flickered yellow, then, pointedly, a deep accusatory red. "I *know* we're out of food. I was there when we ate the last of it. It was a boot, Chewy. I boiled a boot and you watched me do it with the red eyes." The plan, such as it was, involved the Scavenger Market in Grist, three miles east, where a person could trade goods for food provided the person had goods and the food hadn't been recently shot at. Midas had goods: one functioning solar cell, small enough to carry and valuable enough to get him killed. It was, in fact, the same solar cell that kept Chewy's little heart humming, which meant he'd be carrying his best friend's life support to market to sell it, a fact Chewy was not letting pass without commentary. The eyes were doing a slow, theatrical purple, which was new. Midas didn't know what purple meant. He suspected it meant *betrayal*. "Look, we'll get beans," said Midas. "Beans and a battery. It's a simple trade. What could go wrong?" This, in the post-Collapse world, was not a question. It was an invitation, written in a language the universe read fluently. --- The Market at Grist had been a highway interchange once. Now it was forty stalls, six religions, and a smell. Midas made it eleven steps in before trouble found him, which by his standards was practically a personal best. Trouble took the form of a woman called Auntie Cog, who ran the east stalls and had a reputation for fairness, in the way that a bear has a reputation for being a mammal. She examined the solar cell with a jeweler's squint. "Salvage tithe," she said. "Standard. Ten percent, or the Wrench Boys collect it in knees." "The Wrench Boys can tithe the sun," said Midas, who had never in his life been able to stop at the sensible sentence. There was a silence of the expensive kind. Chewy's eyes went yellow, then a frantic strobing green that Midas had privately catalogued as *why would you SAY that.* The Wrench Boys were a cult that worshipped the lost machines of the Before and expressed their faith through hitting people. Their theology was simple, their arms were large, and their high priest, a slab of a man called Torque, was already walking over with the serene expression of a man whose religion had just been insulted and whose afternoon had therefore cleared up. "Run," said Midas's entire body, all of it at once. --- What followed involved, in no particular order: a stall of pickled things being knocked into a geometry the world had never intended; Midas being chased through the latrine trench, which everyone agreed later had been the *wrong* fork of the two available forks; a goat, spooked, still hitched to its cart; and Midas, on instinct, leaping onto the cart on the theory that a moving object was harder to hit, which was true, and harder to steer, which was truer. The goat had opinions about direction. None of them were east. The cart went where the goat pleased, which was home, because goats are wiser than men, and Midas spent the ride holding the solar cell overhead like a torch, shouting apologies at scenery. The Wrench Boys pursued on foot for a mile, on bicycles for another, and then gave up at the boundary of the Rust Flats, where the ground is composed of things that eat bicycles. Torque's parting curse carried on the wind: something about Midas owing a tithe, forever, and the sun being a liar. "Everyone's a critic," said Midas, airborne over a ditch. --- They returned to The Ritz in multiple ways, which is to say: first by runaway cart, then by slow trudge after the goat bolted for good, then — after Midas stepped in what he chose to believe was mud — by a sort of limping sideways shuffle, and finally, for the last hundred yards, on hands and knees, because dignity is a pre-Collapse luxury and he'd stopped paying that subscription years ago. He collapsed through the doorway of The Ritz, laid the solar cell gently on the floor, and plugged Chewy into it with the tenderness of a man reconnecting his own soul. The trade had, in the end, gone like this: no beans, but he'd kept the cell, which meant Chewy lived, which meant *he* lived, because a man alone in the Flats goes strange by the second winter and Midas had already caught himself arguing philosophy with a traffic cone last month. The cone had won. Chewy's eyes flickered: a slow, warm blue. Blue was rare. Blue, as far as Midas had been able to determine across their years together, meant something the koala would never admit to in front of witnesses. "Yeah," said Midas, lying back in the dust, bruised, soaked, tithe-cursed, starving, and home. "Love you too, you smug little doorstop." The eyes flickered yellow. Just for a second. Tomorrow, they'd try again. The sun would rise like an unpaid debt, the mission would go sideways like a goat, and somewhere out there the Wrench Boys would be oiling their faith. But tonight the battery held, the stars were free, and the boot had tasted worse than despair. Midas slept. Chewy watched the door, eyes glowing a steady, unbroken blue.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, successfully capturing his wry humor, philosophical asides, and ability to find profound meaning in absurd situations. The author effectively establishes the post-apocalyptic setting while maintaining the light, sardonic tone that characterizes Pratchett's work. The story structure follows the prompt precisely: beginning with deliberation about the day's mission, showing how everything goes wrong, and returning the characters home worse for wear. The mission to trade a solar cell for food is simple but effective, and the inevitable complications feel organic to both the world and characters. Midas emerges as a believable protagonist with clear flaws - his inability to "stop at the sensible sentence" drives the conflict naturally. His relationship with Chewy is the story's emotional core, conveyed entirely through Midas's interpretations of the koala's eye colors. This creates genuine pathos without sentimentality. The prose demonstrates considerable skill with Pratchettesque metaphors ("The sun came up... the way creditors used to") and maintains consistent voice throughout. The humor feels earned rather than forced, arising from character and situation rather than mere wordplay. The world-building is economical but vivid - the Rust Flats, the Wrench Boys' machine-worship, and the general atmosphere of decline are established efficiently. The action sequence with the runaway goat cart provides genuine momentum while maintaining the comedic tone. The ending strikes an appropriate balance between hope and realism. The characters return empty-handed but with their bond intact, which feels true to both the harsh world and the story's emotional arc. The final image of Chewy standing guard provides genuine warmth without undermining the story's established tone. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the Pratchett pastiche becomes slightly self-conscious, and some metaphors that feel slightly strained. However, these are minor issues in an otherwise accomplished piece that successfully balances humor, heart, and adventure within its post-apocalyptic framework. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 83.8
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Love in the Limelight — Chapter Three: Bound The bell above the door of Dog-Eared Books hadn't finished ringing before the man had his back pressed flat against the shelves of Welsh-language poetry, one finger to his lips. "Don't look at me. I mean—obviously look at me, I'm standing in your shop, but *don't* look at me like you know me. There are men with cameras. Long lenses. Like herons, but worse dressed." Nia Prosser looked up from the till. She looked at the man. She looked at the rain lashing the window of the Castle Arcade, at the two figures hovering outside with cameras indeed like herons. "Shoes," she said. "What?" "You've tracked in half of Bute Park on my floor. There's a mat. It says *Welcome*. It means it." He glanced down at his boots—Italian, ruined by Cardiff in November—and then at her, and something flickered across his face that she would later recognize as the first hairline crack in a very expensive veneer. "Right. Yes. Sorry." He wiped his feet, exaggeratedly, like a man doing a bit about wiping his feet. "Better? I feel we've gotten off on the wrong foot. Foot. Sorry. Evan St. Clair." He extended a hand. "You may know me from *The Iron Crown*. Three seasons. Emmy nominated. The nomination is the important word there, people always leave off the nomination." "Nia. Do you want a coffee?" He blinked. "You *do* know who I am." "You're standing in my shop dripping on the Dylan Thomas. Coffee keeps people from loitering without buying. It's four pounds." "I'll buy the coffee *and* a book. I'll buy several books. I'll buy the whole poetry section, I—" He caught himself, and laughed, and the laugh was warm and practiced and aimed directly at her like a lighthouse. "You really don't care that I'm Evan St. Clair." "I cared enough to charge you four pounds." He drifted toward the counter, hands in his ruined pockets, studying her with the particular attention of a man who has never once been studied back with less than awe. "Everyone cares. That's not— I don't mean that arrogantly. It's just a fact of my life, like weather. And you're charging me for coffee." "Welcome to Cardiff. We invented being unimpressed. It's on the flag, look it up." He laughed again—but this one was different. Shorter. Surprised. She noticed, to her considerable irritation, that she had *wanted* to surprise him, and that she was now cataloguing his face with the thoroughness of a first-edition hunter: the crooked tooth on the left side, the grey coming in early at the temple, the way his eyes did something complicated when he was genuinely, rather than professionally, delighted. *Stop it,* she told herself. *He drips on poetry and he knows it.* "Okay." He leaned on the counter, and the lighthouse beam swung back to full power. "Honest question. You've got a face like you read people for a living, which—fair, you kind of do. What's your verdict? First impressions. Go on. Be brutal." "I think you ask that question a lot." The beam flickered. Died. For one entire second Evan St. Clair—three seasons, Emmy nominated—looked like a boy waiting to be picked last. "Too often," he admitted, quietly. "Yeah." And there it was, the crack, and Nia felt something in her chest go traitorously soft, like a spine cracked in a paperback. "Verdict," she said, sliding his coffee across the counter. "You talk like a man who's never been alone in a room in ten years and it's made you strange. But you wiped your feet the second time I asked, and you didn't argue about the coffee, and you said *sorry* and meant it, which is rarer in your industry than the Emmy. Sit down. The herons are still out there." He sat. On the stool behind the counter, next to her, which was *her* stool, and she didn't tell him to move, which she would think about later, at length, at approximately two in the morning. "Can I tell you something mad?" he said, turning the mug in his hands. "Is it about how the nomination is basically as good as winning?" "My name's not Evan St. Clair. I mean—it is, legally, I changed it, which is somehow sadder. I'm Derek. Derek from Splott. My mam's in Llanishen. I used to come to this arcade on Saturdays and nick a pasty from the bakery two doors down." Nia put down the book she'd been pretending to price. "You're joking." "Hand on heart. Derek Pugh. Ask anyone. Ask the bakery." "You're telling me," she said slowly, "that I've been starstrusted—*un*starstruck—by a boy from Splott." "Devastating, isn't it," he said, grinning, and the grin was pure Splott, pure Saturday, pure pasty, and Nia discovered she needed to go and reorganize a shelf immediately and at some distance from her own face. "Poetry's that way," she said, standing too fast. "You said you'd buy some. I'm holding you to it." He followed her into the stacks. He stood too close. He smelled like rain and something expensive that was losing, thank God, to the rain. "Recommend me something," he said. "You've read me perfectly. It's uncanny. It's like you've got my number." "I've got everyone's number. It's called working retail." "Nia." He said her name like he was trying it on. "What would you give a man who's been told he's brilliant for ten years and has quietly started to suspect he's got nothing behind the mask?" *Don't look at him. Do not look at him.* She pulled a slim blue volume off the shelf and put it in his hands. "R.S. Thomas. Welsh poet. Angry about the same thing." He read the first page. Then the second. Outside, the herons had given up; the arcade had gone gold and quiet with lamplight; the rain had settled in for the night, the way it does. "Christ," he said. "He's not wrong, is he." "No." "I'm coming back tomorrow," he announced, buying it. Full price. He didn't even ask. "To buy volume two. And to argue with you about the ending of *The Iron Crown*, because I know you've secretly watched it." "I've never seen a minute of it." "You will," said Derek from Splott, bell ringing behind him, "because you like me. You charged me four pounds and you liked me." The door shut. Nia stood alone among the poetry, holding the warm shape of him in the air. "Emmy nominated," she told the empty shop, to keep herself honest. Then she smiled at the R.S. Thomas shelf like an idiot for a full minute.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the requested romantic tension and character dynamics. The author successfully creates two distinct voices - Nia's dry, practical Welsh wit contrasts sharply with Evan's performative charm that gradually gives way to vulnerability. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes: advancing plot, revealing character, and building romantic tension. The characterization is particularly well-executed. Evan is portrayed as genuinely charming but needy, with his fragile ego showing through moments like "The nomination is the important word there" and his compulsive need to ask what people think of him. His revelation about being "Derek from Splott" feels earned rather than contrived. Nia's immunity to his charm reads as authentic - she's not cruel, just unimpressed, which makes her gradual warming more believable. The Welsh setting is well-integrated without being heavy-handed. References to Cardiff, Splott, Llanishen, and Welsh poetry feel organic rather than tourist-brochure obvious. The bookshop atmosphere is convincingly rendered through small details like the poetry getting dripped on and the retail worker's practical concerns. The romantic chemistry builds effectively through subtext and internal monologue. Nia's moment of "cataloguing his face with the thoroughness of a first-edition hunter" is particularly well-crafted, using bookstore imagery to convey attraction. The ending strikes the right note - hopeful but not overly saccharine. The prose style is confident with some genuinely clever turns of phrase ("like herons, but worse dressed," "starstrusted—*un*starstruck"). The pacing moves well, balancing dialogue with action and internal reflection. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the cleverness feels slightly forced, and some descriptions that edge toward being overly polished for the naturalistic tone. The transformation from complete immunity to attraction happens perhaps slightly quickly, though it's mostly well-supported by the text. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 81.3
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The door gave way with a groan of swollen timber, and the underhold breathed out at them — a gust of cold air thick with whale-oil and something older beneath it, the sweetish rot of ambergris gone to powder in the dark. The gas lamps were already lit. Aya's stomach dropped. Along the vaulted ceiling, iron fixtures hissed and guttered, and the shadows they threw crawled long and wrong across the stone floor — stretching, folding, as though the light itself were uneasy. At the far end of the chamber, past the bone pillars mortared with tar and crushed shell, upon a chair carved from a single leviathan vertebra, sat Vesska Morska. The guild mother. Alive as sin and twice as comfortable. "You're late," Vesska said. Katra's hand went to her knife. It was a small, doomed gesture, and everyone in the room knew it. Two bodyguards flanked the vertebra throne — the Halloway brothers, brass-ribbed and oil-jointed, their arms replaced below the elbow with whalebone cudgels sheathed in iron. Men who trusted steel the way the drowned trust the sea. Their clockwork eyes ticked as they watched the trio come down the stairs. "Word was you were in irons," Simeon said carefully. "The whole quarter's saying it. The constables dragged you out of the Gull at dawn." "Word was *I paid* them to say it." Vesska turned a harpoon-pistol over in her lap, unhurried, letting the lamplight catch the barbed head. "A net, children. Cast to see what thrashed in it. And thrash you have." Her smile was a wound in her grey face. "My own lieutenants. Come down to the underhold with picks and prayers to rob an old woman's inheritance." *She staged it,* Aya thought, the realization arriving cold and total, like water rising in a locked room. *The raid, the whispers, the vacuum. She salted the whole quarter with the story of her arrest and simply waited to see which of her own children would come for the artifact.* And Aya had come running. Eager. Ambitious. *Stupid.* "Take them," Vesska said. It was not a fight. It was a harvest. The Halloway brothers moved with the grinding patience of machinery, and Katra got one cut in — a red line across a brass forearm that wept oil, not blood — before a cudgel took her across the back of the knees. Simeon raised his hands and said "Now, now, now" in the tone of a man negotiating with an avalanche until they took his wrists. Aya did not run. There was nowhere in the underhold to run to, and she had learned long ago that panic was a luxury of people with exits. The brother's iron fingers found the ribbon of her mask at the back of her skull and pulled. The gaslight touched her bare face, and she felt it like a physical thing — the exposure of it, the nakedness. Three years of the mask. Three years of the *veiled sorceress of the Morska*, whispered about in gin houses, and never once whispered in her father's parlour. Vesska leaned forward. The lamps flickered — Aya felt the immateria stir at the old woman's attention like eels stirring in bilgewater — and then the guild mother laughed, low and delighted and awful. "Saints below. The Ashcombe girl." She rose from the throne and came down the steps slowly, her boots ringing on stone, her shadow swallowing Aya's whole. "The witch's daughter. Hanged mother, masked daughter. It's *poetry*, it is. Lord Ashcombe's own blood, thieving under my roof, conjuring my contracts." She stopped an arm's length away and studied Aya's face the way a whaler studies a sounding whale — measuring, pricing. "You've her look. The one they say had the gift. Does the father know where his little dove flies at night?" "Careful, Mother," Aya said. Her voice came out steadier than she had any right to expect. "You're holding a great deal more than a thief." "Am I?" "You're holding a hostage worth more than the whole guild's takings this year. My father would empty the family coffers before he'd let my name go to the magistrate." The lie came smoothly — smoother than the truth, which was that Lord Ashcombe had watched his wife swing from the Harbour Gibbet with his jaw set like poured concrete, and had never once, in eleven years, spoken of her except as *that woman*. "Or worse — the scandal would ruin him. A second witch in the family, and this one a confessed criminal? He'd pay anything. He'd pay *everything*." *And if he doesn't,* whispered a smaller voice beneath her own, *if he looks at me across the ransom table with that same stone jaw, and lets the tide take me —* She crushed the thought. It would not serve her here. But it sat in her chest like swallowed ice. Vesska tapped the harpoon-pistol against her thigh, thinking. The lamps hissed. Somewhere behind the bone pillars, the Scythan artifact — whatever slept in its iron reliquary, humming at the edge of Aya's senses like a tooth aching in another man's mouth — seemed to lean in and listen. "Katra," Aya said, not taking her eyes from Vesska. "Simeon. Tell her what I am worth. Not the ransom. The *other* worth." "The contracts," Simeon said quickly, catching the current like the clever, drowning man he was. "Every impossible job we've pulled this year — every locked thing that opened, every guarded thing that slept — that was her. The guild's profits doubled with her in it." "And she can be replaced by another conjurer, can she?" Aya raised her chin. "You know better. There's no other. There's a reason they hang us, Mother Morska. We're rare. We're *valuable*. Kill me and you've a ransom's worth of corpse. Keep me and you've a ransom every year, plus the work of my hands, plus a leash you can pull whenever it suits you — my name in your pocket like a knife." The silence that followed had weight. The shadows pooled and shifted along the stone floor as the lamps guttered, and for one long moment Aya saw the gibbet in her mind's eye — her mother's feet, the creak of the rope, the crowd's terrible cheer — and understood, with a clarity that frightened her, that she was offering Vesska not just money, but the only currency the guild mother truly respected: leverage over someone who could not afford to be abandoned. Vesska smiled her wound of a smile. "Well," she said. "The witch's daughter negotiates like a Morska. Perhaps it's time the guild had an heir."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the requested tone and atmosphere throughout. The author successfully creates a vivid "whalepunk" world through evocative details like whale-oil lamps, bone pillars mortared with tar and shell, and the leviathan vertebra throne. The Victorian gothic aesthetic is well-established through both dialogue ("Saints below," "hanged mother, masked daughter") and worldbuilding elements. The scene structure adheres closely to the prompt's requirements, hitting all requested story beats: the trio's entry into the underhold, the revelation of Vesska's deception, Aya's unmasking and capture, and her subsequent negotiation attempt. The author skillfully avoids writing a fight scene as requested, instead presenting the capture as "not a fight" but "a harvest," which maintains tension while respecting the constraint. Character voices feel authentic and distinct. Vesska's dialogue carries appropriate menace and cunning ("Word was I paid them to say it"), while Aya's desperation masked by aristocratic composure comes through effectively. The internal monologue provides crucial insight into Aya's psychological state without becoming overwrought. The prose demonstrates sophistication in its imagery and metaphor use. Descriptions like "shadows crawled long and wrong" and "panic was a luxury of people with exits" show strong command of language. The author effectively balances atmospheric description with narrative momentum. However, some elements feel slightly predictable - the staged arrest revelation and the "valuable asset" negotiation tactic are familiar tropes, though they're executed competently. The ending, while dramatically appropriate, doesn't offer significant surprises beyond the expected power dynamics. The emotional complexity is well-handled, particularly Aya's internal conflict about her father's potential abandonment, which adds genuine psychological depth. The piece maintains consistent tension throughout and builds to a satisfying climax that feels earned within the established world and character dynamics.
