+ Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 79.3
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Seven: The Verdict of the Gel The thermal cycler Wren had built from a defunct toaster oven clicked through its sixty-third cycle of the night, and she watched it the way other people watched a potter's wheel—half craft, half prayer. She called the machine *Oona*. Oona's heating block was salvaged Peltier junctions wired into an Arduino clone with a cracked screen; her lid was a slab of windshield glass weighted with brake rotors; her temperature readouts drifted two degrees hot, which Wren corrected by feel, pressing her palm against the aluminum block the way her grandmother had tested a griddle. Precision was a luxury. Calibration was a rumor. What mattered was that Oona held ninety-four degrees for denaturation, dropped to fifty-eight for the primers to bind, climbed to seventy-two for the polymerase to work, and did it all without catching fire. Most nights. The reagents sat in a rack beside her: forty-liter polymer canisters stamped with the diamond logo of EverSow Agrigenics, the biotech colossus whose engineered crops had fed nine billion people right up until they didn't. The canisters were the only part of EverSow that had survived the Collapse with its reputation intact. Airtight, opaque, chemically inert. Wren had forty of them, cut down and fitted with gasket lids, and inside them lived her whole civilization: master mix in one, buffer in another, primers in four, and in the largest, wrapped in foil and cold packs, the enzyme. Taq polymerase, heat-stable, self-propagating. She'd cultured it from a swab of a hot spring outside Fresno three years ago and she babied that strain like a dairy farmer babies a prize heifer. It was, in a real sense, the last living employee of the old economy. Everything else EverSow had made was dead by design. That was the joke nobody at the settlement laughed at anymore. Obsolescence engineering. Every seed the corporations ever sold had carried a genetic dead-man's switch: one generation of bounty, then a cascade of broken chromosomes, sterility, rot. Guaranteed repeat customers. Guaranteed quarterly returns. Guaranteed that when the supply chains snapped and the servers went dark, the world's food supply would eat itself in a single planting season. They'd sold the famine with the harvest. Which was why Wren did what she did, hunched in a gutted water-treatment plant under a tarp of lead-lined vinyl, splicing heirloom vigor back into salvaged crop lines with pipettes built from inkjet cartridges and a centrifuge whose rotor was a hard-drive motor in a salad-spinner housing. And why Marlow had come to her with the contract. "Six hundred liters of insulin-grade reagent stock," he'd said, laying the seeds on her bench in a tin that had once held breath mints. Twelve seeds, dark and oily. "Plus the antibiotics. Plus, and I want you to hear this part, *Oya's protection debt* cleared for a year. All the Verdant Hand wants to know is whether these are true." True. The word the black market used for the impossible: seeds without the suicide cassette. Seeds that would breed past one generation. Real, heritable, permanent food. The seller—a caravan man calling himself a prophet—claimed they came from a doomsday vault in the Rockies, pre-Collapse stock, never commercialized, never poisoned with the obsolescence gene. The Verdant Hand, being a cartel of former agritech middle managers with a theological relationship to intellectual property, wanted verification before they paid the prophet in weapons. If the seeds were true, the Hand would own agriculture from the coast to the salt flats. If they were false, the prophet would own a shallow grave. Wren had taken the contract because six hundred liters of reagent stock would keep Oona fed for a decade, and because the antibiotics would save the three kids in the settlement coughing up rust-colored phlegm, and because she was curious, and curiosity was the one splice nobody had to sell her. Now the PCR was nearly done, and she was jittering again. The tremor came from the myelin-repair snippet she'd run on herself two winters back, after the fever that had stripped the insulation from her nerves and left her hands useless. Untested gene therapy, self-administered, because the alternative was starving to death with functioning ethics. The fix worked—mostly. She could play a pipette like a violin now, micro-liters at a stroke. But the therapy had opinions. When she was tired, her left hand sang a low-frequency tremolo, and no amount of will shut it up. The other mods had their costs too. The splice that rebuilt her lungs after the spore-plague left her breathing like a bellows—audible across a quiet room, embarrassing at funerals—but she could walk into a grain silo full of Aspergillus and come out whistling. The retinal patch, an off-label night-vision construct she'd pirated from a feline genome, gave her green eyeshine that scared children and made her irises ache in daylight. But she could read a gel by the light of a single UV LED, no headlamp, and in the Collapse, being able to see in the dark was worth a little ache. Everything she was, she'd bought with her own body as the testing facility. Phase one trials, population: one. Oona beeped—her tinny, salvaged doorbell chime—and held at four degrees. Wren pulled the tubes, thumb and forefinger steady through force of ten thousand repetitions, and loaded the agarose gel. The gel ran on a rig built from an EverSow canister lid, wired to a phone charger. She'd stained it with a fluorescent dye she extracted, in a fit of biopunk shamelessness, from highlighter fluid. It worked. Mostly. It also glowed under blacklight at parties, which the settlement's teenagers considered her single greatest contribution to society. She ran the current. DNA crawled through the gel, sorting itself by size, the way truth sorted itself from lies: slowly, and then all at once. Her target sat inside the obsolescence cassette itself—the promoter sequence that every commercial genome ever sold had carried, the trigger for the generational kill-switch. If the seeds were commercial stock, the promoter would amplify: a bright band at 310 base pairs. If they were truly pre-Collapse vault stock, wild-type, uncorrupted— The UV LED hummed. Wren leaned in, green eyeshine flaring off the glass. Lane one: her positive control. Bright. 310. The world as she knew it. Lane two: the prophet's seed. Empty. No band. No cassette. No kill-switch. Her breath went out of her in a long bellows rasp, and behind her, Marlow shifted in the dark, and she heard him ask what it meant, and she heard herself lie before she'd even decided to. "False," she said. "Dead seeds. Junk." Because twelve true seeds in the Verdant Hand's vault meant twelve seeds the world would never taste, patented by men who had already burned it once. And twelve true seeds in Wren's canisters—labeled as buffer, stamped with EverSow's diamond—meant potatoes. She sealed the tin inside her coat, over her traitorous, trembling heart. "Tell the Hand the prophet's a fraud," she said. "And tell them I'll need a week to grieve the loss."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical writing and worldbuilding within the biopunk genre. The author creates a convincing post-apocalyptic setting where corporate genetic engineering with built-in obsolescence has led to societal collapse. The scientific details feel authentic and well-researched, from the PCR process to the jury-rigged equipment descriptions. The protagonist Wren is well-developed, with clear motivations and a compelling backstory. Her physical modifications and their trade-offs (tremors from myelin repair, audible breathing from lung reconstruction, light-sensitive night vision) create a believable character who embodies the biopunk aesthetic. The writing effectively shows her expertise and desperation through her relationship with her equipment and work. The central plot around the black market contract creates genuine tension and leads to a morally complex decision. Wren's choice to lie about the test results and steal the seeds demonstrates character agency and creates an ethically ambiguous ending that fits the dystopian setting. The prose is generally strong, with vivid imagery and technical authenticity. Phrases like "watched it the way other people watched a potter's wheel—half craft, half prayer" and "Everything she was, she'd bought with her own body as the testing facility" are particularly effective. The writing maintains a consistent tone throughout. However, there are some weaknesses. The dialogue is minimal and somewhat functional rather than distinctive. Some exposition feels slightly heavy-handed, particularly the explanation of the obsolescence engineering. The pacing occasionally slows during technical descriptions, though these serve important worldbuilding functions. The ending works well thematically but could have been developed with more emotional complexity. Wren's decision feels somewhat rushed given its magnitude. The piece also relies heavily on technical exposition at times rather than showing through action. Overall, this is a competent piece of genre fiction that successfully fulfills the prompt requirements while creating an engaging narrative with moral complexity. Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Seven: The Weight of Courtesy A small display screen on the wall cycled through various system diagnostics in green text — fuel mass, orbital velocity, cabin pressure — with the placid indifference of a machine that did not know it was carrying a kidnapped man. Or, Arthur Neegan corrected himself, an *invited* man. The distinction, he suspected, was chiefly a matter of vocabulary. The Antares men had been very polite. They had stood in the dust of his homestead with the posture of people who had never once been told no, and their leader — a gray-templed major with insignia that gleamed too brightly for fieldwork — had said, "Mr. Neegan, the Envoy would be grateful for a conversation. This evening, if convenient." Two of them had carried sidearms of Terran manufacture. Arthur had noticed that at once. Antares did not manufacture sidearms. Antares barely manufactured anything, which was precisely its problem. Now the transfer vessel's viewport showed Mars receding, rust-brown and pocked, and ahead of it a ship: long, white, unhurried, with the swept lines of a diplomatic cruiser. It was named the *Concordat*, which Arthur found darkly funny. He was shown aboard without ceremony, down a corridor that smelled of ozone and lemon wax, into a cabin appointed in genuine wood veneer — an extravagance that on Mars would have bought a pressure dome. A woman rose to meet him. She was perhaps sixty, silver-haired, dressed in a plain gray suit with the Antares sunburst at the collar. Her eyes did most of the talking before her mouth began. "Mr. Neegan. I am Livia Saro, Envoy Plenipotentiary of the Antares Compact. Thank you for coming." "I don't recall that refusal was on the menu." The faintest smile. "You're a settler. You know what leases are. So do we. Sit, please. Drink?" "Water," Arthur said, and sat. Saro poured from a decanter with a steadiness that suggested she had done this in worse gravity. "You found Azra," she said. "Eleven days ago. A vein your preliminary surveys rate at forty kilotons minimum, running under your claim and, we suspect, well beyond it. Am I accurate?" "You've read my surveys." "Everyone has read your surveys, Mr. Neegan. The question is who has read them *first*." She settled into the chair opposite him. "Do you understand what your vein represents?" "Money." "An empire." She let the word sit. "Azra accelerates decay. A gram of it, properly shielded, can drive a ship to the Centauri systems in four years. Improperly shielded, it can reduce a city to a memory. The Terrestrial Directorate currently controls eighty percent of known deposits. The Meridian Combine leases most of the rest. Antares — and I mean by that the four systems and eleven million souls of the Compact — controls almost none. We are, in the arithmetic of this century, a guest in our own galaxy, permitted to exist so long as our existence is not inconvenient." Arthur looked at his water. "And my forty kilotons changes that arithmetic." "Your forty kilotons *is* the arithmetic." Saro leaned forward slightly. "Here is our offer. The Compact will register your claim under our flag — a legal instrument the Directorate cannot void without open provocation. You will be granted Compact citizenship, a permanent seat on the extraction board, and a royalty of six percent of gross yield. In exchange, the Compact holds exclusive rights to the vein, and you hold your tongue about its full extent." "Six percent of gross," Arthur said. "The Combine offered me eleven." "The Combine also offers indenture conversions, Mr. Neegan. Ask any of the laborers in your own pits what eleven percent of nothing amounts to." Her voice did not change, but something behind it did. "And consider what the Directorate offers, which is a writ of eminent domain and a thank-you note. They have already drafted it. I have seen the draft." "You've seen a lot, Envoy." "It is my profession to see. It is also my profession to tell you that the last man who found a vein a tenth the size of yours — a prospector named Okonkwo, in the Tharsis fields, three years ago — signed with the Combine and was dead within eight months. Decompression. Faulty lock. The Combine held the lease thereafter through his indentured heirs." She paused. "You are not an indentured man, Mr. Neegan. That is your strength and your danger. You are a citizen of nowhere important, holding the most important piece of real property in the system. Unprotected assets on Mars have a way of acquiring owners." Arthur was quiet for a moment. Somewhere below them, he could hear the thrum of the *Concordat*'s engines — solid, chemical, honest work. He thought of his father, who had come out on the indenture ships from the Dhaka yards and died still owing the passage. "May I ask a question, Envoy?" "You may." "The survey that found the vein. My claim sits in the Utopia basin. The Combine surveyed that basin in '88 and filed it as barren. I always assumed their instruments were poor." He looked up at her. "Were they?" For the first time, Saro's expression moved — a small, genuine disturbance, like wind over still water. "You are sharper than your file suggests," she said. "The Combine's instruments were excellent. Their instruments found your vein in 2088, and the finding was suppressed, because a discovery of that magnitude, disclosed then, would have triggered the Ceres Convention's automatic internationalization clause. Everyone's Azra would have become no one's." She folded her hands. "The file was stolen from Meridian's Luna archives fourteen months ago. It has since circulated. Certain parties have known about your vein for over a year, Mr. Neegan. You were permitted to find it. The only question still open — the only question in the entire system, at this moment — is who you will have found it *for*." Arthur felt the cabin, briefly, as a very small box in a very large game. "And if I say no to everyone," he said, "and sit on it?" "Then you are a one-man nation holding a fission stockpile," Saro said, "and nations holding fission stockpiles have historically short lives. I am offering you a protector, Mr. Neegan. I will not pretend I am offering you a friend. The Compact needs your vein to survive; the Directorate needs it to remain supreme; the Combine needs it to exist. None of us *needs* you, except as the legal accident of a claim registered under Martian colonial law — a body of law, I remind you, that any of three legislatures could amend by Thursday." She rose. The interview, clearly, was over in the way that weather is over. "You have until we make orbit to signal your intention," she said. "I would take the water with you. It is genuine Terran." At the hatch she stopped, half-turned, and the sunburst on her collar caught the light. "Your father came out on the *Praise of Industry*, did he not? 2061?" She did not wait for the answer. "The Compact was the only government that voted against the Indenture Act. We lost that vote. We remember losing it. Perhaps, Mr. Neegan, that is the difference between us and the others: we know what it is to be small, and to be patient." The hatch closed. Arthur sat alone with his water and the green text on the screen, cycling, cycling, patient as anything in the wide and hungry dark.

The characterization is particularly well-executed. Arthur Neegan emerges as a believable protagonist - neither naive nor overly sophisticated, with realistic reactions to his precarious situation. His dry observations ("The distinction, he suspected, was chiefly a matter of vocabulary") feel natural and establish his character efficiently. Envoy Saro is equally well-crafted, presenting as a seasoned diplomat who reveals information strategically while maintaining an air of controlled authority. The dialogue carries the narrative effectively, feeling natural while serving multiple purposes: advancing plot, revealing character, and building the world's political landscape. Saro's exposition about the galactic power structure never feels forced, and her final revelation about Arthur's father adds emotional weight without sentimentality. The prose style successfully emulates Asimov's approach - clean, precise, and focused on ideas rather than ornate description. The imagery is selective but vivid (Mars "rust-brown and pocked," the cabin smelling of "ozone and lemon wax"), creating atmosphere without overwhelming the narrative flow. The world-building demonstrates the requested "big-and-small-picture" approach, moving seamlessly from personal stakes to galactic politics. The revelation that Arthur was "permitted" to find the vein adds compelling complexity to what initially seemed like fortunate discovery. The pacing maintains tension throughout, building to the crucial revelation about the suppressed survey while keeping Arthur (and readers) off-balance about his true position. The ending strikes an appropriate note of uncertainty without false optimism. Minor weaknesses include some slightly predictable elements in the power dynamics setup, though the execution elevates familiar concepts. The piece occasionally borders on exposition-heavy, but this aligns with Asimovian conventions and serves the story's needs. Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
There's a reason I've always loved darkrooms. Outside of them, I know exactly who I am: the girl with the shaved undercut and the combat boots, the one who takes what she wants and apologizes for nothing. In here, under the red light, everything softens. Even me. Elliot doesn't know that. He probably thinks I'm the same person in here as out there. He's nineteen; he's still learning that people have interiors. He's humming again. Something low and tuneless, half a melody he's making up as he goes, while his print drifts in the stop bath like a small ghost. The red light catches the silver rings on his fingers, the chipped black polish, the smear of eyeliner he never quite cleans off his left eye. He hums when he's nervous. It took me three sessions to figure that out. It took me three sessions to admit I'd been cataloguing him at all. "Can I ask you something weird?" he says, not looking up from the tray. I've been waiting all semester for him to say something that wasn't about f-stops. "Weird is my favorite genre." He laughs—quiet, mostly breath. His tongs hold the paper still, but his eyes come up to meet mine, and in this light his face is all planes and shadows, androgynous in a way I don't have a clean word for. "The self-portraits I've been shooting. The ones for the final." He nods toward the enlarger. "You've seen the contact sheet." "I've seen the contact sheet," I confirm. The one where he'd photographed himself in his roommate's slip dress, lace-gloved hands over his face, like he was both hiding and asking to be seen. I'd stared at it for a full minute before pretending I hadn't. "I didn't take those as, like. An art concept." His voice drops. "I took them because I needed to know what I'd look like. And I keep going back to them. And I don't—" The humming has stopped. "I don't know what that means yet. But I didn't want you to think I was doing a bit." My whole body wants to move. That's my thing—when someone's drowning, I swim out and grab them, that's how I've been built since I was fifteen and decided the world was mine to manage. I want to cross this darkroom, take his face in my hands, tell him he's beautiful, tell him whatever he's figuring out, I'll be there for all of it. I want to take charge. I always take charge. But I've learned, slowly and badly, that sometimes taking charge is just taking. So I stay on my stool, close enough that our knees could touch, far enough that he has a whole room to move in if he needs it. "What does it feel like," I ask, "when you look at them?" He exhales like I've asked the real question. "Like... relief. Like the camera's not judging me. It just shows me, and I get to decide." "Then decide slowly," I say. "Nobody's grading you on this part." He laughs again, and this time it's real, and it does something to my chest I'm not prepared for. Here's what I don't say: I've thought about this. Too much. I have a type, historically—women who look like they could win a bar fight, men built like architecture. Defined edges. I've built my whole romantic identity on knowing exactly what I want, and Elliot is none of my categories. He's soft where I expect sharp, uncertain where I expect swagger, and when he tucks a strand of dyed-black hair behind his ear I feel like I'm sixteen again, like my map of desire has been redrawn in red light and I can't read it yet. Maybe that's what's scaring me. Not his questioning. Mine. The timer beeps. He lifts the print—another self-portrait, this one from tonight, taken with the cable release while I was in the other room—and slides it into the fixer. We both lean over the tray as his face surfaces in the chemical bath, blooming up out of white nothing. He's wearing the eyeliner heavier tonight. He's almost smiling. "I like that one," I say. "You can say it's weird." "I think it's the truest thing you've shot all semester." I nudge his shoulder with mine, a controlled collision, the most I'll let myself take. "For what it's worth? Whatever you figure out—it's going to suit you. You have really good instincts. About images, anyway." "And about people?" "Jury's out. You picked me for a partner." "I picked you," he says, "because you're the only person in that class who's never once looked at me like a puzzle." The air in the darkroom goes very still and very warm. I'm aware of the drip of the print, the hum of the exhaust fan, the fact that his hand is resting on the tray's edge and mine is maybe four inches from it, and that four inches has never felt so much like a decision. "Elliot." I keep my voice even, which costs me something. "I want to ask you something, and I need you to know you can say no, and nothing changes." He turns. The red light is in his eyes. "Can I touch your eyeliner? Just—it's smudged. Here." I raise my hand and stop it in the air between us, an offering, not an arrival. He looks at my hand for a long moment. Then he leans in—two percent, maybe three—and closes the distance himself. My thumb, beneath his left eye. His lashes against my skin. His breath. He doesn't hum. He doesn't need to. "Is this okay?" I whisper. "It's the most okay I've been in weeks," he says, and his voice cracks on *okay*, and I don't fix it, because it's not broken. We stay like that longer than the smudge requires. I don't take anything. He gives it. And somewhere in the red dark, a print of his face keeps developing, becoming, second by second, more exactly himself. I've never been patient in my life. I think I'd like to learn.

Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Stolen Moments in Roma** The Vespa missed him by a breath. Ben felt the wind of it, dropped his guidebook into a puddle left by the morning's wash of the piazza, and stumbled backward into a rack of postcards outside a tabaccheria. "*Ma sei scemo?*" The rider tore off her helmet, unleashing a storm of dark hair. "You walk in the road reading a *book*? In *Rome*? We invented the road! We do not invented the... the reading-while-walking!" "I'm terribly sorry—" Ben retrieved his book, dripping. "Mi dispiace. Molto. Er... dispiacere. Grande dispiacere." She stared at him. Then, unexpectedly, she laughed—a full, unguarded sound that scattered pigeons off the Fontana di Trevi's shoulders. "Grande dispiacere," she repeated, savoring it like a wine. "You apologize like a priest who has spilled the communion wine. What is your name, priest?" "Ben. Benjamin. Whitmore." He extended a hand. She looked at it as if it were a curious artifact, then shook it with surprising firmness. "Alessandra. Also grande dispiacere, Ben Whitmore." Her eyes flicked to his book. "Rome for the Cautious Traveler. Dio mio. Who wrote this, your grandmother?" --- The motorcycle was not a Vespa, he learned, but a battered Ducati, and the tour was not sanctioned by anyone. "Get on," she said, tossing him the spare helmet. "Your book tells you the Trevi is beautiful. I show you where the Trevi is *jealous*." They roared through alleys no guidebook would admit existed, and Ben clung to her jacket with the white-knuckled dignity of a man pretending he wasn't terrified. She stopped on a hill he couldn't name, where Rome unrolled below them like a rumpled tapestry of terracotta and gold. "Testaccio," she said. "The made-from-broken-amphorae hill. Two thousand years of garbage. Now it is the best view in the city." She lit a cigarette, offered him one; he declined, so she lit it anyway and tucked it behind his ear. "Souvenir." He noticed, without quite registering it, that she now held a lemon she hadn't had before, taken from a crate outside a fruttivendolo as they'd walked. She tossed it up, caught it, bit into the rind. "You're staring," she said. "I'm—cataloguing. I'm a classicist. It's professional habit." "A classicist." She exhaled smoke at the sky. "So you like old broken things." "Old things, yes. Broken—" He paused. "I find them more honest." Something shifted in her expression, a door opening a centimeter and then firmly shut. "Careful, Ben Whitmore. That is the most dangerous thing you have said all day." --- In the Mercato di Testaccio she moved like weather, sampling everything, paying for almost nothing. A handful of olives. A square of pecorino. Ben watched a small brass saint—San Cristoforo, patron of travelers—migrate from a vendor's tray into her jacket pocket while she argued passionately about the price of figs she had no intention of buying. "Alessandra." A voice like gravel. An old man at a watch-repair stall, spectacles pushed up into wild white hair. "Still stealing, picciridda?" "Orazio." She kissed both his cheeks warmly, without a flicker of guilt. "Still repairing watches nobody wants?" Orazio turned his attention to Ben, looking him over with the frank appraisal of a man pricing a used bicycle. "You are with her? English?" He clucked his tongue. "Listen. I know her since she is tall like this." He held a hand at his waist. "She takes things. Watches. Hearts. Once, my best screwdriver." He pointed a bent finger at Ben. "Check your pockets, inglese. Check them every hour." "My pockets are fine," Ben said politely. Alessandra's smile was pure seraphic innocence. "Orazio exaggerates. It was a *very* small screwdriver." Outside, she was quiet for half a block, which Ben suspected was a record. "He is right, you know," she said finally. "About me. I am not a good person for a cautious traveler." "Perhaps I'm tired of being cautious." She glanced at him sideways, and there it was again—that flicker, the door cracked open. "Perhaps," she said, "you are more interesting than your book." --- By evening she had taken him through a hole in a fence into a closed-for-restoration palazzo courtyard; through a church sacristy where a priest greeted her, alarmingly, by name; onto a rooftop in Trastevere belonging to someone's cousin, where strangers fed them carbonara and wine and someone played accordion badly and beautifully. Ben laughed more than he had in a decade. At some point his tie disappeared. He found it later, knotted around the bronze wrist of a street statue two neighborhoods away. He had no memory of how. Now it was sunset at the Giardino degli Aranci, the sky doing something unjust to the color pink, and they stood at the keyhole-like terrace where the dome of Saint Peter's floated perfectly framed between cypress trees. "I should get you back to your fountain," Alessandra said. "To your cautious book." "Stay for one more day of the uncautious version?" She turned to him fully. The mischief in her face had settled into something harder to read, and for once she seemed to be the one searching for words. "You don't know me, Ben Whitmore. You know a day. A day is a... a postcard. I am the whole city." "Then let me get lost in it." She laughed softly, but her eyes didn't. She stepped close, straightened his collar with maddening gentleness, and kissed his cheek—slowly, close enough to the corner of his mouth that his pulse forgot its Latin. "Domani," she said. "Eight o'clock. Don't read anything." She swung onto the Ducati and was gone into the amber streets before he could answer. Ben stood there, disoriented, delighted, ruined. He reached into his pocket for his notebook and found instead the small brass San Cristoforo, and beneath it a note in looping, triumphant handwriting: *Now you have been stolen too. —A.* He checked his other pocket. His fountain pen was gone. He grinned at the empty piazza like a madman. "Domani," he said to no one, and went to find the wine.

+ Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 84.8
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Last Outpost The recyclers hum their usual off-key lullaby, and I take that as a sign the night will be an easy one. Harlan's three drinks into his shift-end ritual and telling June about the rock he's convinced has a heart of palladium. June's not listening. June's nursing a fizzing plum thing and not-so-quietly deciding whether to forgive her wife for buying a cargo hopper without asking. The usual drama. The good kind. I wipe the bar. Same spot, left of the tap bank, where somebody carved a crude star map into the polymer eight years before I got here. I've never had the heart to sand it out. The rag moves in slow circles whether the bar's clean or not. It's my version of knitting. Then the airlock cycles, and she walks in. Tentacled dreads, the kind of gene-mod you see on deep-void spacers, all of them askew like she's been dragging her head through a gravity storm. She scans the room twice — *twice* — before she takes the stool at the end like it's the only defensible position in the place. Which, for the record, it isn't. That'd be the one by the kitchen door. "Vega whisky, neat," she says. "Better make that a double." "Vega whisky, coming up." I pull the bottle from the middle shelf, where I keep the stuff that's actually drinkable. "Rough docking, or rough life?" "Both. Neither." She rubs a tentacle-dread between her fingers, twisting it like a worry stone. "You're the bartender." "Sharp observational skills. You must be a detective." "Something like that." The double disappears in one motion. She sets the glass down soft, like she's afraid the sound will carry. "Quiet place." "Quietest rock in the belt. That's sort of the brand." "Good." She pushes the glass toward me. "Another." I pour, but I don't slide it over yet. "You want to tell me what's docking behind you? Because people who drink like that are usually being followed, and I like to know what's walking into my bar before it walks in." She looks at me for the first time. Really looks. Her eyes are the flat amber of someone running on stims and fear in equal measure. "Nobody's following me," she says. "Not yet." "Comforting." "Nettle," June calls down the bar, "tell Harlan that finding palladium in a core sample isn't the same as being rich." "Harlan," I say, not taking my eyes off the stranger, "you're not rich yet." "I *will be*," Harlan says, with the serene conviction of a man who's been three drinks wrong about many things. The stranger almost smiles. Almost. Then it collapses and she leans in, voice dropping. "How well do you know the people here?" "Better than they'd like, not as well as they think. Why?" "Because I need a place to—" She stops. Reconsiders. Her dreads coil slightly, an involuntary thing, like a cat's tail. "I need to leave something here. Just for a night. Maybe two. Small. Doesn't matter what." "See, when someone says 'doesn't matter what,' it always matters what." "I'll pay." "Everyone says that too." "Five hundred credits." She's already reaching into her coat. "A thousand." I finally slide her the second double, mostly so she has something to do with her hands. "I don't run a storage locker. I run a bar. People drink, I listen, occasionally I talk them out of bad decisions. That's the whole business model." "You're Nettle," she says. "Nets to my friends." "No." Her voice changes. Loses the frazzle, finds something underneath it — something steady and old and terribly, terribly informed. "Nets. Short for Nettle. But that's not what *he* called you, is it." The rag stops moving. I don't tell it to. It just does. "You've got me confused with somebody," I say. "You ran the Spiral," she says quietly. "Cargo manifesting for the Vantablack run. You could make anything disappear into paperwork. They called you the Ghost of Meridian Station." She takes a slow sip of the whisky, watching me over the rim. "You were the best at it. And then one day you weren't anywhere at all." The recyclers hum. Harlan laughs at something June said. Somewhere in the kitchen, Odo the cook drops a pan and swears in three languages, two of them invented. "That was a different person," I say. "Different life. I'm a bartender now. I make drinks and I mind my own business." "Then you know better than anyone that nobody out here is who they say they are." She sets a small object on the bar between us — matte black, no bigger than a thumb drive, humming at a frequency I can feel in my teeth. She covers it with her hand before I can get a proper look. "The people coming for this are the kind who don't stop at the person holding it. They start there." "I don't want to hear this." "You already heard it." She nudges it an inch toward me. "One night. Two, max. Then I'm gone and you never saw me." "And if I say no?" "Then I walk out that door with it, and the odds of me making it off this rock drop considerably, and you get to live with that." She glances down the bar at Harlan, at June, at old Ptolemy snoring in the booth by the viewport. "Cozy place. Good people. Would be a shame." There it is. The threat wrapped in silk. She doesn't blink, and neither do I, and for a long moment the only sound is the recyclers and my own pulse, which has opinions. Then the proximity chime sounds — soft, polite, the way it always does when a ship requests docking clearance at an hour when no honest ship arrives. The stranger's dreads go rigid. Every one of them, all at once, like coral sensing a predator. "That's early," she whispers. I pick up my rag. I start wiping the same spot, left of the tap bank, over the carved star map that leads nowhere. "Odo," I call toward the kitchen, keeping my voice light as anything. "Better put on a fresh pot." The airlock chime sounds.

The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes - revealing character, advancing plot, and building atmosphere. Nets' voice is particularly well-crafted, with her dry wit and defensive mechanisms coming through clearly. The stranger's dialogue effectively builds menace while revealing just enough information to hook the reader. The background conversations with Harlan and June add authentic texture to the bar setting. The world-building is economical but effective, dropping in details like gene-modded tentacle dreads, Vega whisky, and the Andromeda outer rim without over-explaining. The setting feels lived-in and authentic. The pacing builds tension steadily, from the comfortable opening through the stranger's arrival to the ominous ending with the approaching ship. The author handles the exposition of Nets' past skillfully, revealing her history as "the Ghost of Meridian Station" through the stranger's knowledge rather than clunky backstory dumps. This creates intrigue while maintaining narrative momentum. The prose style is clean and engaging, with some particularly nice touches like describing the recyclers' "off-key lullaby" and Nets wiping the same spot as "my version of knitting." The writing avoids purple prose while still creating vivid imagery. The conflict setup is solid - the stranger brings danger to Nets' sanctuary, forcing her to confront her past. The threat is both personal (to the stranger) and communal (to the bar's patrons), raising the stakes effectively. The chapter ends on a strong cliffhanger without resolving the central conflict. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 83.8
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter Two: The Quarter and Everything After** The strap on my backpack keeps slipping off my shoulder. That's the thing I keep coming back to, hours later, when everything else is too big to hold. The strap. Slipping. Slipping. Like even my own stuff is trying to ditch me. The ride from Tennessee dumped me on Rampart Street at some hour that only exists for people who've made terrible decisions. The sky over New Orleans was the color of a bruise going yellow, and the city smelled like beer and sugar and something rotting sweet underneath, like a fruit bowl nobody emptied. Two states. I did the math on the bus ticket money in my pocket — eighty-seven dollars, a crumpled ten from the coffee can in the kitchen, and the rest in ones from waitressing at the Catfish Shack — and the math said: you are so completely screwed, Taylor. And here's the thing, here's the thing I keep flip-flopping on like a fish on a dock: I felt *free*. Actually free. For the first time since Tuesday night, when Dad's face did that thing — that closing-shutter thing, like a store going out of business — nobody here knew me. Nobody here had ever met *her*. Every person who looked at me on this street saw exactly what I'd been begging someone to see for three years. The strap slips again. I hitch it up. Keep walking. --- By noon I'd learned that New Orleans in June is a wet towel pressed against your whole body, and that Jackson Square is full of people my mother would call "characters" and my father would call "the problem with this country." I sat on a step and ate a granola bar that had melted into a single, unified granola organism. That's where I met her. "You're sitting on my step." I looked up. Girl, maybe seventeen, sunburned shoulders, hair shaved on one side like she'd done it herself with craft scissors, which she probably had. She had a canvas tote that said NEW ORLEANS JAZZ MUSEUM with the word MUSEUM crossed out and *HELL* written in Sharpie. "Sorry." I moved. "I didn't say move. I said it's my step." She dropped down next to me like we'd made plans. "You got a name?" "Taylor." It came out before the fear could stop it, and God, saying it out loud, my real name, to a stranger, felt like shoplifting something expensive. "Taylor." She tested it, nodded. "I'm Dez. You running from something or running to something?" "Does it matter?" "Running *from*, you hide. Running *to*, you plan. You're doing neither, so you're doing the third thing." "Which is?" "Running *out*." She cracked a smile with a chipped tooth in it. "The worst kind. I did that one." I wanted to ask what she'd run out *of*. I didn't. There was a bruise on her arm, older yellow, shaped like fingers, and when she caught me looking she pulled her sleeve down without a flicker of expression change, and I decided we were going to be two people who didn't ask questions. That seemed like the whole economy of this place. Don't ask, and you get to not be asked. --- Dez showed me things. That's what she did all day, like a tour guide for the recently exploded. The French Quarter, where you can be sixteen and nobody blinks, because there's a guy on that corner wearing a diaper and angel wings and *he's* the one drawing crowds. The church on Rampart that does free lunch on weekdays — "sit in the back, look penitent, don't take seconds until the lady with the cross necklace offers." The library on Loyola with AC "cold enough to hang meat" and bathrooms with locks. "And don't," she said, stopping dead in the middle of Decatur Street, "ever go with anyone who says they've got a place for you to crash. Anyone. Nice ones, scary ones, ones who cry, ones who show you pictures of their own runaways like they're their kids. There's a whole food chain down here, Taylor, and everybody's hungry." "You're telling me not to trust people who offer help. From someone who just offered help." She laughed — a real one, sharp and surprised, like it escaped custody. "Yeah. Learn the difference between help and bait. Free lesson." The strap slipped off my shoulder for maybe the hundredth time and she reached over without asking and tied a knot in it, shortening it, quick little fingers like she'd done it before, like she'd fixed other people's broken straps in other lives. "Why are you being nice to me?" I asked. Because I had to. Because Mom's voice was in my head — *strangers, Taylor, strangers* — and because underneath that was the counselor's voice, the smug one on the phone: *concerning behavioral patterns*, and underneath *that* was the fear that the counselor was right, that running was just another pattern, that I was doing something concerning right now, right here, on a street corner with a girl whose arm had finger-marks on it. Dez shrugged. "You looked like me. Day one. Nobody talked to me on day one and I almost—" She stopped. Closed that shutter, same as Dad, and I hated that I recognized it. "Anyway. It's hot. Day one people make dumb choices in the heat." She had secrets. Obviously. The phone that buzzed all afternoon and never got answered. The way she scanned doorways. The way she said "my boyfriend's place" exactly once and never again, like a card she'd accidentally shown and now had to burn. --- It got dark and the Quarter turned loud and glittery and Dez walked me to the church steps where, she said, some nights the side door doesn't latch. "You coming in?" "Nah. I got somewhere." She said it too lightly. "Dez. Is 'somewhere' safe?" She grinned that chipped grin. "Free lesson number two: nobody down here answers that question honestly, including me." She walked off toward Rampart, toward the part of town she'd told me never to go, and I stood there with my backpack — the strap snug now, thanks to her knot — and I realized I don't know her last name, and she doesn't know mine, and I miss her already, which is insane, which is *concerning*, and I sat down on the church steps anyway and watched the streetlights come on over a city that doesn't know me yet. Day one. Strap's holding. So am I.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and emotional authenticity in depicting a transgender teen's first day as a runaway in New Orleans. The writing successfully captures Taylor's voice through a distinctive blend of vulnerability and defensive humor, with internal monologue that feels genuine rather than forced. The characterization is particularly effective. Taylor emerges as a complex protagonist - simultaneously brave and terrified, cynical yet hopeful. The recurring motif of the slipping backpack strap serves as an effective metaphor for Taylor's precarious situation while avoiding heavy-handedness. Dez is equally well-developed, with her own mysteries and damage suggested through subtle details like the finger-shaped bruise and her evasive responses about where she stays. The dialogue feels natural and age-appropriate, capturing the tentative way two damaged teens might circle around trust. Lines like "Running from, you hide. Running to, you plan" demonstrate how exposition can be delivered organically through character voice. The conversation flows with realistic hesitations and the kind of careful probing that occurs when people are testing boundaries. The setting work is strong, with New Orleans rendered through sensory details that avoid tourist clichés. The description of the city smelling "like beer and sugar and something rotting sweet underneath" effectively establishes atmosphere while reflecting Taylor's emotional state. The prose style successfully balances literary ambition with accessibility. Phrases like "the sky over New Orleans was the color of a bruise going yellow" are evocative without being overwrought. The mixed tense approach works well, creating immediacy in the present-tense sections while allowing reflection in past tense. The emotional complexity is handled with particular skill. Taylor's conflicted feelings about freedom versus fear, the simultaneous relief and terror of being seen authentically, and the complicated gratitude toward Dez all feel psychologically authentic. The piece avoids both excessive sentimentality and cynical darkness. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the metaphors feel slightly strained, and the pacing in the middle section could be tighter. However, these are relatively minor issues in an otherwise accomplished piece. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 83.8
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**My Apocalypse Buddy** The sun rose over the Wreckage the way it always did: slowly, with an air of someone who'd seen it all before and hadn't been impressed the first time. Inside the rusted husk of a school bus — the one Midas grandly called Home, when he was feeling optimistic, and *that damned bus* when he wasn't — a council of war was in session. It consisted of Midas, a young man whose talent for catastrophe was widely regarded as the eighth wonder of the old world, and Chewy, an animatronic stuffed koala whose fur had gone the color of regret. "Okay," said Midas. "Today's mission. Batteries." Chewy's head rotated toward him with a sound like a small arthritic god clearing its throat. His eyes, once adorable, now flickered like dying fireflies. *"Where's the beef?"* said Chewy. "See, this is exactly what I mean. You've got maybe two days of power left, and you're spending it asking about beef. There hasn't been beef since the Collapse. There's barely been *bread*." *"Have a break,"* Chewy suggested. *"Have a Kit Kat."* "You're doing it again." Midas rubbed his eyes. "Right. The Mart of Wal. Old ruins, up the ridge. Before time, people went there for everything. Somewhere in that rubble there's a battery aisle, and somewhere in that battery aisle is a D-cell with your name on it." Chewy considered this. Or possibly he was buffering. With Chewy, philosophy and technical failure were difficult to tell apart, and had been for two hundred years. *"Every little helps,"* he said, which Midas chose to take as agreement. --- The Mart of Wal still stood, after a fashion, the way a skeleton still stands. Its great doors had been symbolically chained shut by the Congregation of the Checkout, a sect of robed zealots who worshipped the point-of-sale terminal as the gateway to a lost paradise where everything had cost *so little*. Midas had heard they accepted new members by scanning them. Nobody knew what the scanner did to you. That was rather the point. "Right," whispered Midas, prying open a service door. "In, battery aisle, out. No trouble. Simple." Historians of the Collapse — had there been any — would have noted that the phrase *no trouble, simple*, spoken aloud by Midas, had a failure rate of approximately one hundred percent, and that this was arguably an improvement on his usual odds. They got forty feet into the store before the floor collapsed. It wasn't Midas's fault, in the sense that the floor had been waiting two centuries for *someone*, and Midas was simply the most punctual volunteer. He plunged through rotted tile into the dark beneath, where the supermarket trolleys went to die, and landed in a nest of them with a crash like a percussion section falling downstairs. Chewy, who had been riding in Midas's backpack, poked his head out. *"Falling prices,"* he observed. "Thank you. Very helpful." Midas stood, and something in the dark stood with him. Several somethings. They were small, feral, and they made a sound like a chainsaw being operated by something very angry and very small. The Wreckage's feral chihuahuas had survived the Collapse on a diet of rats, hubris, and one another, and they did not appreciate visitors. Midas ran. This was, at least, a skill he'd practiced. He ran down the trolley graveyard, through a rotten wall, up a fallen escalator, and out into the main concourse of the store — directly into the middle of Congregation of the Checkout's mid-morning service. There were perhaps thirty robed figures, kneeling before a dusty terminal, chanting in a language that was probably English but had the word *loyalty* in it far too often. They all turned. Midas waved. "Hi. Just, ah — shopping." The high priest pointed a withered finger. "*An UNLOYAL CUSTOMER!*" Midas ran again, chihuahuas at his heels, cultists behind the chihuahuas, and somewhere in his backpack Chewy announcing, at maximum volume, *"Cleanup on aisle five!"* — which, to the Congregation, was evidently a sacred invocation, because the chanting behind him redoubled. He burst through the battery aisle, swept an entire shelf into his bag without stopping — D-cells, AAAs, two things that might have been batteries or might have been elaborate sweets — grabbed a shopping trolley from the stack, and hurled himself into it as they crested the collapsed mezzanine, because Midas had one other talent besides catastrophe, and it was an unshakeable faith in downhill. The trolley took the ramp of the loading dock, achieved a brief and glorious flight, and rolled three quarters of a mile down the ridge with Midas screaming inside it and Chewy singing, over and over, *"I'm lovin' it, I'm lovin' it, I'm lovin'—"* until his batteries gave out mid-slogan, with what Midas would later swear was an air of profound satisfaction. --- He returned to home base in three ways. First, the trolley returned him, at speed, because the brakes had rusted off sometime in the previous century. Second, the bus's side door returned him, at speed, through it, in a shower of glass and profanity. Third, physics returned him — off the far wall, onto the floor, and briefly into the ceiling, which is where he found the crack that had been letting the rain in, which was at least useful to know. Midas lay on the floor of the bus, cataloguing his injuries, which was a long catalogue with a supplementary appendix. "Never," he said to the ceiling, "again." He fumbled in the wreckage of his backpack, found a D-cell that had survived the journey, and pried open the panel on Chewy's back with a hairpin. The old koala's eyes flickered. Whirred. Caught. *"Thank you,"* said Chewy, *"for shopping with us."* Midas looked at him for a long moment. Outside, the sun was setting over the Wreckage, and the chihuahuas were probably still coming, and the Congregation knew where he lived, and his ribs hurt in three languages. "Yeah," he said. "Same time tomorrow?" *"Because,"* said Chewy, snuggling into the backpack, *"you're worth it."* And neither of them knew what that meant, exactly. But it was nice anyway.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, successfully capturing his dry wit, observational humor, and philosophical undertones wrapped in absurdist scenarios. The author effectively establishes the post-apocalyptic setting through clever world-building details like the "Congregation of the Checkout" and references to "the Collapse," while maintaining the light tone characteristic of Pratchett's work. The story structure follows the prompt precisely: deliberation, mission gone sideways, and return home "worse for wear." The characterization is particularly strong - Midas emerges as a believably hapless protagonist whose self-awareness about his catastrophic tendencies feels authentic, while Chewy's malfunctioning corporate slogans provide both humor and subtle commentary on consumer culture's persistence. The prose demonstrates genuine elegance in places, particularly in descriptive passages like "The sun rose over the Wreckage the way it always did: slowly, with an air of someone who'd seen it all before and hadn't been impressed the first time." The author successfully balances humor with genuine stakes, making the reader care about these characters despite the comedic tone. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes - advancing plot, revealing character, and providing humor. Chewy's broken advertising slogans are particularly effective, creating both comedy and pathos. The pacing is well-controlled, building tension through the escalating chaos at the Mart of Wal. However, some elements feel slightly forced, particularly the "three ways" return structure, which reads as overly mechanical. The ending, while touching, borders on being too neat given the established chaos. The piece occasionally relies on coincidence (the floor collapse timing) rather than character-driven plot development. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 84.8
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter Three: The Shop at Llanwennol** The bell above the door had barely finished its trembling when the man came in backwards, one hand still on the latch, eyes on the street. "You close at half five," Carys said, not looking up from the till. "It's half two." "Then you've got three hours to buy something or leave." He turned. And there it was—the face from the posters at the Aberystwyth bus stop, the one her niece had Blu-Tacked to her bedroom ceiling. Kit Alden. Soaked to the collar, hair flattened by rain, and grinning like a lighthouse. "Terrible weather out there," he said. "Almost biblical. I was passing and thought, there's a sanctuary." "You thought no such thing. You were followed." His grin flickered—actually flickered, like a bulb going. "How could you possibly—" "Two men out there photographing a parking sign. Nobody photographs a parking sign, Mr. Alden. Not even tourists." "Kit, please." He crossed to the counter, set his hands on it, all easy warmth. "And you are?" "Carys. This is my shop. You're dripping on my floor." "Terribly sorry." He didn't move his hands. "Carys. Lovely name. Do you know, this is my first time in Llanwennol, and already it's my favourite place in Wales. There's something about a proper bookshop—the smell, the—" "Paper and damp. You get used to it." "—the *romance* of it. You must get people coming in from all over." "Mrs. Pritchard comes in from the farm on Thursdays. Big thrill for everyone." He laughed, and it was a good laugh, she'd give him that. Practised, mind. She'd heard practised laughs before, from the chapel soloists. "You know," he said, leaning in as if sharing state secrets, "most people, when I walk into a room, they do a certain thing. A little jolt. Squeal, sometimes. One woman in Cardiff fainted on my shoe." "Was she reading at the time? Might've been the standing up too fast." He blinked. Then he laughed again—but this one was different, less polished, more bark. "You're not going to ask for a photo, are you." "Would you like me to?" "I—" He straightened. She watched something almost fragile cross his face, quickly tidied away. "Most people find it hard to resist." "Most people haven't mopped this floor." He wandered off then, hands in his pockets, and she told herself the flush in her cheeks was from the radiator. It was an old radiator. It ran hot. That was all. She heard him stop in the back alcove. Silence. Then: "Is that a Collins Bird Guide?" "Shop copy. I don't sell my own things." "You birdwatch?" He came round the shelf holding it like a relic, and something had changed in his voice. The lacquer was off it. "I ring." "You—" He frowned. "Ringing. Like, church bells?" "Birds. You catch them at dawn, put a small ring on the leg, record the details, let them go. I do the reed beds past the estuary Tuesdays and Saturdays." He stared at her. Then, quietly: "I've got a life list." "A what?" "Four hundred and twelve species." He glanced at the window, at the rain, at the men with cameras. "I don't tell anyone. If the press found out I'd spent four years' worth of Saturday dawns lying in a ditch in Suffolk looking for a lesser spotted woodpecker, they'd run it under a headline about my *fragile masculinity*." Carys bit down on a smile. It escaped anyway, one corner. "You laughed," he said, delighted, pointing at her like she'd confessed to a crime. "I did no such thing." "You did. Half a millimetre. I saw it." He came back to the counter, and now the charm was gone entirely, and what was underneath it was worse for her, somehow—genuine, bright-eyed, like a boy showing you his conker collection. "Last spring I was filming in Andalusia and I slipped out at five in the morning and saw a hoopoe. A *hoopoe*. On a wall. And I had to sit through an entire day of pretending to care about a car chase when all I could think about was the crest going up and down. Up and down! You know what I mean?" "I know what a hoopoe is, Mr. Alden." "Kit." "I know what one is, Kit." "Say you've seen one." "Seen three. One on Skomer, back in 2019. Nearly fell off a cliff for it." He made a sound like a man being personally blessed. "A woman who's nearly died for a hoopoe. Marry me." "Have you seen the choughs on the cliffs here?" "*Here?* They nest here?" "Eight pairs last count. And in winter, the starlings come in over the estuary. Murmurations. Half a million birds turning like—" she hesitated, annoyed at herself for the next word, "—like one breathing thing." "I've seen it on television," he said. "I've watched it on my phone at two in the morning in hotel rooms. I've *dreamt* about it." He looked at her, and for once he wasn't performing anything. "You see it from your own doorstep." "From the sea wall. If it's not raining." "It's always raining." "Then you learn to love it in the rain." The bell hadn't rung, but he glanced at the window anyway, and she saw the shadow cross him—the other life waiting out there with its lenses. His shoulders dropped half an inch. "I have to go out there eventually," he said. "They'll follow me to the hotel. They'll follow me to the airport. They'll—" He stopped. Looked at her. "Unless there's a back door?" "Past the kettle." "Past the kettle." He smiled, and it was crooked, unguarded, nothing like the poster. "Carys. If I came back Saturday—hypothetically—would the starlings be on?" "The starlings don't take bookings." "Right. No. Of course." He gathered the rain-soaked collar of his coat, hesitated, and the old grin surfaced—one last go at it, and she knew it was his armour going back on. "You will admit, though, before I go, that you're a little pleased I ducked into your shop." "Your three hours are up, Mr. Alden." "Half past two," he said, and she could hear him grinning in the dark of the corridor, "so I'll be back by five." She listened to the back door click. Then she stood a moment with her hand flat on the till, feeling her pulse do something no self-respecting pulse ought to do, and thought: *half a millimetre, and he saw it.* "Saturday," she said to the empty shop. "It's not even a booking. It's a maybe." She got out the shop copy of the Collins anyway, and put it behind the counter, where she could reach it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the requested romantic tension and character dynamics. The author successfully creates two distinct voices - Kit's performative charm masking vulnerability, and Carys's dry, practical Welsh sensibility that conceals her growing attraction. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes: advancing plot, revealing character, and building romantic tension. The Welsh setting is well-established through specific place names (Llanwennol, Aberystwyth, Skomer) and cultural details (chapel soloists, Mrs. Pritchard from the farm) without feeling forced or touristy. The bookshop environment is efficiently sketched through sensory details and Carys's proprietorial attitude. The central conceit works effectively - Kit's charm offensive failing against Carys's immunity creates genuine chemistry. The shared passion for birdwatching provides an authentic connection point that feels organic rather than contrived. The author skillfully shows Kit's facade dropping when discussing his "life list," revealing genuine enthusiasm beneath the celebrity persona. Character development is nuanced. Kit's fragile ego manifests in his need for recognition ("Most people find it hard to resist") while his vulnerability emerges through his secret passion and fear of media ridicule. Carys maintains her defenses while showing subtle signs of attraction - the "half millimetre" smile, her pulse reaction, and her decision to keep the bird guide accessible. The prose is clean and economical, with effective imagery ("grinning like a lighthouse," "charm was his armour going back on"). The pacing builds naturally from initial antagonism through shared interest to mutual attraction. The ending strikes an appropriate note - hopeful but uncertain, with both characters maintaining their essential natures while opening to possibility. Minor weaknesses include some slightly predictable beats in the charm-to-vulnerability arc, and the birdwatching connection, while well-executed, follows a familiar "shared secret passion" romance trope. However, the execution elevates these familiar elements through strong character work and authentic dialogue.
