+ Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 82.5
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The door swung inward on hinges that groaned like a dying whale's ribs, and the smell of the underhold rolled over them: tallow, salt-rot, and beneath it something older — the cold mineral breath of the artifact itself, humming through the stone like a tooth aching in a jawbone. Aya had expected guards. She had expected locks, sigils, perhaps one of the guild's brass-and-oil sentinels with its glass eyes and clockwork patience. She had not expected a lamp. A single whale-oil lamp burned on a table at the far end of the vault, and beside it, seated in a high-backed chair as though presiding over a dinner party, was Mother Marrow. Not shackled in a magistrate's cell. Not swinging from the gibbet at Wrenfield Yard. *Seated*, with a flintlock pistol laid across her lap like a cat, and flanking her, two men the size of harpoon racks — Gorran and the mute, Pell — each with a bar of iron in hand. "Shut the door behind you, loves," said Mother Marrow. "Draughts get into the bones down here." The door boomed shut. Simeon's pocket watch chose that moment to tick, absurdly loud in the vaulted dark — *tick, tick, tick* — like some small brass heart betraying them all. "You're supposed to be in Newgate," Katra blurted. "Newgate." Mother Marrow smiled, and the lamplight made a yellow ruin of her face. "The constables took a woman in my coat, with my rings, weeping my tears. Bought and paid for by sundown. You children thought to divide my kingdom while I yet breathed. I'd admire the nerve of it, if it weren't so *stupid*." Aya's mind raced through the geometry of the room — distance to the lamp, to the artifact's iron reliquary, to the door. Gorran moved first, no warning given, simply crossed the floor and took Katra's wrist and bent it until the knife she'd palmed rang on the flagstones. Pell caught Simeon from behind, one vast arm pinning him, and Simeon went very still, the watch in his waistcoat ticking wildly against his ribs, as though time itself had begun to run. Aya did not run. There was nowhere to run. Instead she raised her chin as her mother had taught her, in the days before the rope, and said: "You'll want to reconsider this, Mother Marrow. Whatever you intend." "Will I." Mother Marrow rose. She crossed the vault slowly, her boots ringing on stone, and stood before Aya, studying the black silk mask, the borrowed coat, the girl-shaped shadow within it. "The summoner. The little nightingale who pulled shrieking things out of the dark and made my rivals piss themselves. I confess, I let you rise because I wanted to know what you were." Her hand came up, rough as a file, and gripped Aya's jaw. "Time to see." The mask came away. The vault went silent except for the watch. *Tick. Tick. Tick.* "Aya Vessant," Mother Marrow breathed. "Lord Aldous Vessant's daughter. The hanged witch's whelp, walking in my house." She began to laugh — a low, delighted, awful sound. "Oh, *bless*. Oh, *providence*. Do you know what the magistrates would pay for you, girl? What your dear father would pay?" Aya's stomach dropped through the earth, into the immateria itself, into the dark where the things she summoned lived. She thought of her father's face at the trial — grey, correct, ruined. She thought of the broadsheets: *THE WITCH OF HARROW LANE SWINGS AT DAWN.* She thought of how quickly a family name burns, and how long it stinks afterward. *They'll hang me like she was hung,* she thought, with a strange, floating clarity. *And Father will watch. And it will be my own doing.* "Whatever you imagine doing with us," she said, and was gratified that her voice did not shake, "you're weighing it wrong. Katra and Simeon are worth nothing — a cutpurse and a tinker. But me? I'm the last living vessel of a hereditary gift the Crown has spent thirty years trying to stamp out. The academies would gut each other for my blood. The Church would burn it. And my father—" her voice caught, traitorously, "—my father would empty his accounts to the last brass farthing before he let the magistrates take my head. You have not caught a thief, Mother Marrow. You've caught an *annuity*. Kill me and you're holding a corpse's value. Keep me breathing, and I'm worth more than the artifact behind you." Mother Marrow's thumb traced her cheek, almost tender. "Pretty words. Aristocrat's words — you were raised on them." "Then weigh them in your own coin," Aya said. "You're a businesswoman. What's the return on three corpses in the underhold? Nothing. Rats' meals. What's the return on the Vessant heir, delivered quietly to a buyer of your choosing — or ransomed, or *leased*?" The word felt filthy in her mouth, and she said it anyway. "You could buy the whole quay." *And I am bargaining myself into a different cage,* she thought, *with a different gibbet at the end of it, and Katra and Simeon dragged down with me, because I wanted — I wanted*— Mother Marrow turned back toward her chair, and for a long moment there was only the lamp's guttering, the artifact's low mineral hum, and Simeon's watch, marking each second like a nail driven into a coffin lid. "Katra, Simeon," she said at last, "go to the cells. Don't fuss; you'll be fed. I've not decided your arithmetic yet." Her eyes stayed on Aya. "You, nightingale — you stay. We're going to talk terms, you and I. And if I see so much as one shadow move that shouldn't — one of your *friends* from the immateria — Gorran shoots you in the belly, and we'll see how much an heir is worth leaking." Aya swallowed. In the deep places behind her eyes, something old and patient turned over, and she felt it look at Mother Marrow the way a whale looks at a rowboat. "Terms," she said. "Yes. Let's." The watch ticked on.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and atmospheric worldbuilding within the whalepunk fantasy setting. The author successfully creates a vivid Victorian-gothic atmosphere through evocative imagery like "hinges that groaned like a dying whale's ribs" and "the cold mineral breath of the artifact itself, humming through the stone like a tooth aching in a jawbone." The whale-oil lamps, brass-and-oil sentinels, and industrial elements effectively establish the steampunk aesthetic. The dialogue feels authentic to the period and characters, with Mother Marrow's voice particularly well-crafted - menacing yet businesslike, befitting a crime boss. Her lines like "Draughts get into the bones down here" and "I'd admire the nerve of it, if it weren't so stupid" capture both her authority and casual cruelty. Aya's aristocratic speech patterns contrast effectively with the underworld setting. Character actions remain believable throughout. Aya's quick pivot to negotiating her value as a hostage demonstrates both desperation and intelligence, while her internal conflict about the consequences feels genuine. Mother Marrow's revelation that she orchestrated a decoy arrest shows cunning befitting her position. The pacing builds tension effectively, moving from the eerie quiet of the entrance to the shock of Mother Marrow's presence, then through the capture and unmasking to the final negotiation. The author successfully avoids writing a fight scene as requested, instead focusing on psychological tension. However, some descriptions border on overwrought, particularly the opening paragraph's layered metaphors. The piece occasionally tells rather than shows emotional states, though this is balanced by strong showing elsewhere. The ending, while appropriately dark, feels somewhat predictable in its setup for further negotiation. The internal monologue effectively captures Aya's aristocratic background conflicting with her criminal activities, and her fear of following her mother's fate adds emotional weight. The piece maintains consistent tone throughout and adheres well to the prompt's requirements. + Fanfic-crossover: Gunpowder Rendezvous — Score: 80.9
Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bar smells like fish sauce and old blood, which Spike figures is just Roanapur's way of saying welcome. He's nursing the cheapest whiskey on the menu—cheap being relative, since he's down to his last few woolongs and the bounty poster in his jacket is worth more than the building he's sitting in. The woman comes in like weather. Door bangs, boots on wet floor, and every drunk in the place recalibrates around her without knowing why. Spike doesn't look up right away. He's learned that the people worth looking at will let you know. She takes the stool one down from his, slaps the bar, and says something to the bartender in a voice like gravel in a blender. Then she lights a cigarette, and her eyes slide over to him like she's already decided he's a problem. Spike pulls out his lighter for his own smoke. It takes three strikes to catch. "Piece of junk," she says. "Sentimental value." He exhales. There's a ring of rust around the middle of the lighter, orange-brown, the kind that only comes from total submersion. She clocks it. He sees her clock it. "That thing's been underwater." "Once or twice." He turns the lighter idly in his fingers. "I drowned once. Kind of." She snorts into her beer. "Kind of." "Whatever happens, happens." He shrugs. "So far, it's happened. I'm still here." "No shit." She leans back, and he gets the full picture: the dragon coiled down her right arm, the twin shoulder holsters riding like they grew there, the shorts that suggest she's never once considered the concept of consequences. "Revy." "Spike." They drink. Somewhere around the third round, she pulls a crumpled flyer out of her pocket and slaps it on the bar. He pulls his out and lays it next to hers. Same face. Same weaselly accountant, same reward. Manny the Ledger. Ran off from the Triads with a hard drive full of account numbers. Worth a fortune dead or alive—though in Roanapur, dead is traditional. Revy looks at the two flyers, then at him, and grins like a shark that's just been told dinner is a swimming contest. "You have got to be kidding me." "Small galaxy," Spike says. "Small my ass. That's my money, cowboy." "I was here first." "You were sitting here *drinking*." She knocks back her shot and orders another. "That's not working. That's just being pathetic in public." He can't really argue with that. He's hungry enough that the bar peanuts are starting to look like a meal. --- The shooting starts at round six, which is traditional. The door opens and four men come in wearing the cheap suits of people who are paid to be bullet catchers. One of them spots the flyers still sitting on the bar—Revy's, since Spike has pocketed his—and everything goes loud. Spike is off the stool before the first shot takes out the bottles behind the bar, moving the way water moves, no wasted motion. Revy is faster, both Cutlasses out and barking, and he registers distantly that she's *good*—not bar-fight good, not even Roanapur good. She's firing two pistols on separate targets with the accuracy most people need two hands and a prayer for. A goon comes around the counter at him. Spike redirects the man's own momentum into the edge of the bar, then through a table, Jeet Kune Do doing what Jeet Kune Do does. Beside him, Revy drops the last two with a smile on her face that he decides not to think too hard about. Silence. Smoke. The bartender already dragging out a mop. "Manny," Spike says, nodding at the back door swinging on its hinges. The accountant had been in the corner booth the whole time, and now he is very much not. They look at each other. Then they run. --- The trail is pathetic and easy—Manny isn't a professional, just a thief with sweaty palms—and it ends at a motel two streets over, a place with a neon sign missing enough letters to spell something ruder. Room 8. They arrive at the door at the same time, which is the problem. "Back off," Revy says, hammers cocked. "You back off." Spike's Jericho is out, though he's holding it low, almost politely. "I tracked him here." "We tracked him here. Plural. I'm feeling generous—we can split it." "Split it?" Her laugh is ugly and genuine. "Listen, you skinny scarecrow, I don't split *checks* at restaurants." "You don't pay for meals, either, I'm guessing." She jabs a barrel at his chest. He doesn't move. That seems to genuinely confuse her—most people move. They stand there in the buzzing neon light, guns on each other, close enough that he can smell gunpowder and cheap tobacco and whiskey on her, and she can smell the same things on him. Her eyes are dark and flat and alive in a way that's familiar, and he hates that it's familiar. "You're not gonna shoot me," Spike says. "Wanna bet?" "You've had four chances since the bar. You keep not taking them." Her jaw tightens. "You've had six." "Whatever happens, happens." "That's the most annoying thing anyone's ever said to me, and I work with a *nun*." Somewhere in the standoff, she's ended up closer. Or he has. The guns are still up but the barrels have drifted—hers pointed at his shoulder now, his at the wall behind her—and the space between them has become a different kind of standoff entirely. "You died once," she says, quieter. "That true?" He looks at her with the eye that sees the past and the one that sees the present, and neither of them blinks. "I'm not a good person, Spike," she says, before he can answer, like she's getting ahead of the question. "Not a bad one either. I'm just here." "Yeah," he says. "Me too." Inside room 8, a window scrapes open. They both hear it at the same instant. Manny, climbing out into the alley, forty million woolongs getting away on spider legs. Neither of them lowers their gun. Neither of them pulls the trigger, either. "Well," Revy says, grin crawling back up her face, guns still locked on him, his still locked on her. "After you, cowboy." "After you," Spike says. "Whatever happens—" "If you say it one more time I'm shooting you for real." The window bangs shut. They move.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong character work and atmospheric writing while delivering on most of the prompt's requirements. The author captures both Spike and Revy's voices authentically - Spike's fatalistic philosophy and laid-back demeanor contrast effectively with Revy's aggressive, profane directness. The dialogue feels natural and character-appropriate, with memorable exchanges that reveal personality through speech patterns and word choice. The setting is vividly established through sensory details like "fish sauce and old blood" and the motel's broken neon sign. The action sequences are well-choreographed, particularly the bar fight where both characters' combat styles are distinctly portrayed. The sexual tension builds organically through proximity, shared danger, and mutual recognition of kindred spirits. However, the piece has some structural weaknesses. The ending feels somewhat abrupt and doesn't fully deliver on the "motel room standoff" promised in the prompt - while there is a standoff outside the room, it doesn't quite achieve the intimate, claustrophobic tension suggested. The bounty hunt plot serves its purpose but remains fairly straightforward without surprising developments. The prose is generally strong with good rhythm and flow, though occasionally veers toward overly stylized descriptions ("comes in like weather"). Character actions remain believable throughout, and both protagonists maintain their established personalities without sudden shifts. The emotional complexity emerges through subtext rather than exposition, showing the characters' attraction and wariness simultaneously. The piece succeeds in creating atmosphere and tension while staying true to both source materials, though it could have pushed further into the psychological complexity of the standoff situation. + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 90.0
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
I still can't hear wind in the pines without turning my head, and I'm telling you this now, all these years later, because Astrid never did. That October, I'd been in the village for four months and hated every grey day of it. Stockholm felt like a story I'd made up. Astrid was the only person who made the place bearable, and she knew it, and she used it the way fifteen-year-olds use everything—carelessly, and to the hilt. She came for me at half past eleven. I'd left my window unlatched, the way I always did, and she stood under it and threw a pinecone against the glass, once. No light, she'd told me at school, whispering across the desk in the middle of a maths lesson as if that were a normal place to discuss it. No torch, no watch, no jewellery. Nothing with your name on it. And you don't tell them where you're going. "Tell who?" I'd asked. "You'll understand tonight." I understood nothing. I understood that my parents were asleep, that the frost had come early that year, and that I followed her anyway. She met me at the edge of the garden with a small canvas sack, and out of it she produced the things her grandmother had left her: a twist of salt in waxed paper, a lump of iron the size of a knuckle—she said it was from a plough, that it had turned up a grave once and been cold ever since—and a strip of cloth, homespun, unbleached. She tied the cloth around my left wrist without asking. "It's so you can find your way back," she said. "Back from where?" She didn't answer. That was Astrid all over. She'd grown up with a grandmother who spoke to the dead as a matter of household management—*ask your grandfather about the leak in the barn roof*—and Astrid had absorbed it the way other kids absorbed their mothers' recipes. It wasn't religion to her. It wasn't even spooky. It was just how certain things were done, and the fact that I found it terrifying and thrilling in equal parts was, to her, faintly ridiculous. "You don't have to come," she said, but she said it while already walking. We went up through the pine plantation behind the village, off the logging road, along a track I'd never noticed though I'd walked that road a dozen times. The frost made the ground loud under our boots. Astrid kept up a low stream of instructions, matter-of-fact, like a driving instructor. "When we get there, we sit on the flat side. Only the flat side. We sit facing north and we don't turn around, no matter what. If you hear something behind you, it's not for looking at. If you hear your name—" and here she stopped, and I heard her swallow, the first crack in her composure all evening—"you don't answer. Not the first time. Not the second. The third time, you put the salt in your mouth and you say *I was not called*." "Say it in Swedish?" "You say it in whatever comes out of you." The mound sat in a clearing the pines had politely refused to enter, a long low swell of earth with a few boulders breaking through the grass like knuckles through old gloves. Flat side, north. I did the maths on that in my head later, lying awake: the flat side faced away from the village. We would sit with our backs to everything living. We sat. She put the iron between us on the ground. And then, for a long time, nothing happened, which I think was the worst part to write down, all these years later, because it's the part people never believe: how ordinary it was. The cold worked up through my jeans. My nose ran. Astrid's breath smoked. Somewhere an owl, or something that wanted to be an owl. Then the wind came up through the plantation. You have to understand the wind in a northern pine forest. It doesn't gust the way it does down south; it moves in long slow pushes through the crowns, and the needles make a sound like—people say *like the sea*, but that's not it. It's more like voices heard through a wall. A murmur that keeps almost resolving into words. "Grandmother said the mound-talk sounds like weather," Astrid said quietly. "That's how you know. Real voices sound like wind. It's the wind that sounds like voices you have to watch for." "That makes no sense." "Nothing out here makes sense. That's the point of sitting on it. You come to the edge of what makes sense and you sit still, and what's on the other side notices you." I laughed then. I remember laughing, a thin city laugh, the kind that means *I'm fifteen and this is a game and you're my friend and nothing is on the other side of anything.* The wind died. All at once, the way a conversation stops when someone walks into a room. And in the silence, behind us, from the steep side of the mound—the side we were not sitting on, the side we were told not to look at—came a sound like a foot settling on frost-hard ground. Astrid's hand closed on my wrist, over the cloth. Her fingers were colder than the night. "Don't turn," she breathed. "I'm not." "Linnea." A voice, soft, from behind us. Her voice, exactly her voice, doing a very good impression of being casual. "Linnea, look at this." Once. The needles above us shivered and the murmur ran through them, and this time it did resolve, just for a syllable or two, into something that had the shape of my name. Twice. Astrid was shaking. That's the detail I've never settled, in all the years since: Astrid, who knew the rules, who'd been raised on the rules, was shaking as badly as I was. Whatever game she'd brought me out here to play, we had, in that moment, both stopped playing it. Or it had stopped being ours. I put the salt in my mouth. It burned the frost off my lips. I said—I don't know what I said. I remember the words in my head but not the sounds that came out, and Astrid swore to me afterward that I'd said it in a language neither of us knew, and I've chosen not to believe her, because it's easier. We didn't run. She made us walk, backwards, facing the mound, all the way to the treeline, and the wind stayed dead the whole way, and the pines said nothing at all, and the silence was worse than the whispering. At the edge of the plantation she finally turned her back to it, and so did I, and she gripped my hand and said, "It's fine. It was probably just the wind." And I said, "Yes," and we both heard the flaw in it: real wind sounds like wind. That's how you know. I moved back to Stockholm two years later. Astrid stayed. Astrid always stayed. But I'm the one who still wakes sometimes, in my flat, in the city, a hundred kilometres from the nearest pine, with the window open, listening to something that is almost, almost voices. I never took the cloth off my wrist that October. I lost it somewhere in the move. Some nights I think that matters more than I know how to say.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates exceptional craft in the folk horror genre, successfully executing the complex prompt requirements while delivering a genuinely unsettling narrative. The author masterfully employs the framing device of adult Linnea recalling teenage events, creating natural distance and credibility through phrases like "I'm telling you this now, all these years later" and "That's the detail I've never settled." The characterization is particularly strong. Astrid emerges as a compelling figure—neither villain nor innocent guide, but a teenager who has inherited dangerous knowledge and treats it with casual familiarity that makes it more frightening. Her matter-of-fact delivery of supernatural instructions ("You say it in whatever comes out of you") creates authentic tension between mundane adolescence and ancient terror. Linnea's voice as narrator is consistent throughout, balancing her past naivety with present-day understanding. The prose quality is exceptional, with elegant constructions like "a few boulders breaking through the grass like knuckles through old gloves" and "the needles make a sound like voices heard through a wall." The author avoids purple prose while maintaining atmospheric richness. The pacing builds tension methodically, from mundane preparation through mounting dread to the climactic supernatural encounter. The supernatural ambiguity is expertly maintained. The voice calling Linnea's name could be psychological suggestion, but Astrid's genuine fear suggests otherwise. The detail about Linnea speaking in an unknown language is filtered through Astrid's potentially unreliable account, preserving uncertainty. The wind metaphor—"real voices sound like wind. It's the wind that sounds like voices you have to watch for"—creates a brilliant inversion that enhances the uncanny atmosphere. The cultural elements feel authentic rather than appropriated, grounded in specific Swedish geography and folklore. The ritual details (no light, no jewelry, salt, iron, facing north) have the weight of genuine tradition without feeling researched or artificial. The ending achieves genuine horror through understatement. The lost cloth bracelet and Linnea's continued sensitivity to wind sounds suggest lasting supernatural contact without overwrought explanation. The final line carries genuine dread. Minor weaknesses include some exposition that borders on telling rather than showing, particularly in explaining Astrid's background, though this is largely mitigated by the retrospective narrative frame. The piece occasionally approaches being overwrought but generally maintains restraint. + Physical-spatial: Therapeutic Boundaries — Score: 88.4
Prompt:
**"Therapeutic Boundaries"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a former professional athlete undergoing mandatory physical therapy after a career-destroying injury, harboring resentment toward recovery itself. Their physiotherapist is not only unnervingly attractive but also a former training partner from their competitive days who has successfully transitioned to a new career while the protagonist's identity remains shattered. We'll lean into the sexual tension of the scene by having her be attracted to him, but both of them attempting to maintain mental distance while being in physical contact as he shows her stretches & movements & manipulates her body, navigating the thresholds of pain. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—every movement, stretch, and manipulation must be anatomically precise and spatially consistent. Paint an exceptionally vivid sensory picture through detailed attention to pain thresholds, involuntary responses to touch. Capture the suppressed, flaring tension of physical proximity, touch, and the controlled infliction of uncomfortable movements. Physical clarity is essential — readers must understand exactly what is happening with the body during each therapeutic technique. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Therapeutic Boundaries** Recovery is a word people use when they mean surrender. Mara uses it constantly. "Your recovery is on schedule," she says, like the schedule isn't the problem. Six months ago my proximal hamstring tore clean off the ischial tuberosity mid-race — three anchors, a scar along the gluteal fold, a career ended in 2.4 seconds. Mara used to run hurdles beside me at the national center. Now she runs her hands over my ruined leg twice a week and calls it her job. She wears compression sleeves on both forearms — faded galaxy print, teal and magenta, our old club colors. I recognize them. She sees me recognize them. Neither of us says anything. "Supine," she says, and I lie back on the plinth, the paper crinkling under my shoulder blades, and she moves to my right hip, standing close enough that I can smell the alcohol wipe still drying on her palms. She slides her right forearm under my calf, cradling the heel, and lays her left hand flat across my left ASIS — the bony point of my opposite hip — pinning my pelvis to the table so it can't cheat. Then she lifts my straight leg. Slowly. Fifteen degrees, thirty, the hamstring sliding under the scar like a cable pulled taut. At fifty-five degrees the burn starts at the sit bone, deep and precise, a lit match held against the tendon's anchor point. "There," I say. "There," she agrees, and holds it. My quad trembles, an involuntary flutter she can surely feel through her forearm, her sleeve's synthetic fabric rough against my calf. She flexes my foot toward my shin — dorsiflexion — and the burn sharpens, travels. "Nerve or tendon?" she asks. "Tendon," I manage. She nods and lowers the leg three degrees, riding the threshold, keeping me exactly at the edge of what I can stand. Then the 90/90. She flexes my hip until the knee points at the ceiling, both hands wrapped around my thigh to hold it vertical, and begins extending the knee, pressing it toward straight. My right leg stops thirty degrees short of full extension, a wall of heat behind my thigh. She stops there too. Her face is above my knee, focused, professional, her breath audible. I stare at the ceiling tiles and count them. "Contract-relax," she says. "Twenty percent. Push down into my shoulder." She wedges her shoulder under my calf — I feel the patterned sleeve against my skin, the warmth of her through it — and I drive my heel down. The hamstring fires against her resistance, shaking immediately, and she holds me immobile with embarrassing ease. Six seconds. "Exhale," she says. I exhale. "Let go." I let go, and she presses the knee toward straight. We gain five degrees. The burn blooms silver behind my eyes. We do it twice more. My leg is quivering like a struck string, and her hand has migrated to my knee to steady it, her thumb finding the soft spot beside my patella and just — resting there. "Roll prone," she says, and her voice has gone a half-tone flatter. Clinical. I know that voice. I used it myself, back when I had to say something true and couldn't. Face down, I feel her before I see her: her left hand flattens over my sacrum, stabilizing, and her right thumb sinks into the tissue just below my sit bone, strumming across the repaired tendon. The pain is a white line, a seven out of ten, and my whole body flinches before I can stop it. "Seven," I grit out. "Breathe," she says, and doesn't ease off. Her thumb crosses the scar itself and stills there — one second, two — longer than palpation requires. I can feel her notice the error too. Then she's moving again, deep longitudinal strokes along semitendinosus, the muscle releasing in reluctant increments, my fists white-knuckled around the plinth's edge, goosebumps rising in the wake of her thumb and spreading up my flank, completely beyond my control. She sees them. She keeps her eyes on the tendon. "Standing hinge," she says. "Last one." I get up. She stands at my left side, right hand on my iliac crest, left hand flat on my sacrum, and walks me through it: ribs down, pelvis tilting posteriorly under her fingers, hips driving back. I hinge to forty-five degrees and the hamstring lights up, that same precise burn, and I hold it while her hands map my pelvis, correcting the tilt, her fingers splayed across the crest of my hip bone. She's close enough that her breath touches the back of my neck, once, warm. Her face is beside my shoulder. Neither of us moves. The pain and the proximity are braided together so tightly I can't separate them — my body alive in exactly two places, the torn tendon and the six points of her hands, and I hate that I can't tell which one is keeping me standing. "Good," she says, stepping back, and the distance she puts between us is a whole language. "That's the threshold we want. Right at it. Not past it." She writes on her clipboard. The galaxy sleeves, the old colors, the new career. Everything she rebuilt, worn casually on her arms. "Same time Thursday," she says, not looking up. "Can't wait," I say, and mean it in every direction at once.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates exceptional technical mastery and sophisticated narrative control. The author delivers precisely what the prompt demanded: anatomically accurate physical therapy sequences rendered with clinical precision while maintaining intense psychological and sexual tension. The medical terminology is deployed expertly - "proximal hamstring," "ischial tuberosity," "ASIS," "dorsiflexion" - creating authentic professional atmosphere without becoming pedantic. The physical descriptions achieve remarkable clarity. Each therapeutic technique is spatially coherent and anatomically sound, from the supine straight leg raise with pelvic stabilization to the contract-relax PNF stretching to the prone manual therapy. The progression follows logical therapeutic protocols while building dramatic tension through proximity and touch. Character development is economical but deeply effective. The protagonist's resentment toward recovery itself is established immediately with "Recovery is a word people use when they mean surrender." The shared history between protagonist and therapist emerges through subtle details - the galaxy-print compression sleeves in "our old club colors" - rather than exposition. Both characters maintain professional facades while their attraction simmers beneath, creating authentic psychological complexity. The prose style is controlled and precise, matching the clinical setting while allowing sensual undertones. Pain descriptions are particularly vivid: "a lit match held against the tendon's anchor point," "the burn blooms silver behind my eyes." The author skillfully braids physical pain with emotional/sexual tension in the climactic moment: "The pain and the proximity are braided together so tightly I can't separate them." The ending strikes perfect ambiguity. "Can't wait" works on multiple levels - dreading the pain, craving the contact, anticipating progress. No false resolution or transformation occurs; both characters remain trapped in their professional roles while acknowledging the underlying tension. Minor weaknesses include occasional slight overwrought moments and some sentences that could flow more naturally. However, these are minimal compared to the piece's substantial achievements in technical accuracy, emotional complexity, and narrative restraint. + Historical fiction: High Seas and Low Vices — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors. Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit. Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The first lieutenant caught me at the gangway with his folded hands behind his back, the way a man holds a fish he doesn't want to touch. "Dispatches again, Merrick?" "Superintendent's business, Pryce. You know how clerks are. They'll want the tide-tables countersigned in triplicate." "You look yellow about the gills." "The sea air," I said, and coughed into my fist — that cough, deep and wet, leaving the taste of copper on my tongue, like sucking a gun-deck fitting. "Whampoa's a swamp in June." "Mind the air doesn't get the better of you," he said, and let me pass. Ah-Po had her sampan waiting at the stairs, as she always did, as if she kept a calendar of my sins. The river was a brown soup of duck boats and night-soil barges, the air thick with tar, rotting shrimp, and the sweetish reek of the scramble boats hauled up under matting. "Mistah," she said, working the scull, "you go same place, every day, all time. You no go factory today, I think." "Mind your tiller, Ah-Po." "Factory lady no want you," she said, and laughed at the water. "I take you pig street, eh?" "You take me where I pay you to take me." "Same thing," she said. Shek's apothecary sat on a lane behind the pork stalls, where the gutters ran pink and flies made a low church of the eaves. Inside it was cool and smelled of ginseng and snake wine — shelves of dried seahorses, deer horn, jars of things with eyes. Shek was fanning himself with a prescription. "Lieutenant," he said. "You have a cough." "The sea air." "The sea is forty li from here." He set the fan down. "You owe me thirty dollars from the last quarter moon." "I'll have it by evening. I've business at Hog Lane first." "Business." He said the word the way a man handles a coin he suspects is clipped. "Your friends at the factories no longer ask after you. The Scottish gentleman, the American — they say, where is Lieutenant Merrick? I say, I do not know this person." He took a small brass scale from beneath the counter. "Thirty dollars, or no more Patna. My own supplier wants silver, not promises." "By evening, Shek. Before the gates close." "Everyone promises by evening," he said. "Evening is a very generous time of day. It never arrives." Domingos's place in Hog Lane was a slit of shadow between a slop-shop and a shoemaker, run by a Portuguese with a squint and no opinions. Fergus Dun was at the back table, a lean man with red eyelids, agent for the receiving ship *Ariel* out at Lintin. He'd bought me a bottle of Madeira once and spent the evening explaining, with great patience, that opium was simply trade and trade was simply nature. "Merrick," he said. "Sit down before you fall down. You've the complexion of a church candle." "The sea air." "Of course." He poured two glasses without asking. "I hear the *Vigilant*'s boats are going to sweep the river. Some zealous soul at the factory has discovered his conscience, and now we're all to be improved." "I hadn't heard." "No? And you aboard her." He drank and watched me over the rim. "A man with your access, Merrick, could name the night. Name the number of boats. Name who'd be commanding them. A man like that might find himself thirty dollars richer by supper, and no one the wiser." "You're asking me to sell my own ship." "I'm asking you to sell a schedule. Ships get sold every day in this river — hulls, cargoes, crews, occasionally a captain's honour. The market is brisk." He turned his glass a quarter-turn on the table. "The *Ariel* has six hundred chests riding at anchor and a fleet of scrambling dragons waiting to run them up the creeks. One night's warning and the whole parcel slips past your gunboats like eels through a net. You'd not be hurting anyone, Merrick. You'd be helping commerce find its level." "Christ, Dun." "Forty dollars," he said. "I'd go higher, but we both know you'd sell it cheaper. You always do." I told him the date. I told him the boats — six, with a launch from the marine party. I told him Hartley would have the command, and that Hartley trusted his charts and never trusted the fog. Dun counted out the coins on the wet table like a man dealing cards, and when I swept them into my pocket he said, mildly, "You know what's remarkable? You're cheaper than the drug you're buying. The drug at least goes up in price." Shek weighed the dollars one by one, his lips moving. Then he brought the ball from the back room — Patna opium, dark as toffee, wrapped in its scarlet leaves, heavy as a sparrow's heart in my palm. "You cough worse," he observed. "The sea air." "Mm," said Shek. "Forty li away." The house behind the coffin-maker's was quiet by the third hour of the afternoon. The gurgle of pipes came from the bunks like rain in a drainpipe. I lay back on the mat with the spirit lamp beside me, worked the pill over the flame on the needle's point until it swelled and glistened like a beetle's back, and drew it into the bowl. The smoke tasted of scorched sugar and burnt flowers and something older underneath, and my chest opened like a shutter and the cough loosened its grip, and the copper on my tongue turned sweet. The lamp flame stood very still in its glass. Somewhere down the lane a coffin was being planed, the long strokes of it, and I thought: tomorrow I'll stand my watch. I thought it the way a man thinks a phrase in a language he has forgotten — knowing the shape of it, and none of the meaning. The sea air, I told the ceiling. It was the sea air.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and atmospheric writing, successfully creating an immersive portrait of a naval officer's descent into opium addiction in 1830s Canton. The author effectively uses the first-person perspective to create intimacy while maintaining the character's self-deception through his repeated excuse about "the sea air." The dialogue feels authentic to the period and reveals character efficiently. Each conversation serves multiple purposes - advancing the plot, revealing Merrick's deteriorating condition, and building the world of colonial Canton's opium trade. The exchanges with Ah-Po, Shek, and particularly Fergus Dun are well-crafted, with each character having a distinct voice and relationship dynamic with Merrick. The sensory details are particularly strong, from the "brown soup" of the river to the apothecary's smell of "ginseng and snake wine" to the final description of opium smoke tasting like "scorched sugar and burnt flowers." These details create vivid sense of place without feeling forced or overwrought. The structure follows Merrick's degrading day effectively, moving from his lie to escape duty, through his desperate scramble for money, to his betrayal of naval intelligence, and finally to his temporary relief in the opium den. This progression feels natural and inevitable given his addiction. The prose style is controlled and period-appropriate, avoiding modern anachronisms while remaining accessible. Metaphors like "folded hands behind his back, the way a man holds a fish he doesn't want to touch" are fresh and effective. However, the piece occasionally relies on somewhat predictable beats - the corrupt naval officer selling secrets is a familiar trope, and some of the moral degradation feels expected rather than surprising. The ending, while well-executed, doesn't offer particular insight beyond the obvious tragedy of addiction. The character work is solid but not exceptional. Merrick's self-deception is well-portrayed, but we don't get deep psychological complexity beyond his addiction and denial. The supporting characters serve their functions well but remain somewhat archetypal. + Humour: Sisyphus Gives Advice — Score: 87.5
Prompt:
Sisyphus Gives Advice Write a comedic scene in the style of Terry Pratchett featuring Sisyphus, who has started an advice column while continuing his eternal boulder-pushing. Rather than being bitter about his punishment, Sisyphus has developed a comfortably zen emotional intelligence and wisdom from his centuries of repetitive labor. Not in the cliche ways you might expect -- he's actually very grounded, warm & connected with the everyday human plight. He dictates responses to "Crow," his feathered familiar who serves as both scribe and mail carrier. The piece should include Sisyphus thoughtfully answering several advice-seekers' letters about everyday problems (relationship troubles, work-life balance, dealing with difficult people, life purpose doubts) while periodically returning to his boulder-pushing duties. His advice should be surprisingly insightful and practical. The humor should emerge naturally from the messages he receives, from mundane to risque. Sisyphus should genuinely enjoy helping others, finding meaning in this new pursuit while maintaining his boulder routine. The humour should be *understated and not forced*. Contrary to expectation, almost none of his advice involves boulder rolling metaphors (though he does sneak *one* subtle in there), nor a treatise on stoicism. We are also going against the obvious fish-out-of-water trope; in fact, he's surprisingly a natural at this. In all of this , it's important to *show, don't tell*. The format should be largely epistolary, with the occasional interjection for scene setting. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The hill had been Sisyphus's address for some time now, and he kept it tidy. There was a flat stone near the bottom for correspondence, a crevice where Crow nested, and a groove worn into the mountainside so deep you could shelter in it during rain, if you didn't mind the smell of ten thousand years of granite dust. The trick — and Sisyphus had learned many tricks, most of them the hard way — was to do his dictating on the way *down*. The way up was for breathing. "Right," he said, as the boulder settled into its resting place at the summit and began, as it always did, to think about leaving. "Read me the next one." Crow hopped onto the boulder, which was the closest thing to a desk either of them had, and unrolled a letter with one claw. *Dear Sisyphus: My husband has been saying he will fix the roof since before we were married. We have now been married eleven years. Last week I looked up during dinner and saw the moon. — Perplexed of Piraeus.* "Ah," said Sisyphus, starting down the hill after the departing boulder. "Tell her this: 'Dear Perplexed — He is not going to fix the roof. This is not because he doesn't love you. It is because in his mind, the roof is already fixed. Men complete tasks by announcing them. Hire a roofer, pay him from the household money, and when your husband objects — he won't — tell him the roof got tired of waiting too. Also, eleven years of moonlight at dinner is quite romantic. Some couples pay for that.'" Crow took this down in beak-scratches on a slate.¹ *Next letter. Dear Sisyphus: I am a married woman. Last month at the harvest festival I discovered that my neighbour's husband and I share an interest in beekeeping, and also several other things. My husband hates bees. What do I do? — Buzzing in Thebes.* Sisyphus paused, one hand on the boulder, considering. "Tell her: 'Dear Buzzing — You've noticed, I expect, that you spent the whole letter telling me about the beekeeping and none of it about your marriage. That's not nothing. That's data. I'm not here to judge anyone; I once cheated Death twice, and he still sends me a card at midwinter.² But ask yourself what the bees are standing in for. If the answer is *joy*, then the problem isn't the bees, it's that your marriage has a hole where the joy goes, and holes can be patched, though not by anyone who hates bees. If the answer is *escape*, then be honest and get out first, because the worst thing you can do to a man who hates bees is let him find out he's been living in a hive.'" "Very balanced," said Crow. "I've had a lot of time to think," said Sisyphus, "and very little to do with it but this." --- It was around mid-morning — a purely ceremonial term on the hill, since the sun did the same thing every day regardless of anyone's schedule, which Sisyphus found restful — that a small god appeared at the bottom of the slope. He was god of door hinges that squeak at exactly the wrong moment, and he was called Creakus, and he was important in the way that a splinter is important. "You're supposed to be *suffering*," said Creakus, falling into step. It wasn't hard; Sisyphus was moving at the pace of a man who has learned that hurrying is a tax you pay twice. "Am I?" "The punishment is eternal, pointless labour! It's in the writ! I've seen the writ! It's very clear about the futility!" The god had to hop over a loose stone. "This column undermines the whole *tone* of the exercise. It's — it's off-brand." "Mm," said Sisyphus, and gave the boulder a good shove at the tricky bit near the halfway ledge, where it always wanted to drift left. "You could at least look wretched. The other condemned do it properly. Tantalus has a whole *method*." "Tell you what," said Sisyphus pleasantly, as the boulder began its slow roll back down and he fell in behind it. "If the writ says I can't answer my mail, I'll stop. Until then, I've got a letter here from a woman in Corinth whose mother-in-law moved in 'for a fortnight' four years ago, and frankly her problems are more urgent than mine." Creakus hovered, opened his mouth, produced a squeak not unlike his portfolio, and departed in a huff to go afflict a barn door. *Dear Sisyphus: I am a potter. I make forty amphorae a day. My hands are clay to the elbow. My dreams are clay. Last night I dreamt I was an amphora and I was *slightly lopsided*. My wife says I should rest. My foreman says rest is for other, worse potters. Who is right? — Cracked in Corinth.* "Tell him: 'Dear Cracked — Your wife. Your foreman is a man who will say anything to keep forty amphorae a day coming, and one day you will be the man at the wheel who can no longer feel the wheel. Here's a thing I've noticed: nobody on their deathbed says I wish I'd made more pots. They say I wish I'd been home more, or I wish I'd learned the flute, or I wish I'd told Cracked he was a good potter. Tell your foreman the kiln's running fine without him being dramatic about it. And take an afternoon. The clay will still be clay on Thursday.'" Crow scratched it out. "And the mother-in-law one?" "Tell her: 'Dear Besieged — You cannot evict your husband's mother, but you *can* become extremely boring to her. Take up an interest she disapproves of. Weave. Philosophy. Get a small dog. She'll find her own fortnight somewhere else, and your husband will believe it was his idea, which is the only way anything gets done in a marriage.'" --- The last letter came at the top of the hill, at that held-breath moment when the boulder teeters and decides, as it always decides, to come back down. *Dear Sisyphus: Every day I get up, go to my work, come home, sleep, and do it again. I feel like I'm going nowhere. What is the point of a life that just repeats? — Restless of Rhodes.* Sisyphus stood with his shoulder against the stone and looked out over the valley, where the olive trees went silver in the wind, and a hawk was doing something unhurried and perfect in the thermals, and somewhere below, a great many people were getting up, going to their work, coming home, and sleeping. "Tell her: 'Dear Restless — You're asking what the point is, as if the point is somewhere at the top of the hill. It isn't. I've been to the top of a hill or two. There's a nice view and a lot of wind. The point is the hawk you didn't look at this morning because you were busy going nowhere. Nowhere is where everyone lives. The trick is to notice you're there.'" He set his shoulder to it and started down. "Sign it, 'Sisyphus.'" --- ¹ Crows cannot write in the human sense, but they have excellent memories and a strong sense of professional pride, and the letters went out verbatim, which is more than can be said for most scribes. ² He did. It said *Thinking of You*. Death was nothing if not gracious in victory.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of both Terry Pratchett's style and the complex prompt requirements. The author successfully captures Pratchett's distinctive voice through dry wit, footnotes, and observational humor while avoiding forced comedy. The characterization of Sisyphus is particularly well-executed - he's genuinely wise and grounded rather than bitter, and his advice feels earned through experience rather than philosophical posturing. The epistolary format works effectively, with each letter presenting relatable human problems that allow Sisyphus to demonstrate his practical wisdom. His responses are genuinely insightful - the advice about the roof repair, the beekeeping metaphor, and the pottery burnout all feel authentic and useful. The author wisely avoids the obvious boulder metaphors (except for one subtle instance as requested) and doesn't lean into tired stoicism tropes. The prose flows naturally with Pratchett's characteristic rhythm and pacing. Descriptive passages like the hill's geography and the moment of the boulder's decision feel lived-in and authentic. The dialogue between Sisyphus and Crow feels natural, and Crow's personality comes through despite limited lines. The scene with Creakus adds welcome texture and humor while reinforcing that Sisyphus has found genuine purpose in his new role. The final letter about repetitive life provides a perfect thematic capstone without being heavy-handed. The footnotes are perfectly Pratchettesque, adding humor and world-building without disrupting flow. The piece maintains consistent tone throughout and demonstrates genuine emotional intelligence in both Sisyphus's character and his advice. Minor weaknesses include some moments where the wisdom feels slightly too polished, and the piece could have pushed the humor slightly further in places. However, these are minor quibbles with what is otherwise a highly successful execution of a complex creative challenge. + Coming of age: Lost & Found in Osaka — Score: 80.7
Prompt:
Lost & Found in Osaka Slice of Life / Coming-of-Age: First Connection. Write one scene within a larger story set in Osaka, Japan. A shy, introverted teenager & synthesizer nerd, is browsing the electronics district of Den Den Town. She is drawn to the sound of an electric guitar. A girl, slightly older and radiating confidence, is busking near the entrance to a crowded arcade, playing a blistering rendition of a classic anime theme. The scene takes us through their initial awkward interaction, transitioning into a surprisingly easy conversation. The busker, intrigued by the teenager's quiet intensity and knowledge of music, suggests they grab some sushi at a nearby kaitenzushi (conveyor belt sushi) restaurant. Write primarily in dialogue, capturing the distinct voices of the two characters: the teenager's hesitant and -- initially -- awkward speech, and the busker's more outgoing and playful tone. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The afternoon sun carved canyons of shadow between the towering electronics stores of Den Den Town. Mika adjusted the strap of her messenger bag, heavy with a secondhand MIDI interface she’d spent three months’ allowance on. She was hovering outside a shop window displaying vintage Roland modules, mentally calculating the impedance matching required for her setup at home, when the sound sliced through the urban hum. Not just any sound. A guitar. Not the polite, chiming tones usually drifting out of instrument shops, but a furious, precise assault. The notes were familiar, impossibly familiar, and it took her a full eight bars to place the shredded, harmonic-minor reinterpretation of "A Cruel Angel's Thesis." Her feet moved before her brain gave permission. The source was near the entrance to a sprawling arcade, the electronic cacophony of rhythm games and claw machines spilling out behind her. A girl, maybe eighteen or nineteen, stood with a confident width to her stance, fingers dancing over the fretboard with a speed that made Mika’s synapses fire in sympathetic recognition. The busker wore a cropped leather jacket over a band tee, her hair tied back in a high ponytail that swung with the rhythm. A portable amp buzzed at her feet, fed by a battery pack that looked suspiciously cannibalized from an electric scooter. The final note rang out, sustained with a whammy bar dive that simulated the sound of a jet engine. A smattering of applause rose from the arcade-goers clutching crane game plushies. The girl took a theatrical bow, pocketing a few coins. Mika stood frozen, ten feet away, caught between the instinct to flee and the overwhelming urge to ask about her signal chain. The girl straightened up, catching sight of her. "You’re either gonna ask for a request or you’re waiting for me to notice the drool. Which is it?" Mika’s mouth opened. "Your phrasing. In the bridge. You shifted the mode." The girl blinked, then a slow grin spread across her face. "Ah. A scholar." "Sorry. I didn’t mean to—" "You didn’t interrupt. I finished. Big difference." She began winding up her cable, movements efficient. "Most people just hear the ‘wooosh’ at the end. You caught the modal shift?" "The harmonic minor run," Mika said, the words coming out faster now, her filter momentarily offline. "It shouldn’t work over those changes, but the pedal… is that a modified Boss SD-1? The clipping sounds different. Asymmetric?" "Full points." The girl pointed a finger gun at her. "My friend modded it. Swapped the diodes. What’s your poison? You talk like a schematics manual." "I… I don’t play guitar. Mostly synths. Hardware. Analog." "A hardware girl in a software world. I respect that." The girl slung her guitar case over her shoulder, the worn fabric covered in patches from bands Mika had only seen in obscure import catalogues. "Name’s Rin." "Mika." "All this theory is making me hungry, Mika." Rin tilted her head towards the neon-lit street. "Kaitenzushi? There’s a good one around the corner. 100 yen plates. You can tell me why my pedal tone is ‘objectively mid’ or whatever you were thinking." Mika’s social anxiety, a constant hum in her chest like a 60-cycle ground loop, spiked. But the thought of going home to her bedroom studio, alone, after this… this *connection*… felt worse. "I… okay." --- The restaurant was a chaotic symphony of beeping touch screens and the mechanical whir of the conveyor belt. Rin grabbed a booth by the window, dropping her case under the table with a thud. "Grab that salmon. It’s making eyes at you." Mika snatched the plate as it passed, fumbling slightly. Rin had already stacked three plates of tuna and was shoving soy sauce dishes towards her. "So, analog synths," Rin said, chopsticks gesturing. "You mean like, actual knobs? Not just an app on your phone?" "Actual voltage. Oscillators. Filters." Mika took a bite of the salmon, the fat melting on her tongue, grounding her slightly. "The drift. Digital is perfect, but analog… it breathes." "Breathes. I like that." Rin studied her for a moment, a playful glint in her eye. "You walk up to a stranger to talk about modal shifts, then you look like you’re about to dissolve into the booth when I ask your name. You’re a walking contradiction, Mika." Mika stared at her plate. "I just… don’t usually have a lot to say. To people." "But you had a lot to say to me." "You were playing the Evangelion theme. Like… like you meant it. Most people play it ironically." "Nothing ironic about shredding." Rin flagged down a passing plate of ikura, the orange orbs glistening. "You watch stuff? Anime?" Mika nodded, picking up a piece of tamago. "Soundtracks, mostly. I don’t watch the shows as much as I… study the scores." "Okay, hotshot. Best soundtrack. Go." Mika hesitated, the usual fear of being judged for her niche taste bubbling up. But Rin was watching her, not with the polite patience of classmates, but with genuine interest. "Serial Experiments Lain." Rin’s chopsticks froze halfway to her mouth. "The Cyberia Mix?" "The club scenes. The layered, detuned saw waves." Mika’s voice gained a slight heat, the passion overriding the hesitation. "It’s not just music. It’s like… data streams. The way the arpeggios sync with the background animation. It’s perfect." "You have taste." Rin pointed at her with a piece of tuna. "Most people just know the opening theme. I tried to rip off that specific pulsing bass sequence for my band’s demo last month. Failed miserably." "You have a band?" "Garage band. Literally. My garage. We’re called ‘Static Null’." "That’s a good name." "Right? We need a synth player." Rin leaned forward, elbows on the table, a mischievous smile playing on her lips. "You know anyone who breathes analog?" Mika’s heart stuttered. She looked at Rin, at the easy confidence radiating from her, at the guitar case under the table, at the empty plates stacking up between them. The conveyor belt hummed on, carrying its endless loop of possibilities past their booth. "I… might know someone." "Tell them to bring the drift," Rin said, grabbing another plate. "I’ll bring the noise." Mika smiled, small and genuine, into her tea.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and adherence to the prompt requirements. The author successfully creates two distinct character voices - Mika's hesitant, technical speech patterns contrasting effectively with Rin's confident, playful dialogue. The setting of Den Den Town is authentically rendered with specific details about electronics shops, arcade sounds, and the kaitenzushi restaurant atmosphere. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes: establishing character, advancing the relationship, and providing exposition about their shared musical interests. The technical music terminology is woven in organically rather than feeling forced or show-offy. Both characters have clear motivations and distinct personalities that come through in their speech patterns and actions. The pacing works well, moving from the initial encounter through their conversation to the restaurant scene without feeling rushed. The author effectively uses Mika's internal monologue to establish her social anxiety while showing her passion for music overriding her shyness when she finds someone who shares her interests. However, the piece has some minor weaknesses. Certain descriptive passages lean toward purple prose ("The afternoon sun carved canyons of shadow") and some metaphors feel slightly overwrought ("social anxiety, a constant hum in her chest like a 60-cycle ground loop"). The transformation from shy to engaged happens quite quickly, though it's reasonably well-motivated by their shared musical passion. The ending feels earned rather than artificially positive - Mika's gradual warming up to Rin is believable given their connection over music. The technical details about synthesizers and guitar equipment add authenticity without overwhelming the narrative. The piece successfully captures the slice-of-life genre while building toward a meaningful first connection between the characters. + Teen horror: Tick Tock (Goosebumps) — Score: 83.2
Prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style) Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter 3: Ten Seconds Back** The watch arrived in a box with no return address. Okay, that's a lie. It arrived in a box with a return address, but when I Googled it, the address turned out to be a cemetery in Ohio. Which, in hindsight, should have been my first clue. My name is Miles Fenwick, I'm twelve years old, and for four days last month, I was the most powerful kid at Jefferson Middle School. It started in the cafeteria. Derek Boone "accidentally" dumped his chocolate pudding cup on my head, and everyone laughed, and I sat there with pudding dripping off my eyebrows thinking, *I wish I could take back the last ten seconds.* The watch buzzed against my wrist. The screen flickered — just for a second — and instead of the normal watch face, I saw a number: **00:00:10** And then the whole world hiccupped. One second I'm covered in pudding. The next, I'm sitting at my table, my hair clean and dry, and Derek is *just now* reaching for the pudding cup. I watch it happen. I watch it happen and I don't move, and the pudding splats onto the table six inches to my left, because this time I flinched. "Nice reflexes, Fenwick," Derek sneered, but nobody laughed, because there was nothing on my head. I looked down at the watch. The screen flickered again. A countdown, ticking: **00:00:09... 00:00:08...** Then it went back to showing the time, like nothing happened. You'd think a normal person would have thrown the watch in a lake. But you have to understand — I'm twelve. And a twelve-year-old who discovers he can rewind time does not throw *anything* in a lake. I used it on my math test. Rewound ten seconds right before Ms. Patel read out the answers to the warm-up problems, which she did every single morning, out loud, like a maniac. Then I "guessed" perfectly on the actual test. I used it when I tripped in the hallway in front of Priya Nair, who I have liked since fourth grade and who has never once noticed I exist. Rewound. Didn't trip. Played it cool. She said "nice shirt." I nearly died. I used it when my mom asked who broke the garage window. Rewound. It wasn't me that time. It was never me that time. Here's the thing nobody tells you about magic: it always costs something. You just don't find out the price until you've already paid it. It was Priya who noticed first. "Whoa," she said on Thursday. "Did you get taller over the weekend?" I had. Two inches. My mom had to buy me new shoes because my toes were cramping and I'd told her I must have "a growth thing." She'd laughed and said puberty hits some kids like a freight train. Puberty. Right. By Friday, I had to shave. Not, like, a full beard. But there was *hair on my chin* and my voice had dropped so low it came out of my mouth like it belonged to somebody else. An acne breakout exploded across my forehead overnight. My hands looked like baseball gloves. And people started treating me weird. Not bullying-weird. *Different*-weird. The lunch lady gave me the high school portion. A teacher called me "sir." When I walked past a group of eighth graders, one of them nodded at me like I was one of them, and another one said, "Hey, isn't that the freshman who—" "I'm in sixth grade," I said. They stared at me. Then they laughed, because obviously I was joking, because look at me. That night I stood in the bathroom with the door locked and really looked at myself. My face was *longer*. My jaw was heavier. There was a dark shadow along my jawline that no amount of shaving seemed to fix, and — I'm just going to say it — there was hair on my chest. I'm twelve. Twelve-year-olds do not have chest hair. The watch flickered. **00:00:03** Three. Three what? Three *rewinds* left? I'd been keeping count. The pudding. The test. The hallway. Mom. That was four uses, and I'd started with ten, and now— The screen flashed again, and this time it wasn't a countdown. It was a date. My birthday. And a number next to it that made my stomach drop through the floor and keep going: **AGE: 16** Four rewinds. Four years. One year per rewind. I was sixteen years old standing in my parents' bathroom, and my whole body went cold, because I did the math and the math was this: I had three rewinds left, and every single one of them would make me older, and I didn't know if it could go backward, and I didn't know what happened when the countdown hit zero, and— And then my mom knocked. "Miles? You in there? Your brother's game is—" "I'll be right out," I said, in my new freight-train voice. Silence. Then, quieter: "Who is this?" "Mom. It's me." "...Miles?" But she said it like she was *checking*. Like she wasn't sure. Like her own memory had a smudge on it. Here's what I figured out later, standing in the dark of my brother's treehouse, hiding from a house where everyone kept looking at me sideways: every rewind didn't just change *me*. It rewrote the world around the change. And the world had been rewriting me to match. The school records. The yearbook photos on the shelf — I checked, and in every single one, I was taller, older, wrong. The world was catching up to the lie. And when the world catches up to a lie, it doesn't stop halfway. The third-to-last rewind, I used it to save my little brother. Sam ran into the street after his soccer ball. A delivery truck. I didn't even think. The watch buzzed, the world hiccupped, and I grabbed his arm and pulled him back, and he looked up at me and screamed, because a nineteen-year-old stranger had just grabbed him, and I was a nineteen-year-old stranger, and when I got him home my dad asked why I was walking with Sam, and he called me "buddy," and he did not know my name. The timeline shifted with a sound like a zipper. I heard it. I *felt* it. And in the new version of the world, Miles Fenwick had run away four years ago. My own bedroom was a home office now. **AGE: 19**, said the watch. **00:00:02** Two left. One more year off my life to fix anything. And after that, one more. And then zero. So here's my problem, and why I'm writing this down in a treehouse that isn't mine anymore, in a body that doesn't belong to me, with hands that shake like an old man's: I know exactly what I have to do. I have to rewind one more time — back to the cafeteria, back to the pudding, back to the first moment, and *not move*. Let Derek Boone humiliate me. Eat the ten seconds. Stay twelve. But the watch only goes back ten seconds at a time. To get back to that day, I'd have to rewind over and over and over, thousands of times, and every single rewind is a year, and if I'm right about the countdown— The screen flickers. **00:00:02** It's still two. For now. But it's been flickering more often lately. And last night, for just a second, I swear it showed something else. Not a number. A picture. My face. Old. Really old. Smiling. I have two rewinds left to fix everything. I'm just not sure "everything" includes me. *Tick.* *Tick.* *Tick.* --- *To be continued...*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the Goosebumps-style teen horror prompt, successfully incorporating all required elements: a middle schooler with a time-rewinding smartwatch, physical aging consequences, changing social treatment, timeline disruption, and the setup for a final reversal attempt. The author captures the appropriate voice for the genre - conversational, slightly sarcastic, and authentically middle-grade in perspective. The narrative structure is well-crafted, using a retrospective first-person narrator who reveals information strategically. The opening hook with the cemetery return address immediately establishes the supernatural tone, while the progression from small uses (pudding incident) to major consequences (brother's accident) creates effective escalation. Character development is particularly strong for Miles, who feels genuinely twelve in his initial decision-making (using magic for tests and impressing crushes) while showing realistic horror as consequences mount. His voice remains consistent throughout, even as his physical form changes.
