+ Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 85.2
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The darkroom smells like fixer and cold coffee, and under the red safelight Elliot's face looks like something I'd want to photograph—except I can't photograph it, because we're supposed to be photographing *something*, a final project, twenty percent of our grade, and instead I've spent forty minutes watching him hold a print in the developer tray like it's a small animal he's afraid of drowning. "So I've been thinking," he says, and then stops. The enlarger hums behind him. His nails are painted black, chipped, and his rings click against the tray's plastic lip. "This is going to sound like a weird thing to say in a darkroom." "I like weird things said in darkrooms. It's basically a confessional with chemicals." He laughs, quiet, and looks at the print instead of me. "I don't think I'm—like, a guy. Exactly. I don't know what I am. I've been trying on different words and none of them fit yet." His voice drops lower, like he's confessing to shoplifting. "The way I dress, the eyeliner, all of it. It's not a bit. It's me trying to figure out what me is." I should say something supportive and normal. I'm good at supportive and normal. I'm the person who takes charge, who knows what she wants, who has a type—tall, confident, people who walk into rooms like they own the lease. My friends tease me that I've never dated anyone who didn't already have their whole personality assembled, like IKEA furniture, all the parts included. And here's Elliot, nineteen, unassembled, holding himself up to the red light like a contact sheet, asking *which frame is me?* My first instinct is to take over. That's my whole operating system. I want to say, *Okay, let's workshop this, here's a plan, here's vocabulary, I'll drive.* But something in his shoulders—the way he's braced for me to react badly—makes me swallow all of it. "Thank you for telling me," I say instead, and it comes out softer than I planned. "That's a big thing to hand somebody." "I haven't told anyone. At school, I mean." "You picked a darkroom. Good instincts. Low light, no eye contact, plausible deniability." I nudge the print in the tray. "This one's done, by the way. It's going to overdevelop into regret." He fishes it out and I show him the stop bath, and for a while we work in that easy silence that only exists at two a.m., the kind where you stop performing. I'm aware of his arm next to mine. I'm aware that I'm aware of it, which is worse. Here's my confusion, laid out flat like a print in the rinse: I've always liked *definition*. Sharp edges. People who knew exactly what they were. And Elliot is soft in a way I don't have a category for—the thrifted mesh shirt under his flannel, the smudged eyeliner, the way he said *I don't know what I am* like it was an apology. My attraction has a filing system and he doesn't fit in any drawer. It's terrifying and it's also, God help me, the most interested I've been in anyone in two years. Watching someone become themselves in real time turns out to be the best show in town. "I have a question," I say. "You can tell me it's none of my business." "You're going to ask about the eyeliner." "I was going to ask if you want me to actually learn your pronouns or if you're still—he/him for now, whatever you figure out later?" He blinks. "Oh. Yeah. He's fine. For now. That's—" He exhales like he'd been holding it since September. "Nobody's asked it like that. Like it's just logistics." "It is just logistics. The rest is the interesting part." "The rest is the terrifying part." "The terrifying parts are usually the good ones." I'm being too much again. Dial it back, Dani. Give him the wheel. "What do you want to try first? When you figure out the words. Not what you think you should want." He thinks about it, actually thinks, red light pooling in the hollows under his cheekbones. "Skirts, maybe. Longer hair. I found this slip at the thrift store on Fifth and I've bought it twice and returned it twice." "Twice?" "Twice." "Elliot." I lean against the counter. "Buy the slip. Worst case, it's a very comfortable rag." He laughs for real this time, head tipped back, and something in my chest goes sideways. I'm used to being the confident one, the one who moves first and decides for both of us, and I'm realizing I don't want to do that here. I want to watch him decide things. I want to be the room he decides them in. That's when I ruin the paper. I reach over to switch on the enlarger timer and hit the wrong switch—the main lights—and the darkroom detonates into white. Elliot yelps. I kill it in half a second, but the box of photo paper is open on the counter because I'd been mid-pull when he started talking about the slip, and forty sheets of Ilford are now fogged into expensive black rectangles. "Oh no," I say. "Oh no, that's the whole box, that's *forty dollars of*—" "Wait, you made a mistake?" His voice is delighted. "You? The person who color-coded our entire production schedule?" "The red light made the switches look the same, don't—" "You're never letting me live down my blurry test strips and you just flash-fried our entire inventory." "Okay. Fair. I'm demoted. You're in charge of the paper now." "Finally," he says, "a promotion," and we're both laughing, too loud for two a.m., and when it settles he's closer than he was, and neither of us moves away. "We can split the cost of new paper," I say. "Or I'll model for the rest of the project. Free labor. I have excellent bone structure and a very tolerant attitude toward experimental lighting." "You'd do that?" "I'd like that." I mean it in both registers—the project one and the other one, the one I'm still not sure how to name. Whatever I am, someone who likes sharp edges and finished products, I'm apparently also someone who's fallen for a person mid-draft. "For the record, I don't need you to figure out the words to know what I'm looking at." "What are you looking at?" "Someone worth waiting for." I hand him the tongs. "Developer's at ninety seconds. Your turn to drive." He takes them. Under the red light, he smiles like a print coming up in the tray—slowly, then all at once.

Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Stolen Moments in Roma** The near-miss happened at eleven in the morning, in front of the Trevi Fountain, between a man reading a guidebook and a woman who never read anything except the road. Ben Whitfield had been standing precisely where *Rome on Foot* recommended—third column from the left, best light, best angle—when the motorcycle came around the corner like a wasp with a grudge. It missed him by the width of his guidebook. "*Ma sei scemo?*" The rider flipped up her visor, revealing eyes the color of espresso and considerably more caffeinated. "You stand in the street to read about the street? Inglese?" "I'm—terribly sorry. *Mi dispiace. Molto.*" He fumbled the syllables like wet soap. "I should have—*dove si*—where does one *look*—" She killed the engine. Up close, the bike was a scarred little thing, cherry-red, with a long rainbow-colored scrape along the left fairing, dented in some adventure she clearly had no intention of explaining. "That's the worst Italian I've ever heard," she said, switching to English, "and I once heard a German tourist ask a nun for a divorce." "I'm an academic," Ben offered, as though that explained anything. "Ah." She looked him over—corduroy, sensible shoes, guidebook clutched like a life vest. "So you are here to study Rome. Rome does not like being studied. Rome likes being *survived*." She should have ridden off. Instead, she looked at the fountain, at him, at the scrape on her bike, and something mischievous settled into her face like a cat deciding to stay. "I'm Alessandra. Get on." "I beg your pardon?" "You nearly died here today. Very bad luck. The only cure is to go somewhere else. I have no deliveries until two." She tossed him the spare helmet. "You can hold the book while we ride, professore. Consider it fieldwork." --- They ate supplì on a wall in Trastevere at one o'clock, feet dangling over a lane no wider than the bike. Alessandra talked with her hands, which meant she talked constantly and nearly knocked the food off the wall twice. Ben learned that she was Roman the way other people were stubborn, that she'd been a courier since she was nineteen, and that she considered traffic laws "suggestions with paperwork." He also learned, without being told, that she stole things. He watched her pay for the supplì—and then, laughing at something he'd said, casually lift a brass lighter from the counter of the friggitoria, spin it once, and make it vanish into her jacket like a magician's dove. She met his eyes a half-second later, daring him to say something. He opened his mouth. He closed it. "Good," she said, biting into her supplì. "You're learning." "Learning *what*, exactly?" "That some things in Rome," she said, "are not for tourists." --- At three, she took him somewhere no guidebook would ever send him: through a gap in a construction fence, up a rusted service ladder, onto the roof of a shuttered palazzo near Campo de' Fiori. It was trespassing. It was definitely trespassing. "I really don't think—" Ben began, halfway up the ladder. "Then don't think. You do it too much. Come." The roof was a sprawl of broken terracotta and satellite dishes, and the whole city lay beneath them like something spilled and gorgeous. Ben stood very still, breathing hard, his heart doing something arrhythmic that wasn't entirely from the climb. "You are afraid," Alessandra observed, pleased. "A reasonable person would be." "Yes. Very reasonable." She said *reasonable* the way other people said *tax audit*. She walked to the roof's edge without hesitation and sat, legs over the void. "Sit with me, professore. The reasonable view is from the ground. This one is stolen." He sat. His hands were shaking slightly. She noticed, and grinned, and for a moment—just a moment—her expression softened into something he couldn't catalogue, something that didn't fit her mischief at all. "What did the dent come from?" he asked, nodding toward the thought of the bike below. "The rainbow one." Alessandra was quiet for exactly as long as it took to decide not to answer. "A night I don't tell strangers about." "I'm not a stranger anymore. I'm a hostage." She laughed then, loud and unguarded, head thrown back. "*Ostaggio.* Yes. The most polite hostage in Rome." --- By dusk they were at a wine bar in Testaccio, where Ben drank too much and told her about his sabbatical, his research on Renaissance trade routes, his flat in Bath, his ex-fiancée, and his talent for "schedules, mostly." Alessandra stole a sprig of rosemary from a neighboring table's centerpiece and tucked it into his breast pocket like a medal. "You are a man who has never once been late for anything," she said. "Once. 2019. There were floods." "Ben." She said his name for the first time all day, and it landed strangely warm. "Tomorrow you will go back to your fountain and your columns and your book. And you will be *comfortable*." She said it like a diagnosis. "Unless." "Unless?" She didn't answer. She just looked at him over the rim of her glass, and let the word hang there, glowing. --- They parted at the Trevi Fountain at midnight, because of course they did—Rome circles back, Alessandra said, like a dog chasing its own tail. "So," Ben said, hands in his pockets, absurdly reluctant. "Fieldwork concluded." "Concluded." She straddled the dented red bike and looked at him a long moment—the rosemary still in his pocket, the brass lighter, he'd later realize, somehow in his jacket too. "Turn around, professore." "Why?" "Because you're supposed to throw a coin over your shoulder. You haven't. Terrible luck, leaving Rome without throwing. Now turn." He turned. He heard the coin splash. He heard the engine snarl to life. When he turned back, she was already gone into the dark, taillight winking out past the column where they'd met. It was only later, in his hotel room, that Ben reached for his guidebook and found it gone. In its place, tucked into his coat, was a postcard of the Trevi Fountain—clearly lifted from a souvenir stand, price sticker still on it. On the back, in slanted, impatient script: *Stolen. Like your coin, which I threw for you. Like your Tuesday, which you will now give me. Same corner. 10 a.m. Don't bring the book. —A* Ben Whitfield, a man who had never once been spontaneous in his life, stood in the middle of his room, holding a stolen postcard, grinning like a thief. He was, he realized, completely smitten. And somewhere across the city, so was a woman who never gave anything back—except, apparently, once. To an Englishman with terrible Italian and a rosemary sprig in his pocket, which she'd also stolen, and which she had absolutely no intention of telling him she wanted returned.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and creative flair in crafting a contemporary romance set in Rome. The author successfully creates two distinct, compelling characters whose personalities emerge naturally through action and dialogue rather than exposition. Alessandra's kleptomaniac tendencies are woven seamlessly into the narrative without heavy-handed revelation, while Ben's transformation from rigid academic to willing accomplice feels organic and well-paced. The prose style is particularly noteworthy, employing crisp, evocative imagery ("motorcycle came around the corner like a wasp with a grudge") and clever metaphors that enhance rather than overwhelm the narrative. The dialogue crackles with authenticity, capturing both Alessandra's sharp wit and Ben's endearing awkwardness. The author demonstrates excellent control of pacing, moving between intimate moments and broader action sequences with natural rhythm. The structure effectively uses the episodic format requested, with each scene building character development and romantic tension. The theft motif serves as both character trait and plot device, culminating cleverly in the stolen guidebook revelation. The ending strikes an appropriate balance between resolution and anticipation, avoiding saccharine romance clichés while delivering emotional satisfaction. The writing shows sophisticated understanding of "show don't tell" principles, revealing character through behavior and subtext. The cultural clash between the protagonists feels authentic without relying on stereotypes. The author maintains consistent voice throughout while allowing each character's distinct personality to emerge through their speech patterns and actions. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose edges toward being overly clever, and some descriptions that, while beautiful, occasionally slow the narrative momentum. However, these are minor quibbles in an otherwise polished piece that successfully balances literary quality with genre expectations. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 80.0
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The slow shift at The Last Outpost has a rhythm to it, and I know every beat. Hask takes his stool at the far end at nineteen hundred sharp, orders the same thing he always does—algae beer, no head—and complains about the price of fuel. Dreebo slides in twenty minutes later, smelling of engine grease and cheap cigars, and argues with him about it. Old Marta plays cards with whoever's foolish enough to sit at her table. Somewhere around the third hour, a glass breaks, somebody laughs, and I sweep it up while pretending to be annoyed. Tonight starts exactly on script. "Fifty credits a drum," Hask says, shaking his head at me like I set the prices. "Fifty. When I started hauling ore out here, it was twelve." "Everything costs more when you live at the ass end of a spiral galaxy, Hask." I slide his beer across. "You want cheap, move to the Core." "Move to the Core," he mutters. "The Core. The woman's telling me to move to the Core." Dreebo cackles from two stools down. "She's got you there." "She's got nothing. She's got a bar on a rock." "And you're drinking in it," I say sweetly. That's when the door cycles and the stranger comes in. I notice three things at once, because bartending out here teaches you to triage. One: she's not a miner, not a merchant, not anyone I've seen on the dock manifests this month. Two: her tentacled dreads are askew—actually askew, half of them pinned up in a knot like she dressed in a hurry, or in the dark, or in fear. Three: she scans the room before she sits. All of it. Corners, exits, faces. People who scan like that are running from something. I used to scan like that. She plops onto the stool in the middle of my bar—dead center, where she can see both doors—and says, "Vega whisky, neat." A beat. "Better make that a double." "Rough transit?" I ask, reaching for the bottle. "You could say that." I pour. Vega whisky is the good stuff, the only import I splurge on, and I watch her knock back half of it in one motion. She's got a tremor in her hand. Small, but there. "You docking long?" I keep it light. Bar-small-talk light. "Depends." "On?" She looks at me then, really looks, and something in her expression goes sharp and uncertain at the same time. "On how long it takes to say what I came to say." Behind us, Marta's table erupts in laughter and there's a bright, tinkling crash—one of my glasses, gone to pieces on the floor. Dreebo's cackling, Marta's swearing in three languages, and I make a show of rolling my eyes. "I'll get the broom," I call over. "Leave it!" Marta bellows. "I'll clean it. My fault, my mess." I turn back to the stranger. She's watching me in the mirror behind the bottles, the way you watch someone when you already know the answer to the question you're about to ask. "You're Nettle," she says quietly. "Nets. The bartender." "Most people just call me the bartender." "Most people don't know your name." She finishes the whisky and pushes the empty glass toward me like a chess move. "Most people don't know you used to have a different one." The bar noise goes distant, like someone turned the whole room down. Hask is still griping about fuel. Dreebo is still arguing. Nothing has changed except everything. "You've got me confused with somebody," I say. My voice comes out level. I'm almost proud of it. "Rill." She says it softly, just for me. Just a name. A name I haven't heard spoken aloud in four years. "I'm not confused." I set the bottle down. My hands are steadier than hers, but not by much anymore. "Who told you that name?" "Rill told me that name. Before—" She stops. Her dreads shift as she glances at the door, then back to me. "Before they took him." The floor of my bar has never felt thinner. Underneath it is rock, and underneath the rock is vacuum, and right now I understand exactly how little there is between me and falling. "Took him where?" I hear myself ask. "That's the thing." She laughs, and it's an awful sound, nothing in it. "Nobody knows. That's why I'm here. He gave me coordinates. A contact. Said if anything happened, find the bartender on the Last Outpost. Find Nets." She taps the bar twice with one finger. "You." "Whatever Rill was into, I got out of. Years ago. I'm a bartender. I pour drinks and break up fights over card games. That's the whole job." "You think I didn't say that to myself the whole way here?" Her voice cracks. She pulls it back together, but I can see the cost of it. "I run cargo. He was my navigator. He was my *friend*. And three weeks ago a customs cutter flagged us, and he told me to run, and I ran, and I've been running ever since, and I keep thinking somebody's going to come out of the dark behind me and there never is, which is somehow worse." I pour her another double without being asked. My hands do it on their own. "Why me?" I say. "He knew where I was. He could've sent a message. Anything." "He said messages get read." She leans in. "He said the only person in the galaxy he trusted to hand-deliver something is a woman who doesn't exist anymore." She reaches into her jacket, slow, careful, the way you move when you don't want anyone to think you're reaching for a weapon. She sets something on the bar between us: a small black case, no bigger than a matchbox, humming faintly against the wood. "He said you'd know what it is. And he said—" her voice drops, "—he said don't let them follow you here." "Them." My mouth is dry. "Who's them?" "I don't have a name. Cutter crew had no registry. Black hull, no markings." She looks at the door again. "But I've been sitting here twenty minutes, Nets, and I've docked at a lot of stations in my life, and I've never felt a place go quiet like this one just did." I don't want to look. I look anyway. Through the viewport over the door, out past the landing lights, a ship is easing into the far berth. Black hull. No markings. The stranger's glass sits empty between us. Nobody says anything for a long moment. "So," she says. "How's your night been?" The slow shift at The Last Outpost has a rhythm to it, and I know every beat. Hask takes his stool at the far end at nineteen hundred sharp, orders the same thing he always does—algae beer, no head—and complains about the price of fuel. Dreebo slides in twenty minutes later, smelling of engine grease and cheap cigars, and argues with him about it. Old Marta plays cards with whoever's foolish enough to sit at her table. Somewhere around the third hour, a glass breaks, somebody laughs, and I sweep it up while pretending to be annoyed. Tonight starts exactly on script. "Fifty credits a drum," Hask says, shaking his head at me like I set the prices. "Fifty. When I started hauling ore out here, it was twelve." "Everything costs more when you live at the ass end of a spiral galaxy, Hask." I slide his beer across. "You want cheap, move to the Core." "Move to the Core," he mutters. "The Core. The woman's telling me to move to the Core." Dreebo cackles from two stools down. "She's got you there." "She's got nothing. She's got a bar on a rock." "And you're drinking in it," I say sweetly. That's when the door cycles and the stranger comes in. I notice three things at once, because bartending out here teaches you to triage. One: she's not a miner, not a merchant, not anyone I've seen on the dock manifests this month. Two: her tentacled dreads are askew—actually askew, half of them pinned up in a knot like she dressed in a hurry, or in the dark, or in fear. Three: she scans the room before she sits. All of it. Corners, exits, faces. People who scan like that are running from something. I used to scan like that. She plops onto the stool in the middle of my bar—dead center, where she can see both doors—and says, "Vega whisky, neat." A beat. "Better make that a double." "Rough transit?" I ask, reaching for the bottle. "You could say that." I pour. Vega whisky is the good stuff, the only import I splurge on, and I watch her knock back half of it in one motion. She's got a tremor in her hand. Small, but there. "You docking long?" I keep it light. Bar-small-talk light. "Depends." "On?" She looks at me then, really looks, and something in her expression goes sharp and uncertain at the same time. "On how long it takes to say what I came to say." Behind us, Marta's table erupts in laughter and there's a bright, tinkling crash—one of my glasses, gone to pieces on the floor. Dreebo's cackling, Marta's swearing in three languages, and I make a show of rolling my eyes. "I'll get the broom," I call over. "Leave it!" Marta bellows. "I'll clean it. My fault, my mess." I turn back to the stranger. She's watching me in the mirror behind the bottles, the way you watch someone when you already know the answer to the question you're about to ask. "You're Nettle," she says quietly. "Nets. The bartender." "Most people just call me the bartender." "Most people don't know your name." She finishes the whisky and pushes the empty glass toward me like a chess move. "Most people don't know you used to have a different one." The bar noise goes distant, like someone turned the whole room down. Hask is still griping about fuel. Dreebo is still arguing. Nothing has changed except everything. "You've got me confused with somebody," I say. My voice comes out level. I'm almost proud of it. "Rill." She says it softly, just for me. Just a name. A name I haven't heard spoken aloud in four years. "I'm not confused." I set the bottle down. My hands are steadier than hers, but not by much anymore. "Who told you that name?" "Rill told me that name. Before—" She stops. Her dreads shift as she glances at the door, then back to me. "Before they took him." The floor of my bar has never felt thinner. Underneath it is rock, and underneath the rock is vacuum, and right now I understand exactly how little there is between me and falling. "Took him where?" I hear myself ask. "That's the thing." She laughs, and it's an awful sound, nothing in it. "Nobody knows. That's why I'm here. He gave me coordinates. A contact. Said if anything happened, find the bartender on the Last Outpost. Find Nets." She taps the bar twice with one finger. "You." "Whatever Rill was into, I got out of. Years ago. I'm a bartender. I pour drinks and break up fights over card games. That's the whole job." "You think I didn't say that to myself the whole way here?" Her voice cracks. She pulls it back together, but I can see the cost of it. "I run cargo. He was my navigator. He was my *friend*. And three weeks ago a customs cutter flagged us, and he told me to run, and I ran, and I've been running ever since, and I keep thinking somebody's going to come out of the dark behind me and there never is, which is somehow worse." I pour her another double without being asked. My hands do it on their own. "Why me?" I say. "He knew where I was. He could've sent a message. Anything." "He said messages get read." She leans in. "He said the only person in the galaxy he trusted to hand-deliver something is a woman who doesn't exist anymore." She reaches into her jacket, slow, careful, the way you move when you don't want anyone to think you're reaching for a weapon. She sets something on the bar between us: a small black case, no bigger than a matchbox, humming faintly against the wood. "He said you'd know what it is. And he said—" her voice drops, "—he said don't let them follow you here." "Them." My mouth is dry. "Who's them?" "I don't have a name. Cutter crew had no registry. Black hull, no markings." She looks at the door again. "But I've been sitting here twenty minutes, Nets, and I've docked at a lot of stations in my life, and I've never felt a place go quiet like this one just did." I don't want to look. I look anyway. Through the viewport over the door, out past the landing lights, a ship is easing into the far berth. Black hull. No markings. The stranger's glass sits empty between us. Nobody says anything for a long moment. "So," she says. "How's your night been?"

+ Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Gone South — Chapter Two: Powdered Sugar** The trucker's taillights disappear around the corner and I stand there on Royal Street with my backpack straps digging into my shoulders, thinking: *this is the dumbest thing I have ever done, and I once lit a firework in Coach Pruitt's mailbox.* That was past tense. Everything before this moment feels like past tense now. Present tense: New Orleans smells like sugar, piss, and old water. The heat sits on my chest like a cat that's decided I'm furniture. And somewhere behind me, a saxophone is playing something slow and slurred, the musical equivalent of a shrug, like the guy playing it knows exactly how stupid my life is and finds it funny. I have sixty-three dollars and a Ziploc bag of granola bars Mom doesn't know is missing. I have a phone at 41% that I already turned to airplane mode, because airplane mode means nobody can find me, right? That's how airplanes work. Probably. The sax pulls me down the block like a leash. I don't fight it. The player is an old Black man with a Saints cap, eyes closed, and the crowd around him is doing that thing crowds do here — just *flowing*, everyone moving and nobody going anywhere. I stop in the shade of a balcony dripping with green plastic beads and I listen, and for about forty seconds I forget that my mother called me a phase. Her exact words. "This is a phase, and I am *exhausted* by it." Like I'm a fad diet she tried in 2009. "You've got that just-got-here look." The voice belongs to a girl leaning on the wall next to me, maybe seventeen, eating something out of a paper bag that's bleeding powdered sugar. She's got a shaved head, a sunburn peeling on her nose, and a duffel bag that looks like it lost a fight with a lawnmower. "What look," I say. Not a question. Questions invite conversation. I know better. I've been "concerning behavioral patterns" since fourth grade. "The look," she says, "of somebody standing in the shade going *oh no*." She holds out the bag. "Beignet? Guy at the market gave me the end-of-day batch. They're only mostly stale." My stomach makes a decision before my brain does. I take one. It's like eating a donut that went to art school. "I'm Saint," she says. "Like the football team?" "Like everybody out here gets a new name and that's mine." She watches me chew. "What's yours?" And here's the thing. Here's the whole entire thing. I've said it exactly once out loud, in the kitchen, two days ago, and it got turned into a *phase* before it finished leaving my mouth. My whole life is a name nobody's let me have yet. "Taylor," I say. Saint squints. "That your real name or your street name?" "Real one. First time I've said it where somebody didn't interrupt." She nods like this is normal, like people tell her this stuff every day, and maybe they do. "Then it's your street name too, Taylor. Out here you get to pick. That's like the one rule that's actually a rule." She pushes off the wall. "The rest of the rules are: don't take anything free from a man named Uncle Ray, don't sleep in Louis Armstrong Park after dark, and don't tell anybody where you keep your money." She points her chin at my backpack. "Which pocket?" "None of your business." "See, you're a natural." We walk. I don't know why I walk with her. That's a lie — I know exactly why. Because the alternative is standing on Royal Street until dark, alone, in a city where my entire support network is a saxophone player who doesn't know I exist. Saint talks with her whole body, narrating the Quarter like a tour guide for people with no money: *that's the good water fountain, that's the bathroom that doesn't lock, that church hands out sandwiches on Thursdays, that guy right there will tell you he's got work for you and the work is not work.* The guy she's pointing at is maybe forty, clean shirt, too-nice smile, posted up by the fence like a spider that learned to wear cologne. He waves at Saint. She doesn't wave back. She also — and I only catch it because I've spent sixteen years watching people's faces for early warning signs — stops breathing for a second when she sees him. Interesting. So Saint has rules for herself she's not telling me either. Her phone buzzes in her pocket. Fourth time in an hour. She silences it without looking, jaw tight. "Boyfriend?" I ask. "Baton Rouge," she says, which is not an answer, and also — "Didn't you say you were from Lafayette?" "No." Beat. "I said Baton Rouge." She said Lafayette. Outside the sandwich church, twenty minutes ago, a whole story about a crawfish boil in Lafayette. I don't call her on it. I'm carrying a phone in airplane mode and a name my own mother won't use; I understand that everyone out here is running from a story they keep telling wrong on purpose. We end up on the riverfront as the light goes orange, sharing her second bag of beignets, powdered sugar on our fingers like we're eight years old. The river is huge and brown and indifferent, which I find comforting. Back home the biggest body of water is a creek that once ate a golf cart. "So," Saint says. "You got a plan, Taylor from Nowhere?" "I have sixty-three dollars and a plan to get more dollars." "Bold. Detailed." She brushes sugar off her knees. "Look. There's a spot under the Claiborne bridge, couple of us, it's not *safe* safe but nobody's bothered us yet. You can come, or you can not. I'm not being nice, I'm being practical. Somebody watching your back means somebody watching *my* back." Every alarm I own goes off at once. This is the part in the after-school special where I get trafficked. This is also the part where I sleep on a riverbank alone with sixty-three dollars, and I've done the math on that, and the math is bad. "Practical," I say. "Sure." "Cool. Walk behind me, not beside me. Looks less like we're together." Way ahead of you, I think, and follow her anyway. Somewhere back on Royal the sax is still going, that same slow shrug of a melody, and I realize I've been humming it for three blocks. First day. New name, said out loud, and nobody interrupted. Tomorrow I figure out the rest. Tonight I just keep walking.

[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and authentic voice work. The author successfully captures Taylor's perspective as a transgender teen runaway with a distinctive narrative voice that blends vulnerability with defensive wit. The mixed tense approach works effectively, creating temporal layers that reflect Taylor's psychological state of being caught between past trauma and uncertain future. The characterization is particularly strong. Taylor feels genuinely sixteen - simultaneously naive and street-smart, making impulsive decisions while maintaining sharp observational skills. The internal monologue authentically captures adolescent thought patterns, mixing profound insights with mundane concerns. Saint emerges as a compelling secondary character with her own mysteries and contradictions, avoiding the trap of being merely a plot device. The dialogue crackles with authenticity. Conversations feel natural and reveal character efficiently - Saint's casual wisdom about street rules, her deflection when caught in inconsistencies, and Taylor's guarded responses all ring true. The author avoids exposition dumps, instead weaving necessary information through organic interactions. The New Orleans setting is rendered with sensory specificity without falling into tourist-brochure clichés. Details like "sugar, piss, and old water" and the saxophone as "the musical equivalent of a shrug" create atmosphere while serving the narrative's emotional landscape. The prose style is confident and distinctive. Metaphors feel fresh ("heat sits on my chest like a cat that's decided I'm furniture") and the rhythm varies effectively between short, punchy observations and longer, flowing passages. The author demonstrates restraint, avoiding overwrought emotional manipulation while still creating genuine pathos. However, some elements feel slightly convenient - Saint appearing exactly when needed with exactly the right knowledge and resources. The pacing occasionally rushes through potentially deeper moments, particularly around Taylor's processing of family rejection. While the chapter establishes mood and character well, the plot advancement feels somewhat predictable in its beats. The emotional complexity is well-handled, showing Taylor's conflicted feelings about trust, safety, and identity without resolving them neatly. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - neither falsely optimistic nor gratuitously dark, but realistically uncertain. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 85.2
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# My Apocalypse Buddy The end of the world, Midas had concluded some years ago, was less an event and more a lifestyle. It came with a dress code (tattered), a cuisine (canned), and a roommate (furry, battery-operated, and insufferable before his morning charge). "I'm just saying," said Chewy, "that statistically speaking, we are going to starve." "You don't eat." "I contain multitudes. One of them is hungry." Midas looked out over their home base — a toppled water tower on its side like a drunk tin of beans — and considered their predicament. The predicament was this: three cans left, one of them labeled only MEAT*, and winter coming down from the hills with its usual lack of diplomacy. Then he considered the graffiti. They'd found it two days ago, scrawled across a dead bus shelter in letters that had once been artistic and were now merely urgent: **THE GARDEN IS REAL. PAST THE TEETH OF THE CITY. BRING NOTHING. KNOCK THRICE.** "Past the teeth of the city," Midas said, for the fortieth time. "The dental college," said Chewy. "The one with the giant tooth on the sign. I've been saying this for two days. My file corruption can't explain why you don't listen." "Refuges don't exist. Every 'sanctuary' we've found has been a raccoon nest or a cult." "Or both. Wonderful days, those." Chewy's servos whirred in a way that, in a creature with eyebrows, would have been an eyebrow. "But a garden, Midas. A *garden*. Seeds. Green things. Things that make more things, which is the entire economic philosophy of the old world in one sentence." And that was how, at noon, they set off toward the giant tooth. --- The mission began going sideways approximately eleven minutes in, which was a personal record; Midas's usual record was seven. First there were the Teeth People — not a cult, exactly, more of a club with opinions — who had claimed the dental college as sacred ground and demanded a toll. Midas had nothing to offer except the MEAT can, and a short negotiation established that the Teeth People were more interested in Chewy. "Pre-Collapse animatronic," said their leader, eyes gleaming with the specific gleam of a man who has just found something he can unscrew and sell. "Servos alone would feed us for a month." "Chewy is not for sale." "Everything is for sale. That's what collapse means." "It's the collapse of *markets*," said Chewy, "if anything," which was not helpful, and there followed a scuffle in which Midas employed the ancient martial art of Running Away While Holding Something, and Chewy employed the equally ancient art of Biting, which his zoo programming had never authorized but which his spirit had clearly always wanted. They escaped through the college's collapsed atrium, past forty porcelain training jaws grinning at nothing, and out the far side — where, to their mutual astonishment, the graffiti's promise held. There *was* a garden. Walled, guarded by green, breathing, actual *growing* things, behind a door of riveted steel. Midas, bleeding modestly and in several tasteful locations, remembered the second instruction. He set down his pack. He put the remaining cans on the ground. He raised his fists to knock thrice. The door opened first. A woman stood there, holding a shotgun in the manner of someone who has thought carefully about where to point it. Behind her, Midas could see rows of vegetables standing at attention, and perhaps twenty people with the tanned, wary look of those who eat well and trust nobody. "You brought nothing," she said. "Nothing," Midas agreed. "You brought *him*." The shotgun indicated Chewy. "He's not a thing. He's a—" "Machine. Metal. Plastic. Old-world poison." She smiled, and it was the smile of someone who would compost you and consider it a moral act. "The rule is bring nothing. Machines are what *got* us here. Bring him inside for dismantling, or bring yourself back never." Now, Midas had faced starvation, cults, weather, and on one memorable occasion a badger with ambitions, and in each case his instinct for self-preservation had arrived promptly and been shouted down by his instinct for trouble. He scooped up Chewy under one arm, grabbed the nearest thing off the ground — a fistful of pea vines, ripping them up by the roots, which produced a sound from the woman like a kettle achieving enlightenment — and ran. What followed was not, strictly speaking, an escape plan. It was a sequence of poor decisions at speed: through the potato rows, over the compost heap (which had opinions), into the goat enclosure, where Midas had the presence of mind to open the gate behind him so the goats would share their opinions with everyone. Goats, it turns out, are nature's anarchists. The garden's defenders, discovering their sanctuary suddenly full of screaming brassicas and triumphant livestock, did not pursue far. --- They returned home in several ways. They returned *physically*, at dusk, limping, bitten by goats, compost-stained, and — in Midas's case — wearing a potato that had lodged itself somewhere personal during the fence vault and which he chose, in the end, to regard as cargo rather than injury. They returned *philosophically*, having confirmed that every promised paradise comes with a door policy, and that the words BRING NOTHING are written by people who mean *bring nothing I disapprove of*, which is to say by people. And Chewy returned *mechanically altered*, because somewhere in the scuffle his zoo programming had crossed wires with something older and stranger, and now, at unpredictable intervals, he said things like *please keep your bread dough in a warm place until doubled in size* in the voice of a very calm, very dead corporation. Midas found this deeply unsettling. He also found it useful, because folded inside Chewy's chest panel, where the Teeth People had been fumbling, was a seed packet the woman had dropped — tomatoes, a whole varietal, a small paper envelope of the future. They ate the MEAT can that night† and planted the seeds in an old helmet by the door of the water tower. "Statistically speaking," said Chewy, watching the dirt, "we are going to starve." "Statistically speaking," said Midas, "the world ended. And yet." The koala's eyes glowed faintly in the dark, the way they had glowed since a forgotten before-time, over gift shops and strollers and a species that had loved things that weren't real and made them real anyway. "Welcome to the San Diego Zoo," Chewy said softly, to no one. "Please don't feed the animals." Outside, winter came on. Inside, something was going to grow. --- \* Not a brand. An assertion. † It was, in defiance of all hope, meat. This was widely considered the day's greatest tragedy, as it removed all grounds for complaint.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, capturing his dry wit, philosophical asides, and footnote humor effectively. The author successfully creates a post-apocalyptic world that feels both bleak and absurdly comedic, maintaining the required tone throughout. The story structure follows the prompt precisely: deliberation about the mission, inevitable complications, and return home "worse for wear." The characterization is particularly strong - Midas as the hapless protagonist with a talent for trouble, and Chewy as the sardonic animatronic koala with glitching programming that adds both humor and pathos. The dialogue crackles with Pratchettesque wit ("I contain multitudes. One of them is hungry") and the narrative voice maintains consistent dryness while delivering genuine insights about human nature and survival. The world-building is economical but vivid - the toppled water tower home base, the Teeth People cult, and the garden sanctuary all feel lived-in and believable. The mission's progression feels organic rather than forced. Each complication (the Teeth People, the garden's anti-technology stance, the goat chaos) escalates naturally from character decisions rather than arbitrary plot devices. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - they've gained something (seeds) but lost something (Chewy's further deterioration), avoiding unearned optimism. The prose demonstrates genuine elegance in places ("winter coming down from the hills with its usual lack of diplomacy") while maintaining accessibility. The footnotes are perfectly deployed Pratchett pastiche. Some minor weaknesses include occasional over-explanation of jokes and a few moments where the Pratchett imitation becomes slightly self-conscious, but these don't significantly detract from the overall achievement. The piece succeeds in being both entertaining and subtly moving, particularly in its treatment of the relationship between Midas and Chewy, and the final image of planting seeds despite statistical doom captures the resilient absurdity that defines good post-apocalyptic fiction. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter Three: The Shop at the End of the High Street** The bell above the door of Siop Llyfrau Tŷ'r Dderw gave a bright, indifferent jangle, and a man came through it backwards, one hand holding the door ajar as he scanned the street through the rain-streaked glass. "You're letting the weather in," said the woman behind the counter, without looking up from her ledger. "Thirty seconds." He shut the door. "There are men out there with cameras. Long lenses. Like herons, but with less dignity." "Heron with cameras," she repeated, in the tone of someone confirming an order. "That's a new one." He pulled off his cap, and there it was—the face that had sold roughly nine hundred million cinema tickets. Rhys Bevan. Two franchises, one Oscar nomination, a perfume deal he'd been trying to live down for six years. He gave her the smile, the *good* one, the one that had made a Late Night host cry actual tears. "Do you mind if I hide here a bit? Just till they get bored. They've got the attention span of—well, of me, honestly, so it won't be long." She looked at him properly for the first time. Grey cardigan, reading glasses pushed up into dark hair, a mug of tea with a Welsh dragon on it that had faded to something closer to a Welsh gecko. "Do you mind if I keep doing my accounts?" she said. "It's you they're after, not me." "Right. Yes. Obviously." He blinked. People did not usually say *obviously* to him. People usually said *oh my God.* "I'm Rhys, by the way." "Carys." "You don't—no, you don't know who I am." "Should I?" "No! God, no, that's—" He laughed, and it came out slightly higher than he'd planned. "That's refreshing, actually. Most people at least pretend. There's usually a gasp. Once, in Osaka, a woman fainted, which was flattering until I realised she'd just been standing in the sun for four hours." "Mm," said Carys, and carried a two. Rhys wandered, because wandering was what he did when a room wasn't orbiting him. He picked up a paperback, put it back, picked up another. His fingers were doing the thing they did at parties—touching everything, looking for purchase. "You're from here," he said. "Llanfeurig. The accent. I'm from Ebbw Vale myself, originally. Left when I was nineteen." "Everyone leaves," Carys said, mild as milk. "It's practically the town motto. It's on the sign, under the Welsh. *Welcome to Llanfeurig. Everyone Leaves.*" "That's a bit bleak." "It's a bit true." He grinned despite himself. "You know, I've done three press tours where I've charmed entire nations, and I've been in this shop four minutes and I'm losing ground. What's your secret?" "Nothing secret about it. I just don't much care for people who walk into shops and touch every book like they're fruit at a market." He put the book down so fast it was almost a salute. "Understood. Hands where you can see them." "Diolch." "*Diolch*," he returned, in Welsh, watching her face for the flicker. There. Tiny, but there—a small softening at the corner of her mouth, gone almost before it arrived. He felt absurdly pleased with himself, the way you feel finding a tenner in an old coat. "Don't look so smug," Carys said. "Half the county speaks Welsh. You're not special here." "I'm not special anywhere," he said, and heard the joke land wrong—too true, too quick—and heard himself rush to fill the silence after it. "That's—forget that. That came out wrong. I'm very special, ask anyone, they've done studies." Carys looked up over her glasses. And Rhys Bevan, who had once talked his way out of a Moroccan jail cell, discovered he could not, for the life of him, read this woman's face. "Can I ask you something?" he said. "Honestly." "You've been asking me things since you came in." "Why aren't you—look, I'll just say it. I'm usually better at this. People like me. It's sort of my whole thing, it's the *job*, I make people like me, and I'm quite good at it, and you're standing there doing long division like I'm the man come to read the meter." Carys set her pen down. For a moment he thought he'd genuinely offended her, and something in his chest went cold and hollow, because that was the thing, that was always the thing— "My father," she said, "was a slate man. When the quarry closed, he was fifty-four and he'd never once in his life been out of Gwynedd. He was terrified of the ferry to Ireland. Terrified. Wouldn't cross water, wouldn't get on a train south of Machynlleth. He died without ever seeing London, and I promised myself I'd never be afraid of a thing as small as another person." She shrugged. "So I'm not. Frightened of you, I mean. You're just a man in a wet coat." Rhys stood very still among the paperbacks. "That's the most honest thing anyone's said to me in about four years," he said finally. "And you said it about you, and it still somehow made me feel like the interesting one. How did you do that?" "Practice. I run a bookshop. People come in here having revelations all day. You get good at holding the ladder." He laughed then, a real one, unguarded, and Carys found—entirely against her will, and with some alarm—that she was laughing too, and that her pulse had been doing something unprofessional for several minutes now, and that she was very glad of the counter between them, because her hands were not to be trusted. "Can I tell you something equally honest?" he said. "Since we're doing that." "If you must." "My father never came to a single premiere. Not one. I sent tickets, I sent a car, I sent—once I sent the plane, and he said, *don't get above yourself, Rhys.* That was it. So now, every film I make, I read every review. Every one. Even the Portuguese ones, I run them through a translator at three in the morning. Because if a stranger in Lisbon likes me, then maybe—" He stopped. Cleared his throat. "Anyway. That's why the herons. That's why I need everyone to like me. It's not a good feature. It's a hole." The rain had gone soft against the window. Outside, a long lens had drifted off toward the chip shop like a bored dog. "They've gone," Carys said quietly. "Right. Yes." He didn't move. "Do you—look, this is mad, but is there any chance this shop needs, I don't know. A famous customer. Tuesdays, maybe. Tuesdays are quiet." "Tuesdays are quiet because nobody comes." "Exactly. Perfect. I'll be the nobody." Carys looked at him for a long moment—wet coat, ridiculous smile, hole and all—and thought, *oh, no. Oh, no, no.* "Tuesday," she said. "We open at nine. Don't be above yourself." "I wouldn't dream of it," said Rhys Bevan, and walked out into the rain grinning like a man who'd just found the tenner in the coat.

Rhys is convincingly portrayed as someone whose charm is both genuine and desperate - his need for validation comes through in natural ways, from his compulsive touching of books to his late-night review reading. Carys is effectively written as someone who appears unimpressed while actually being affected, shown through subtle physical cues and her eventual agreement to see him again. The dialogue carries the scene effectively, with distinct voices for each character. Rhys speaks with the practiced charm of someone used to performing, while Carys has a dry, understated Welsh sensibility. Their exchanges feel natural and reveal character efficiently. The writing avoids purple prose while maintaining literary quality. The pacing builds tension appropriately through their verbal sparring. However, there are some minor weaknesses. The emotional complexity is well-developed - both characters have believable vulnerabilities that drive their attraction. Rhys's father issues and Carys's determination not to be intimidated create authentic psychological depth. The chemistry builds convincingly through their conversation. The piece succeeds in creating genuine romantic tension while avoiding clichés. The Welsh setting feels authentic rather than decorative, and the class/fame dynamics add realistic complexity to their interaction. Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The door gave way with a groan of swollen oak, and the underhold breathed out at them — a long, cold exhalation that smelled of whale oil, brine, and something older beneath both. Whalebone ribs arched overhead, scrimshawed with the names of dead ships and deader men, and between them hung lamps of ambergris that burned a sickly gold. At the far end, behind a vault door studded with cold-iron sigils, waited the Scythan artifact. Aya counted the steps to it out of habit. Twenty-two. Perhaps twenty-three if the shadows lied. The shadows were lying about something else entirely. "Shut the door behind you, dearies," said a voice from the dark. "Draughts give me the rheumatics." Lamps flared along the bone-ribbed walls, and there, enthroned upon a chair built from a leviathan's vertebrae, sat Yeva Morska. Not swinging from an Admiralty gibbet. Not rotting in a magistrate's cell on the Strand. Alive, upholstered in black silk, her grey hair coiled like a nest of eels, a scrimshaw cane across her knees. Behind her stood two men — one flesh, one mostly brass, the clockwork one ticking softly in the silence, its harpoon-rifle levelled at Simeon's chest with a patience no living thing could counterfeit. *The raid. The arrest. All of it theatre,* Aya thought, and her stomach dropped like a gutted whale sinking. *She fed her own arrest to the broadsheets to see which of her children would come crawling toward the vault.* "Evening, Mother Morska," Simeon said carefully, hands already open at his sides. "You're looking remarkably well preserved." "Pickling, Simeon. It's the secret." Yeva's smile was a knife pulled from a sheath of wrinkles. "Katra, love — don't. You'll embarrass yourself." Katra's hand had drifted toward her boot. It stopped. The clockwork thing ticked once, loudly, the way a clock does when it is deciding whether to strike. It was over in moments and without a single blow, which was somehow worse. The flesh-and-blood guard — a slab of a man with a face like a hull plate — took Katra's knives with the boredom of a customs officer confiscating gin, and bound all three of them back-to-back against a rib of the great bone arch. Aya felt the cord bite her wrists and told herself it was only rope. Only rope. Not the hangman's silk her mother had worn. Yeva rose, cane clicking, and crossed the underhold at her leisure. She smelled of myrrh and lamp oil. She stopped before Aya, tilted her head, and studied the mask — the plain porcelain thing Aya had bought off a Bogg Street costumier a lifetime ago. "Let's see what the tide washed in," Yeva said, and pinched the mask away. The air touched Aya's bare face like a confession. Yeva's eyebrows climbed, slow and theatrical. "Well, sink me. The little lordling's daughter. Aya Vasiliev, of the Vasilievs — the house with the silver mines and the seat on the Admiralty board." She turned Aya's chin left, then right, appraising her like a flenser appraises a carcass. "I'd half hoped you'd be somebody interesting." "Don't," Katra snarled from beside her. "Don't you touch her, you hag—" "Mind your betters, gutterling." Yeva didn't look away. "Your betters are worth more than the pair of you salted." *She knows. Of course she knows.* Aya's pulse hammered in her throat. *How many nights did I laugh at them all, the aristocracy in their drawing rooms, while the whole time I was one dead woman's secret away from the gallows?* "Mother Morska," Simeon said, his voice smooth as tar, "whatever you're weighing, weigh it slowly. Nothing here needs to end badly." "Doesn't it?" Yeva tapped her cane against the floor, once, twice. "Here's my arithmetic, Simeon. I have three traitors lashed to my wall on the very night they came to rob my vault. The magistrates pay handsomely for guild blood these days — the new Commissioner is a hungry man. And for *witch-blood*—" her eyes slid back to Aya, bright and terrible, "—oh, they pay in pardons. In charters. A guild mother could buy herself a decade of legitimacy for one red-haired girl who summons things out of the immateria. Your mother swung for less, girl. I attended. Lovely woman. Screamed in a language nobody living could speak." The underhold seemed to lean in. Somewhere in the ambergris lamps, the flames guttered, and Aya felt — she was almost sure she felt — something on the far side of the immateria press its face briefly against the skin of the world, curious, the way deep things are always curious about the ones who call them. "Or," Aya said. Her voice came out steadier than she had any right to expect. "You could consider the market value of a hostage, Mother." "Could I." "My father is Lord Konstantin Vasiliev. His word moves the Admiralty. His debts are paid in whale-oil contracts, and there are men on that board who would rather their dealings with him never saw the light." She held Yeva's gaze, and beneath the mask of her own calm she was screaming. *And there it is. The moment I say it aloud, I am no longer bored. I am a commodity. Sold by thieves to lords, or by lords to the rope.* "A ransom demand to Vasiliev House is worth more than any pardon the Commissioner can scribble. And it costs you nothing but a sealed letter and the patience not to gut me." "Bold," Yeva mused. "You've been slumming with us for what, a year? A year of thieving under my roof, and now you'd price yourself like a prize carcass." "She's right, though," Simeon said quietly. "The arithmetic favours her alive." "Shut up, Simeon," Katra hissed. "Don't you dare sell her—" "Nobody's selling anybody. I'm *buying time*," Simeon snapped, the first crack Aya had ever heard in his composure. Yeva said nothing for a long while. She paced a slow circle around the three of them, cane ticking, her shadow thrown huge and hunched across the whalebone wall like something that had crawled up from the immateria itself. Beyond the guild walls, out in the grey harbour, a foghorn sounded. Once. Twice. Three times — a long, mournful bellow that shivered in Aya's ribs and rolled away over the water. Yeva stopped. She looked up, as if listening to it, and then she smiled down at Aya with something almost like fondness. "Tide's turning," she said. "And so, my clever little witch, is my mind. Take them down to the holding cells — all three, gently, the Vasiliev girl *gently* — and fetch me paper and a good sealing wax." She leaned close to Aya, and her breath smelled of the deep ocean, of things that drown and things that don't. "You'll write to your father, dear. And you'll pray he loves you more than he loves his reputation. Because if he doesn't — well. The Commissioner pays in pardons, and the Commissioner is *so* very hungry."

[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the requested tone and atmosphere throughout. The author successfully creates a vivid whalepunk setting with evocative details like "whalebone ribs arched overhead, scrimshawed with the names of dead ships and deader men" and "ambergris that burned a sickly gold." The Victorian gothic atmosphere is well-established through both descriptive language and dialogue patterns. The characterization is particularly strong. Yeva Morska emerges as a compelling antagonist with authentic voice - her dialogue feels natural and menacing without being overwrought. Lines like "Pickling, Simeon. It's the secret" and "Mind your betters, gutterling" establish her personality efficiently. Aya's internal struggle between her aristocratic identity and criminal activities creates genuine emotional complexity, especially in her realization that she's become "a commodity." The plot beats are executed smoothly - the reveal that the arrest was theater, Aya's unmasking, and her desperate negotiation all feel earned and logical within the story's framework. The author avoids the trap of writing an action sequence as requested, instead focusing on psychological tension and dialogue-driven conflict. The prose strikes a good balance between atmospheric description and narrative momentum. While occasionally leaning toward the ornate ("something on the far side of the immateria press its face briefly against the skin of the world"), it generally serves the gothic tone without becoming purple or overwrought. Some minor weaknesses include moments where the internal monologue could be more seamlessly integrated, and occasional phrases that feel slightly forced in their attempt to maintain period voice. The pacing is generally strong, though the middle section with the binding and unmasking moves perhaps too quickly given its importance to the character arc. The dialogue authentically captures different social classes and relationships, from Simeon's careful politeness to Katra's fierce loyalty. The ending maintains appropriate darkness while setting up future conflict, avoiding unearned positivity. Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. Model Output:
The bar is called the Rusty Nail, which Spike thinks is optimistic. Rust implies the place was ever clean. He's three fingers into a bottle of something that tastes like engine degreaser, nursing it slow because his wallet holds exactly one more drink and a crumpled IOU from Jet. The bounty on his screen — a syndicate accountant named Marcello Vex, wanted alive, 30,000 woolong — is supposed to walk through that door sometime tonight. Spike has been waiting two hours, smoking, watching the door in the mirror behind the bottles. The jukebox in the corner is neon pink and half its tubes are dead. It plays the same scratchy rock track on a loop, some garage-band garbage about bad women and worse whiskey, skipping at the same spot in the second chorus every forty seconds. Spike has counted. Then the door bangs open and a woman walks in like she owns the place and intends to burn it down for the insurance. She's got a dragon coiled down her right arm, cutoff shorts that qualify as a legal opinion rather than clothing, and two pistols riding her hips like old friends. She scans the room, and her eyes snag on Spike — not on his face, but on the bulge of his Jericho under his jacket. "Well, shit," she says, dropping into the stool beside him without asking. "Don't tell me. Skinny guy, weird hair, looks like he slept in a dumpster on purpose. You're after Vex." "Marcello Vex," Spike says. "Forty-something, bad combover, talks too much." "Thirty thousand, alive." She raps her knuckles on the bar. "Hey! Bottle of Bacardi and two glasses. He's paying." She jerks a thumb at Spike. "I'm not paying." "You are, because if you're not, this gets loud." She grins, and it's all teeth. "Revy." "Spike." "That it? Just Spike?" "Names are like attachments." He lights a cigarette. "More trouble than they're worth." The jukebox skips. *Bad women and worse whiskey.* Revy pours herself four fingers and drinks half in one swallow, watching him the whole time over the rim of the glass. He watches her back. She's beautiful the way a drawn gun is beautiful, and about as safe. "So here's the thing," she says. "I don't split bounties." "Neither do I." "Then one of us is going home disappointed, cowboy." She knocks her shoulder into his. He doesn't sway. She likes that. Most men sway, or flinch, or start apologizing for existing. He just exhales smoke toward the ceiling like she's weather. The jukebox skips again. Spike checks the mirror. The door opens. Marcello Vex walks in with two bodyguards and bad cologne, and both bounty hunters move at the same instant — which is to say, into each other. "Move," Revy snarls, hand on her grip. "After you," Spike says, not moving. The bodyguards, being professionals, notice two armed strangers having a whisper-shouting match at the bar and draw first. That's their mistake. Revy clears leather and drops both of them before Spike finishes exhaling; Spike puts a round through Vex's knee as the accountant bolts for the back door, which is a problem, because the bounty says *alive*, and shooting a man in the knee is very much alive but also very much not walking. "Nice," Revy says, meaning it. Then they both reach for the handcuffs at the same time, and their hands touch, and the jukebox skips, and something in the room's chemistry goes sideways. "Back off," she says. "He's mine." "I bled for him." "I aimed for him." They stare at each other over the groaning accountant, guns half-drawn, and the neon jukebox paints them both in dying pink, and neither of them blinks, and neither of them shoots, and that's the strangest part. Revy has shot men for less. Spike has been shot for less. Instead she says, low, "You wanna take this outside?" Spike considers it. "There's a motel across the street." "Wow. Subtle." But she doesn't say no. --- The motel room costs the last of Revy's cash and smells like insecticide and old sin. Vex is zip-tied to the radiator, unconscious, negotiated collateral — split fifty-fifty in the morning, which they both agreed to and neither intends to honor. Revy sits on the bed with the Bacardi between her legs. Spike leans against the window, cigarette going, watching her in the glass. Somewhere down the strip a different bar is playing the same song, scratchy and skipping, like it followed them. "So what's your deal?" she says. "You move like somebody taught you. Not cop-taught. *Syndicate*-taught." "Old news." "You got a dead eye. I can tell. You watch me with one side of your face." Spike turns from the window. "I died once," he says. "A woman I loved. Another man she loved. A church, and a lot of blood. Whatever happens, happens." "Poetic." Revy takes a long pull from the bottle. "Me, I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here. Nobody's waiting on me and I'm not waiting on anybody. That's the whole story." "That's not a whole story. That's a first chapter." "Careful." Her voice drops an octave, goes flat and dangerous. "Guys who look too close end up eating through a straw." "Whatever happens, happens," Spike says again, and sets his cigarette down, and crosses the room. Revy's gun is out before he takes his second step. His Jerecha is out before her hammer settles. Muzzle to her forehead, muzzle to his chest, four feet apart, and the air conditioning rattles, and Vex snores against the radiator, and the song skips somewhere down the street. "You always draw on men who buy you nothing?" Spike asks. "You always hit on women holding a gun on you?" "Only the interesting ones." She could shoot him. He's fast, but she's faster at this range, and they both know it. He could take the shot anyway, because some part of him has never really expected to survive anything, and they both know that too. It's the most honest either of them has been all night. "You're not going to shoot me," Revy says. "No. Are you?" Long pause. The song skips. "Shit," she says, and lowers the gun, and grabs a fistful of his jacket, and the distance between them stops being four feet and becomes nothing at all. It's less a kiss than a gunfight conducted at contact range — all pressure and no surrender, her free hand finding the scar tissue over his ribs, his hand flattening against the dragon on her arm like he's reading it. Then she shoves him back and levels the pistol again, breathing hard. "Nobody stays," she says. "You get that? Nobody *stays*." "Wouldn't dream of it." In the morning, Vex is still tied to the radiator and the room is empty on both sides, and the fifty-fifty split is settled by a coin someone left on the nightstand, heads-up, next to a single cigarette and a spent shell casing, and neither of them ever says the other one's name out loud again — except sometimes, when the jukebox skips.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and atmospheric writing that successfully captures the noir aesthetic of both source materials. The author establishes an evocative setting with the Rusty Nail bar, using concrete details like the broken jukebox and its skipping song as both atmosphere and recurring motif. The prose style is lean and effective, avoiding purple prose while maintaining literary quality. Character portrayal shows solid understanding of both protagonists. Spike's fatalistic philosophy and casual demeanor are well-captured through his dialogue and actions, particularly his "whatever happens, happens" attitude and smoking habits. Revy's aggressive sexuality, profanity, and violence-first approach are authentically rendered. The author successfully maintains their distinct voices throughout.
