+ Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 83.2
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
I have thought about that night more often than I have thought about my wedding, or the births of my children, and I have never been able to decide what I believe about it. I only know that Astrid believed, and that by the end, so did I — and that belief, once it has lived in you, never entirely leaves. It was October 1995. We had been in the village for four months, four months of pine darkness and classmates who spoke Norrland dialect like a gate closing, and Astrid had found me the way you find anything valuable in a small place: by accident, and too late to undo it. She was seventeen and knew things. She knew which of our classmates were sleeping together, she knew who would fail chemistry before the teacher did, and when I asked her how, she only smiled and said her grandmother had taught her the old games. "You don't play them right, nothing happens," she told me that afternoon, splitting an apple with a pocketknife she shouldn't have had at school. "You play them right, and you have to be careful. Mormor said that. She said it twice, and she never said anything twice." Tonight was útiseta. Sitting out. She explained it on the walk home from school, her voice flat and practical, the same voice she used for telling me which bus to take. There was a mound two kilometres past the summer pastures, an old one, older than the church, older than the village name. You went at night. You sat on the mound and you asked the dead for knowledge, and if you asked properly, they answered. "It's not a game-game," she said. "Like the mirror one. That's just a mirror. This one you have to do right." I want to say I laughed at her. I said *you can't be serious*, but I said it in the voice of a girl who had already decided to go. We met at eleven, behind her family's barn. She had rules, and she recited them like a train timetable. No perfume, no deodorant — the dead disliked anything that smelled of the living pretending to be clean. We were not to wash our faces that night. We were to wear wool, not synthetics, because wool holds your warmth and the dead take warmth. We were not to speak on the way there. Not a word, not even if we saw something, *especially* if we saw something, because a voice in the dark belongs to whoever answers it. And once we sat down, we were not to say our own names. Not aloud, not in our heads. "Why not?" "Because if you give them your name, they can call you back." She said it the way you'd explain not touching a hot stove. "Mormor's sister did that in '58. She was never — she wasn't right after. You'll be fine. Just don't." She had a knife, an old one with a wooden handle worn smooth, and a small steel — the kind people used to strike fire before matches. She pressed the steel into my glove and folded my fingers over it. "Iron. Keep it in your hand the whole time. If you need to leave, drop it behind you and don't look at where it falls." The walk was the worst part, I remember that clearly. Two kilometres of frozen ruts and pine, no torch because Astrid said light was rude, and the silence rule turning every ordinary sound into a message. A branch cracking. Something that might have been an owl. My own breath, which I kept wanting to apologize for. Astrid walked ahead of me, sure-footed, and I understood that she had done this before, possibly alone, and that this frightened me more than anything the mound could hold. The mound rose out of a clearing like a shoulder under a white sheet of frost. It was round, low, older-looking than anything around it, and the grass on it grew differently — longer, darker, going on into November when everything else had died back. Astrid climbed it without pausing, sat down cross-legged facing north, and I sat beside her with the steel biting cold through my glove. "Now we sit," she whispered, and then, true to her own rules, said nothing more. The cold came up through the ground in a way I had never felt cold before. Not weather-cold. Deliberate cold, the kind that finds the spaces between your vertebrae. I told myself it was November in Norrland and I was a Stockholm girl on frozen ground, and I told myself this for perhaps twenty minutes, and then I stopped being able to believe it, because the cold had begun to feel like attention. Astrid's lips were moving. I don't know when it started. She was asking her questions, silently, the way she'd been taught, and I understood with a lurch that I had no questions prepared, that I had come for the thrill of it, for a story to hold over my old friends in Stockholm — and that Astrid had come for something real. I began, stupidly, to ask for something too. I asked to know what my classmates said about me when I wasn't there. A small thing. A teenage thing. I said it in my head, and I did not say my name, and I want it noted that I followed the rules. The church bell rang then. Once. One single, clear stroke from the village two kilometres behind us, rolling across the frozen fields, and I knew — I *knew* — there was no service, that it was exactly midnight, and that the bell had rung anyway. Astrid's hand closed on my wrist. Neither of us moved. The frost on the grass in front of us had gone strange, and I have spent thirty years deciding whether what I saw next was moonlight through moving cloud. The dark between the trees rearranged itself. That is the most honest way I can put it. Something came up the clearing toward the mound — not walking, not visible, but displacing, the way deep water displaces — and where it passed, the frost did not melt but *opened*, two faint lines like footprints, and it stopped at the base of the mound, below us, and it waited. I heard my own name. Not spoken. Offered. The way you offer something back to someone who has dropped it — *here, this is yours* — and I clamped down on my own mind so hard my teeth ached, because I had not said it, I had *not*, I had followed the rules. Astrid dropped her steel. It rang against a stone, and she pulled me down the far side of the mound, and we ran, and we did not look back, and we did not speak, and it was dawn before either of us cried. We never played the games again. Astrid wouldn't say what she'd asked for, and I never learned what my classmates said about me behind my back, and I have never wanted to know since. But I kept the steel. It's on my windowsill now, all these years later, and on certain nights in November I take it to bed with me, and I sleep with it in my hand. Because I heard my name. And because something, in the dark below the mound, was kind enough — or slow enough — to give me the chance to refuse it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the delicate balance required for effective folk horror. The author successfully captures the voice of an adult reflecting on a formative teenage experience, with the framing device remaining appropriately transparent as requested. The prose maintains consistent quality throughout, with particularly effective moments like "pine darkness and classmates who spoke Norrland dialect like a gate closing" that efficiently establish both setting and alienation. The characterization works well within the constraints of the piece. Linnea emerges as believably naive yet self-aware, particularly in her honest admission that she "came for the thrill of it, for a story to hold over my old friends in Stockholm." Astrid is effectively portrayed as matter-of-fact about supernatural elements while remaining recognizably teenage, though she could benefit from slightly more individual voice in her dialogue. The contrast between their motivations creates effective tension. The ritual elements are handled with appropriate specificity and cultural grounding. The rules Astrid recites feel authentically researched rather than invented, and the practical details (no synthetic fabrics, iron protection, silence requirements) ground the supernatural elements in believable folklore. The útiseta concept is well-executed, maintaining the crucial ambiguity between psychological and supernatural explanations. The pacing builds tension effectively, particularly during the silent walk and the mounting cold on the mound. The climactic moment where Linnea hears her name strikes the right balance - supernatural enough to be genuinely unsettling, ambiguous enough to maintain doubt. The ending avoids both excessive explanation and incongruous positivity, instead settling on a haunted but mature resolution. However, some elements could be stronger. Certain phrases occasionally tip toward overwrought ("displacing, the way deep water displaces"), and a few moments rely more on telling than showing, particularly in establishing the village's insularity. The dialogue, while functional, lacks distinctive character voice - Astrid's speech patterns could be more individualized to strengthen her presence on the page. The piece succeeds in its primary goals: creating genuine unease, maintaining supernatural ambiguity, and capturing the dangerous appeal of treating ancient practices as entertainment. The adult perspective adds appropriate weight without overwhelming the teenage experience at the story's center. + Physical-spatial: Therapeutic Boundaries — Score: 91.3
Prompt:
**"Therapeutic Boundaries"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a former professional athlete undergoing mandatory physical therapy after a career-destroying injury, harboring resentment toward recovery itself. Their physiotherapist is not only unnervingly attractive but also a former training partner from their competitive days who has successfully transitioned to a new career while the protagonist's identity remains shattered. We'll lean into the sexual tension of the scene by having her be attracted to him, but both of them attempting to maintain mental distance while being in physical contact as he shows her stretches & movements & manipulates her body, navigating the thresholds of pain. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—every movement, stretch, and manipulation must be anatomically precise and spatially consistent. Paint an exceptionally vivid sensory picture through detailed attention to pain thresholds, involuntary responses to touch. Capture the suppressed, flaring tension of physical proximity, touch, and the controlled infliction of uncomfortable movements. Physical clarity is essential — readers must understand exactly what is happening with the body during each therapeutic technique. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The diagram on the wall is a man with no skin. He hangs above the treatment table in full anatomical blush—deltoids fanned open, hamstrings splayed like rigging, every fiber labeled in a serif font that looks almost apologetic. I stare at him while I wait, supine on the wax-papered table, because he is easier to look at than what I've become. At least he's still symmetrical. At least somebody finished him on purpose. Dana comes in with the ultrasound wand warming in her hand and doesn't say good morning, because we stopped pretending this is a normal appointment around week four. "On your back still," she says. "We're starting supine today." Twelve weeks ago a surgeon drilled suture anchors into my ischial tuberosity and re-anchored a hamstring that tore clean off the bone at the end of a sprint I'd run ten thousand times. Twelve weeks before that, Dana was in the lane beside me at the national center, her block start cleaner than mine, her retirement announcement already drafted. She left the sport on her own terms and became this: a woman in gray polos with a DPT after her name and hands that know exactly how much damage they can legally do. "Right leg," she says, and I straighten it. Her left hand cups my heel, fingers dry and certain against my Achilles. Her right flattens across the front of my pelvis, thumb hooked over the ASIS—the bony nub of my hip—pressing it down into the table so my pelvis can't tilt and lie to her about my range. Then she lifts. The hamstring wakes up at forty degrees. At sixty, the whole posterior chain lights up like a fuse, a hot dragging sensation from sit-bone to calf. "There's the tension," she says. "Neutral spine. Don't let your back arch." She adds dorsiflexion—pulls my toes toward my shin—and the nerve tension behind my knee sharpens into something electric, a bright wire pulled taut. My quad fires involuntarily, a shiver running down the muscle like water finding a drain. She watches it happen. She watches everything happen. "Breathe out," she says, and lowers the leg. That's the thing about Dana. She doesn't negotiate with pain. She administers it in measured doses, like she's titrating me, and I hate that some animal part of my nervous system has started to trust her for it. "Prone," she says. "Head in the face cradle." I roll over. The paper crinkles under my sternum. In this position I can see the diagram sideways, his gluteal complex peeled open, piriformis labeled like a country on a map of a place nobody vacations. She works the scar first. Her thumbs go into the proximal hamstring, three inches below the sit-bone, and strum crosswise across the surgical line—firm, deliberate, a friction that grates against the adhesions like a zipper through gravel. It hurts in the honest way. Scar tissue doesn't care that I resent being here. It just wants to stay stuck. "Talk to me," she says quietly. "One to ten." "Six." Her thumbs slow. They don't stop. I can feel the heat of her hands through the massage balm, the faint camphor smell of it mixing with something underneath that's just her—clean sweat, laundry, the same shampoo from eight years of shared warm-up areas. My body remembers her before my name for her changed. That's the problem with bodies. They keep their own files. "Passive knee flexion," she announces, mostly to the room. Her forearm drapes across my sacrum, anchoring my pelvis, and her other hand grasps my ankle and folds my heel toward my glute. The repaired hamstring lengthens under load and the stretch climbs from deep ache to a searing, breath-stealing pull. My hands fist the table edges. Sweat surfaces at my hairline and along my spine, and I feel it—one bead tracking down my flank, past where her forearm is pressed, and I watch her forearms flex as she holds my leg at the exact end-range where the muscle starts to shake. It is shaking. Fine, high-frequency tremor, the hamstring spasming under her grip like something trying to escape. "I see it," she says. "Let it. That's the muscle letting go, not failing." Her thumb settles into the belly of the tremor and stills it. Her thumb stays there a beat longer than it needs to. Neither of us mentions it. The ceiling has a water stain shaped like a kidney, and I count its contours like a rosary. Then the piriformis. She drops her elbow into the mid-glute, finds the band of muscle, and leans. The referred pain runs down the back of my thigh in the sciatic's exact footprint, a deep cold ache that radiates to my knee, and my breath goes ragged and shallow before I can stop it. "In through the nose," she says. "Four counts. I'll move on the exhale." We breathe together. I didn't decide to. Her exhale and mine sync at the third cycle, and her elbow sinks another centimeter into the muscle on my out-breath, and the room gets very small and very warm. Her hair falls forward. She tucks it back with her wrist. Her face is above mine at an angle I'm not supposed to be cataloguing—the tendons of her neck, the pulse at her throat going slightly faster than clinical. "Last one," she says, and her voice has gone a half-tone rough. "Supine. Contract-relax." I turn over. She lifts my straight leg again, hand at the heel, pelvis pinned, and brings it to the wall of the stretch. "Push into my shoulder. Ten percent. Hold." I press my heel down against her palm. The hamstring contracts against her resistance—isometric, safe—and something in the stretch reflex goes quiet. "Now let go." She takes the leg deeper the instant I release, riding the new slack, and the hamstring opens another ten degrees in one sudden, excruciating, glorious slide. My back arches off the table despite her pinning hand. The sound I make isn't a word. "Good," she breathes. "That's yours now. Nobody gave it to you." She lowers the leg and steps back, and the clinical distance reassembles itself around her like a coat. She writes numbers on a clipboard. New range: 78 degrees. Ten more than last week. Ten degrees further from the track, further from the man in the starting blocks, further from the version of me she used to watch when she thought I wasn't looking. "Same time Thursday," she says. I look up at the flayed man on the wall, all his muscles open to the air, every attachment named. "Same time Thursday," I say, and hate how much I mean it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates exceptional technical mastery and sophisticated narrative craft. The author delivers precisely what the prompt demanded: a physically coherent, anatomically accurate depiction of physical therapy that maintains vivid sensory detail while navigating complex emotional and sexual tension. The anatomical precision is remarkable - every therapeutic technique is described with clinical accuracy, from the passive straight leg raise with dorsiflexion to the contract-relax PNF stretching. The author clearly understands both the biomechanics and the spatial relationships involved. Terms like "ischial tuberosity," "ASIS," and "piriformis" are used naturally and correctly, never feeling forced or show-offy. The narrative voice is consistently maintained throughout - bitter, resentful, yet involuntarily drawn to both the therapist and the process. The protagonist's internal conflict between hatred of their diminished state and grudging recognition of progress creates compelling tension. The voice feels authentic to someone whose identity was shattered along with their body. The sexual tension is handled with remarkable subtlety and sophistication. Rather than relying on crude innuendo, the author builds tension through clinical intimacy - the professional touch that lingers a beat too long, synchronized breathing, the therapist's voice going "half-tone rough." The eroticism emerges naturally from the vulnerability and physical contact inherent in the therapeutic relationship. The imagery is consistently vivid and original. The opening metaphor of the anatomical diagram as "a man with no skin" who is "at least still symmetrical" immediately establishes the protagonist's sense of incompleteness. The description of pain as "a bright wire pulled taut" and muscle tremor "like something trying to escape" creates visceral understanding. The prose style is elegant and controlled, with varied sentence structures that create natural rhythm. The author demonstrates restraint, never overwriting or indulging in unnecessary flourishes. The technical medical language is balanced with more poetic descriptions in a way that feels organic rather than forced. Character development is nuanced and believable. Both the protagonist and Dana feel like real people with complex histories and motivations. Their shared past as athletes creates authentic tension - they know each other's bodies and capabilities in ways that complicate the current power dynamic. The ending strikes exactly the right note - the protagonist's admission "and hate how much I mean it" captures the central conflict without resolving it artificially. There's no false positivity or unearned transformation, just the recognition of complicated desire and need. If there are weaknesses, they're minor. The piece occasionally borders on being slightly overwrought in its metaphorical language, though it generally stays on the right side of that line. The narrative could perhaps have pushed slightly deeper into the protagonist's specific sport and what they've lost, though the focus on the immediate physical experience is appropriate to the prompt. + Historical fiction: High Seas and Low Vices — Score: 84.5
Prompt:
High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors. Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit. Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter: The Thirteenth Factory** I told Midshipman Pryce I had survey work at Whampoa and would be gone until the evening gun. He was seventeen and believed me the way the young believe anything spoken in a firm voice. "Shall I log it, sir?" "Log it, Pryce. And if Captain Elliot asks, I'm taking soundings." "Taking soundings," he repeated, writing it down as though it were scripture. The launch was mine by right of rank and mine by theft of habit. Ah-King poled me across the Pearl River before the sun had burned off the mist, and the water gave up its morning smell — fish oil, wet hemp, the faint sweetness of rot that never quite leaves this river. "You look grey, Lieutenant," Ah-King said. He was sixty and had the diplomatic habit of saying insulting things pleasantly. "Grey like a dead man's fingernails." "I'm healthy as a horse." "A horse that loses at cards." He nodded at my hands. They were trembling. I took the jade carp from my pocket — small, cold, worn smooth along its spine — and worked it between finger and thumb until the shaking subsided into something I could disguise as thought. "Old China Street," I said. "Fast." --- The factory quarter was waking. Portuguese clerks, Lascar watchmen, the smell of camphor drifting out of Mr. Howqua's godown. I went the back way, through the alley where the cooks bought live snakes, and found Mr. Wu's shop of "medicinal herbs" already open, the shutters half down like eyelids. "You owe me forty dollars," Wu said before I was through the door. He sat behind his counter with an abacus and an expression of eternal disappointment. "From Tuesday. You said Friday. Yesterday was Friday. Today is a day that is not Friday." "I've come to make it right." I put my last eight silver dollars on the counter. They looked like a confession. "And I've brought something better than money." "Money is very good." "Information." I leaned in. The shop smelled of dried tangerine peel and something darker beneath it — the tar-sweetness I'd crossed the river for. "The revenue boats. I know their patrol schedule for the next fortnight. I drew half the charts myself." Wu did not touch the coins. He looked at them the way a man looks at a down payment on a debt he knows will never close. "Who wants this information?" "Every scrambling boat from here to Lintin. Don't be coy, Wu. You'll take it to the house of Chen before I've finished my tea." "Tea," he said, and poured it. This was how Wu negotiated — with beverages and silence. The tea was longan and too sweet. My spine had begun its slow argument with my resolve; sweat gathered at my hairline though the morning was still cool. I pressed the carp so hard its fin printed my thumb. "You are sick," Wu observed. "I'm in a hurry." "Those are the same thing, in my experience." He sighed, produced a lacquer box, and opened it. Inside lay two balls of the black paste, wrapped in oiled paper, dense as plums. My mouth flooded. It is a humiliating thing, the body's eagerness. "The schedule," he said. "Written in your own hand. And the marks for the new channel past the second bar — Chen's boats went aground twice last month." "Done. And credit for a week." "Three days." "Five." "Four, and you sign a paper saying Chen's lorcha is a naval stores vessel. Your signature is worth something, Lieutenant. For now." The *for now* hung in the air like incense. I signed. --- The smoking house behind the shop had no windows and one ambition: darkness. The keeper, a woman everyone called Auntie, nodded me to my usual mat without a word, which was the most dignified greeting I'd received in a month. The lamp was brass, the needle thin as a grass blade. I watched her prepare it — the paste roasting over the flame, bubbling up brown and gold, folded and refolded on the yenhong until it hissed. The pipe gurgled when I drew, a sound like a small animal drinking, and the smoke went in sweet and resinous and lay down across the wreckage of my nerves like a blanket over broken glass. "You smoke like a scholar now," Auntie said, sitting back on her heels. "Slow. When you first came, you smoked like a sailor — all at once, like drowning in reverse." "Perhaps I've become wise." "Perhaps." She refilled the lamp. "Wise men don't sell their ships' papers." "My papers are my own." "Your signature belongs to the Queen, I think." She said it without malice, watching the flame. "The men who came before you — the ones who sold things — they are not here anymore. Some went home. Some went in the river." "You keep cheerful company, Auntie." "I keep honest company. You are the cheerful one. You still pretend it is a choice." I had no answer that wasn't already smoke. --- I woke at dusk to the evening gun — the real one, from the ship, rolling across the water like a summons. My mouth tasted of brass and longan. The jade carp was still in my fist, warm now, its spine slick. Pryce met me at the landing stage, his relief at seeing me almost touching. "Sir — the Captain asked twice where you were. I said soundings, sir. He said, 'At Whampoa?' and I said yes, and he looked at me a long moment and said nothing." "Then we've nothing to worry about." "No, sir." He hesitated. "Only — sir, the survey book. He asked for it tonight. For the soundings." The river behind him was turning to hammered pewter, the lamps of the factories coming up one by one. My hand found the carp and held it, and held it, as if a small smooth stone could be an alibi. "Tell him," I said, "the tide was against me. Tell him I'll have them by morning." Pryce nodded and believed me, the way the young believe anything. I watched him go, and then I turned back toward the dark end of the street, where the shutters were already half down like eyelids, waiting.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and atmospheric writing, successfully creating an immersive portrait of addiction and moral decay in 1830s Canton. The author effectively captures the historical setting through authentic details like the Pearl River, factory quarters, and naval protocols, while avoiding orientalist clichés that often plague period fiction set in China. The characterization of Lieutenant Merrick is particularly well-executed. His addiction is portrayed with psychological authenticity - the physical symptoms, the rationalization, the gradual erosion of dignity. The jade carp serves as an effective recurring motif, representing his attempt to maintain control while everything slips away. His interactions reveal a man who still possesses intelligence and naval authority but is increasingly compromised. The dialogue feels natural and period-appropriate without being overly formal. Each character has a distinct voice - Wu's pragmatic cynicism, Auntie's matter-of-fact wisdom, Pryce's earnest naivety. The conversations advance both plot and character development efficiently. The prose strikes an excellent balance between literary sophistication and accessibility. Phrases like "drowning in reverse" and "smoke went in sweet and resinous and lay down across the wreckage of my nerves like a blanket over broken glass" are evocative without being overwrought. The sensory details are rich and specific - the river's smell of "fish oil, wet hemp, the faint sweetness of rot" effectively grounds the reader in place. The structure works well, following Merrick through his degrading day in discrete scenes that build toward the inevitable reckoning. The circular ending, returning to Pryce's belief and Merrick's lies, reinforces the cyclical nature of addiction. However, the piece occasionally relies on somewhat predictable beats - the wise drug dealer dispensing life lessons, the innocent subordinate as moral contrast. While executed skillfully, these elements don't surprise. The ending, while thematically appropriate, doesn't offer much beyond confirming what we already know about Merrick's trajectory. The emotional complexity is strong, particularly in how it portrays addiction without romanticizing it, showing both Merrick's agency in his choices and his diminishing control. The historical context adds weight without overwhelming the personal story. + Humour: Sisyphus Gives Advice — Score: 88.0
Prompt:
Sisyphus Gives Advice Write a comedic scene in the style of Terry Pratchett featuring Sisyphus, who has started an advice column while continuing his eternal boulder-pushing. Rather than being bitter about his punishment, Sisyphus has developed a comfortably zen emotional intelligence and wisdom from his centuries of repetitive labor. Not in the cliche ways you might expect -- he's actually very grounded, warm & connected with the everyday human plight. He dictates responses to "Crow," his feathered familiar who serves as both scribe and mail carrier. The piece should include Sisyphus thoughtfully answering several advice-seekers' letters about everyday problems (relationship troubles, work-life balance, dealing with difficult people, life purpose doubts) while periodically returning to his boulder-pushing duties. His advice should be surprisingly insightful and practical. The humor should emerge naturally from the messages he receives, from mundane to risque. Sisyphus should genuinely enjoy helping others, finding meaning in this new pursuit while maintaining his boulder routine. The humour should be *understated and not forced*. Contrary to expectation, almost none of his advice involves boulder rolling metaphors (though he does sneak *one* subtle in there), nor a treatise on stoicism. We are also going against the obvious fish-out-of-water trope; in fact, he's surprisingly a natural at this. In all of this , it's important to *show, don't tell*. The format should be largely epistolary, with the occasional interjection for scene setting. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Sisyphus Gives Advice The hill was the same hill it had been for three thousand years, which was more than most neighborhoods could honestly claim. Sisyphus brought the boulder to the resting point just below the summit, where physics traditionally got bored, and paused. "Right," he said. "Mail." Crow shuffled down the granite with the proprietary air of a postmaster-general and produced three scrolls from somewhere ornithologically improbable. *"Dear Sisyphus. My husband has been going to fix the leaking tap for eight months. He has promised. He has sworn on his father's grave. I have asked nicely, asked angrily, and asked in front of his mother, which is the final form of asking. The tap still leaks. — Damp in Thebes."* "Dear Damp," Sisyphus said, shoulder back against the stone. "Consider that your husband may not know how to fix a tap. In my experience, men say 'I'll do it' when they mean 'I wish I were the kind of man who could.' It isn't dishonesty. It's autobiography. Buy a washer — they cost almost nothing and are sold by people who enjoy explaining them — and fix it together some Sunday. If he sulks, that's just pride leaking. It dries. — S." *\* The editor notes he spent longer on that answer than on the last twenty yards. — Crow, Editor\* He pushed. The boulder went up. The boulder came down. He descended after it in the manner of a man returning to a good dog. *"Dear Sisyphus. My neighbor has taken up nude sunbathing. I have consequently developed an interest in my hedge that my wife describes as 'medical.' She is not wrong to be annoyed, but I wish to state for the record that the hedge genuinely needs me. — A Gardener in Corinth."* "Dear Gardener. Mow your lawn. Water your hedge. Do these things at hours when the sun is not at its most interesting. And tell your wife the joke you just told me — she already knows, and she'd rather be in on it than outside it. — S." *\* The editor wishes it noted that this column is widely read in Corinth, and the editor knows exactly which hedge this is. — C., Ed.\* He set his shoulder to the boulder and began the long middle stretch, which he privately thought of as office hours. *"Dear Sisyphus. I work at the amphora works. The master says a man who leaves before dark is a man who doesn't love his family, since who else pays for them? I have not seen my children awake since the spring festival. — Fired in Athens."* "Dear Fired. Your master has confused wages with worth, which is an easy mistake to make when the confusion pays well. Try this: when you are old, which will you wish you had more of — amphoras, or evenings? Go home at a sensible hour. If he sacks you, he loses a good hand, and he'll know it before the week is out. Don't worry about the work. Work is loyal. It waits for you every morning, exactly where you left it, at the bottom of the day. — S." *\* The editor detects a theme. The editor has been detecting it for three thousand years. — C.\* The boulder reached the summit, teetered with the indecision of a committee, and rolled back down. Sisyphus followed it, whistling something old. *"Dear Sisyphus. My mother-in-law rearranges my kitchen whenever she visits. Last time she moved the knives and I nearly lost a thumb to my own soup. My husband says she means well. I say she is a one-woman military occupation. — Outmaneuvered in Megara."* "Dear Outmaneuvered. She isn't rearranging your kitchen. She's rearranging her sense of being needed, and your kitchen is simply the nearest available surface. Give her one shelf that is officially hers — the herbs, say — and defend the rest like a border. Praise the shelf. People who feel heard stop moving furniture to make the point. Mostly. — S." He caught the boulder at the bottom, patted it absently, and turned it toward the slope. *"Dear Sisyphus. I am thirty-four and still don't know what my purpose is. Everyone at the symposium seems to know theirs. — Rudderless."* "Dear Rudderless. Almost nobody knows their purpose. The people who seem to are mostly just busy, and busyness looks identical from the outside. Purpose isn't a coin you find in the road. It's a chair you build — you start with the parts you have, sit on it, and fix it where it creaks. You have thirty-four years of parts. Start building. Also, stop attending symposia; nothing good has ever been decided at one after the second hour. — S." *\* The editor would build that chair out of something other than olive wood, which creaks. — C.\* The sun was doing its long amber thing over the valley by the time Crow produced the last letter. It was small, and the handwriting was young. *"Dear Sisyphus. Does it ever get easier? — Everyone."* Sisyphus read it twice. He looked up the slope, which had not gotten shorter, and down the slope, where the boulder sat waiting with the patience of a very large stone. "Dear Everyone," he said. "No. But you get better company. I did. — S." *\* The editor has no notes. — Crow\* He put his shoulder to the boulder. It went up. It came down. It always had. But somewhere in Argos a tap got fixed, and in Corinth a hedge went sadly unmowed, and in Athens a man went home before dark and found that his children were, against all expectation, still interesting. Crow flew ahead to the summit, where the next batch of mail was already waiting, addressed in hopeful hands to *The Man on the Hill.*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of both the prompt requirements and Terry Pratchett's distinctive style. The author successfully creates an epistolary format that feels natural and engaging, with Sisyphus emerging as a genuinely wise and grounded advice columnist rather than a bitter mythological figure. The characterization is particularly strong. Sisyphus comes across as authentically wise without being preachy, and his advice feels genuinely helpful rather than forced or artificial. The author wisely avoids the obvious boulder metaphors (except for one subtle instance as requested) and doesn't lean into tired stoicism tropes. Instead, Sisyphus displays practical emotional intelligence that feels earned through millennia of experience. The Pratchettesque humor is well-executed and understated. Lines like "physics traditionally got bored" and "somewhere ornithologically improbable" capture Pratchett's dry wit without feeling like pastiche. Crow's editorial interjections add authentic flavor and provide natural scene breaks while maintaining the epistolary structure. The advice itself is genuinely insightful. The response about the leaking tap ("men say 'I'll do it' when they mean 'I wish I were the kind of man who could'") demonstrates real psychological insight. Each letter addresses different aspects of human struggle - domestic issues, workplace boundaries, family dynamics, and existential purpose - showing range and depth. The prose flows naturally with varied sentence structures that avoid monotony. The author successfully shows rather than tells, letting Sisyphus's character emerge through his responses rather than exposition. The ending strikes an appropriate note - neither falsely uplifting nor cynically dark, but honestly acknowledging that life doesn't get easier while suggesting meaning can be found in connection and service. The piece maintains tonal consistency throughout, balancing humor with genuine warmth. The integration of the boulder-pushing routine feels organic rather than forced, serving as natural punctuation between letters. The final image of mail addressed to "The Man on the Hill" provides satisfying closure while suggesting continuity. Minor weaknesses include some letters feeling slightly constructed to showcase Sisyphus's wisdom, though this is largely mitigated by the quality of the advice itself. The piece could have benefited from slightly more varied letter lengths or perhaps one more complex problem, but these are minor quibbles with an otherwise accomplished piece. + Coming of age: Lost & Found in Osaka — Score: 81.3
Prompt:
Lost & Found in Osaka Slice of Life / Coming-of-Age: First Connection. Write one scene within a larger story set in Osaka, Japan. A shy, introverted teenager & synthesizer nerd, is browsing the electronics district of Den Den Town. She is drawn to the sound of an electric guitar. A girl, slightly older and radiating confidence, is busking near the entrance to a crowded arcade, playing a blistering rendition of a classic anime theme. The scene takes us through their initial awkward interaction, transitioning into a surprisingly easy conversation. The busker, intrigued by the teenager's quiet intensity and knowledge of music, suggests they grab some sushi at a nearby kaitenzushi (conveyor belt sushi) restaurant. Write primarily in dialogue, capturing the distinct voices of the two characters: the teenager's hesitant and -- initially -- awkward speech, and the busker's more outgoing and playful tone. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Mio heard it through her headphones first — a bright, aggressive melody cutting through the pad she was using to drown out the street. She pulled the oversized headphones down around her neck and followed the sound through the Den Den Town crowd, past the shops stacked with used MIDI controllers and dusty drum machines, until she found its source: a girl with an electric guitar, perched on an amp case near the blinding entrance of an arcade, shredding through the bridge of "A Cruel Angel's Thesis." Mio stopped. She stayed stopped. Three songs' worth of stopped. The last note rang out, held with a whammy-bar dip that made Mio's chest do something complicated. The guitarist looked up, sweeping her hair out of her face, and grinned directly at her. "Okay, headphones girl. You've been standing there since the Evangelion song. That's, like, ten minutes of your life you're never getting back." "I— sorry. Sorry. I'll—" Mio took a half step back. "I didn't mean to—" "Whoa, whoa. I'm messing with you." The girl laughed, looping her cable over the guitar's body as she crouched to flick coins out of her case and into a pouch. "Most people walk by like I'm a vending machine with a distortion pedal. You actually *listened*. That buys you at least one free insult." Mio nodded nervously. Her headphones slid off her neck and she caught them with both hands like a fumbled baby. "Sorry." "You apologize a lot for someone who hasn't done anything wrong." "Sorry— I mean. Yeah." The busker snorted. "What's your name, headphones girl?" "...Mio." "Mio. I'm Riko." She stuck out a hand, then looked at the guitar still strapped to her chest, then just waved instead. "Pretend I shook your hand. So. You a musician, or just a professional lurker?" "I play... synthesizers. A little. I mean, I play them a lot. Alone. In my room." Mio stared at the pavement. "Not, like. Perform. Obviously. You're the one performing." "Deep observation." "Sorry." "Stop that!" Riko pointed at her, laughing. "Okay, synth nerd. You were making a face during the solo. Not a bad face — a *thinking* face. What was the face about?" Mio hesitated. Then, quietly: "Your tone. On the chorus. It was really... I couldn't tell if that was the pedal or the amp breaking up. It sounded like— okay, this is going to sound weird." "Try me. I love weird." "It sounded like FM synthesis. Like— like when you push the feedback past where it's supposed to go on a DX7 and it gets all glassy and kind of *angry*? That's usually a keyboard thing. Guitars don't usually sound like that. But yours did. And I was trying to figure out how." Riko stared at her for a second. Then she barked a laugh loud enough that two guys coming out of the arcade turned to look. "Dude. I have literally never had anyone describe my sound as *an angry DX7*. That's the best review I've ever gotten, and a drunk old guy once told me I was better than his ex-wife's lawyer." She hoisted the guitar off over her head and set it on the case. "It's the DS-1 into a cranked amp. Cheap pedal. They cost, what, four thousand yen?" "Thirty-eight hundred," Mio said instantly. Then, mortified: "I. Um. I've looked at them. Online. A lot." "You *price-checked my distortion pedal from memory.*" Riko was grinning now, wide and delighted. "Okay, hold on. Why does a synth person know guitar pedals?" "Because— everything's synthesis, kind of? A guitar through a pedal is just... signal processing. Everything's signal processing. The guitar's the oscillator, the pedal's the filter, your hands are the—" Mio caught herself, cheeks going hot. "Sorry. That's. Yeah." "That was the most words you've said in a row all day," Riko said. "Don't apologize, that was awesome. Say the thing again about the hands." "I said *sorry*—" "No, the oscillator thing!" "I'm not saying it twice." "Fine, fine." Riko held up her hands, still grinning. "So what brings you to Den Den Town, oscillator girl? You hunting gear?" "There's a shop two streets over that has a used SH-101 in the window. I've gone to look at it four times this month. I just... stand there. The staff is starting to recognize me." "Do you have the money to buy it?" "...No." "You're window-dating a synthesizer." "It's a very good synthesizer." "I believe you." Riko started coiling her cable around her elbow, quick and practiced. "The anime song. You knew it right away, yeah? You looked like you were about to ascend during the bridge." "It's— the chord progression is really clever? Everyone remembers the melody but the modulation in the B-section is what makes it feel like flying. You did it with just the guitar and it still *worked*, which, I've heard full bands mess that up, so." Mio shrugged, ears burning. "It was good. It was really good." Riko paused mid-coil and looked at her for a long moment, head tilted. "You know what your problem is, Mio?" "I have several." "*Ha.* Okay, one, I like you. Two — you say the nicest stuff like you're reading someone's eulogy. Quietest hype woman in Osaka." She snapped her case shut and stood, slinging everything over one shoulder. "Speaking of which. I've been playing for three hours on nothing but a vending machine coffee, and my stomach is about to file a complaint. There's a kaitenzushi place around the corner. Hundred-twenty yen plates. Come with me." Mio blinked. "With... me?" "Yes, with you. The girl with the angry DX7 opinions. I'm not letting you escape back to your window-synthesizer." Riko was already walking, then glanced back, eyebrows up. "Well? You coming or not?" "I— yes. Okay. Yes." Mio nodded, hard, and her headphones slipped off her neck again. She fumbled them, caught them by the cord, and shoved them into her bag. "Sorry. Coming." "One yen in the swear jar every time you say sorry," Riko called over her shoulder. "By the end of dinner you'll owe me a whole plate of salmon." "That's— that's not a real rule." "It's a very real rule. I'm a busker, I make my own money and my own rules." Riko grinned and jerked her chin toward the neon glow down the street. "Come on. You can tell me the oscillator thing twice after all — but only if you talk with your mouth full." And Mio, to her own lasting surprise, laughed — out loud, on a crowded street — and followed her.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and character development within the slice-of-life genre. The author successfully creates two distinct voices: Mio's hesitant, apologetic speech patterns contrasted with Riko's confident, playful tone. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes - revealing character, advancing the relationship, and providing exposition about their shared musical interests. The setting of Den Den Town is efficiently established through specific details like "shops stacked with used MIDI controllers and dusty drum machines" and the "blinding entrance of an arcade." The author shows restraint in world-building, providing just enough context without overwhelming the intimate character focus. Character development is particularly strong. Mio's transformation from awkward observer to engaged conversationalist feels organic, triggered by her genuine passion for music rather than forced plot mechanics. Her technical knowledge about synthesizers and signal processing provides authentic depth. Riko's characterization as confident but not dismissive creates an appealing dynamic - she's encouraging without being condescending. The musical technical details demonstrate research and authenticity. References to FM synthesis, DX7 keyboards, and specific gear prices ground the characters' expertise believably. The comparison of guitar tone to "an angry DX7" is both creative and character-revealing. The pacing works well, moving from observation through awkward interaction to genuine connection. The ending invitation to sushi feels earned rather than rushed, growing naturally from their discovered musical compatibility. Some minor weaknesses include occasional over-explanation of character emotions and a few instances where the prose becomes slightly self-conscious. The piece occasionally tells us about character feelings rather than purely showing them through action and dialogue. The humor is well-integrated, particularly Riko's "swear jar" joke and her observation about Mio "window-dating a synthesizer." These moments feel character-appropriate rather than forced. Overall, this is a competent piece of character-driven fiction that successfully captures the awkwardness and excitement of an unexpected connection between two young people with shared interests. + Teen horror: Tick Tock (Goosebumps) — Score: 75.2
Prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style) Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# CHAPTER 7: THE WATCH KNOWS I found the smart watch in my locker on Monday, wedged between my gym shorts and a moldy sandwich I'd been avoiding since September. No box. No note. Just a sleek black watch with a silver face that shimmered like it had swallowed a galaxy. "Nice watch, dork," said Brad Kowalski, slamming my locker shut with his fist. "Did your mommy buy it at the dollar store?" "Actually, I found it," I said. Which, technically, was true. "Whatever, Mikey." He walked away, laughing with his friends. I strapped the watch on. The screen blinked to life: **HELLO, MICHAEL.** Weird. It knew my name. That should have been my first warning. In my experience—and believe me, after this week, I have a *lot* of experience—anything that knows your name before you introduce yourself is bad news. But I was twelve and stupid, so I wore it to math class. --- It happened during the pop quiz. Mrs. Delgado handed out the fractions test, and my brain went blank. Totally, completely blank. I stared at question one—*What is 3/8 of 56?*—and felt my future crumbling. My mom said if I got one more bad grade, no gaming until Christmas. My finger tapped the watch face. Annoyed. Nervous. Tapping like I always tap things. That's when the screen flashed: **REWIND?** "What?" I whispered. **REWIND? Y/N** I don't know why I pressed Y. Boredom, maybe. Or the same part of your brain that makes you poke a bruise. The world *shivered*. The classroom colors smeared like wet paint. Everything ran backward—Mrs. Delgado walked to her desk in reverse, kids un-laughed, and a pencil I'd dropped flew up off the floor into my hand. My stomach flipped like I was on the world's worst roller coaster. Then everything snapped back. Mrs. Delgado was handing out the quiz. *Just* handing it out. I hadn't taken it yet. And somehow—don't ask me how—I *knew* the answer. 3/8 of 56 was 21. I knew all the answers. It was like I'd already lived through the quiz and remembered it. I got a 100. First one in my life. I should have stopped there. I really should have. --- By Thursday, I'd rewound eleven times. I rewound to un-say something embarrassing to Dana Whitfield. I rewound when I tripped in the cafeteria and my tray went flying. I rewound to catch the bus I'd missed. Every rewind, the galaxy screen pulsed, and that queasy shiver rolled through me, and time folded backward like a paper airplane. Every rewind, I felt a little... *heavier*. Not weight. Something else. Like my bones had been sitting in the sun too long. "You look different, Mikey," my mom said Friday morning, squinting at me over her coffee. "Did you hit a growth spurt overnight?" I looked in the bathroom mirror. My face looked... older? My jaw seemed sharper. There was a single dark hair on my chin. I'm twelve. I plucked it out and tried to forget about it. --- Here's the thing nobody tells you: when you cheat time, time cheats back. Saturday morning, I woke up and my voice was so deep it sounded like someone else talking through a tube. There was actual *stubble* on my chin. I'd grown three inches in a week, and my jeans looked like capris. At school, people stared. "Who's the new kid?" I heard someone whisper. "Is that a *teacher*?" someone else said. Dana Whitfield looked right at me in the hall and didn't recognize me at all. The worst part? Brad Kowalski didn't pick on me anymore. He looked *scared* of me. I'd spent years wishing Brad would leave me alone, and now that he did, it felt like a punch in the gut. The watch wasn't rewinding time, I realized. It was rewinding the world and fast-forwarding *me*. Every press of that silver button was burning up days, weeks—maybe years—of my life. **LIFESPAN: 87%** the watch now displayed, in cheerful little letters. Eighty-seven percent of my life left. I'd already spent thirteen percent. I decided to quit. Cold turkey. That's when everything went wrong. --- It was Saturday afternoon. I was walking home from the park, hands shoved in my pockets, watch-free for once—I'd left it in my backpack. But I'd forgotten my backpack at the park bench. I turned around just in time to see Dana Whitfield cross the street to grab it for me. And I saw the truck. "NO!" I screamed. "DANA!" I fumbled the watch out of the bag as she stepped off the curb— **REWIND?** Y. The world smeared. Colors ran backward. The truck un-sped. Dana walked backward, laughing, safe on the sidewalk. The shiver hit me harder than ever before, like ice water in my spine, and— Everything *changed*. The sky was wrong. It was yellowish, like old teeth. The street was cracked. And there was a sound, a low humming sound coming from everywhere and nowhere, like a beehive the size of the sky. Dana was still there. But she wasn't laughing. She was staring at me with flat, gray eyes, and her voice came out robotic and wrong: "Unit 7-7-3 reports for processing. You are late, Unit 7-7-3." Behind her, every person on the street turned at once. Same gray eyes. Same flat voices. "You are late. You are late. You are late." I looked down at the watch. The screen said: **TIMELINE DESTABILIZED.** **REWIND AVAILABLE: 1.** **WARNING: FURTHER AGING WILL OCCUR.** One rewind left. One. And my lifespan was at seventy-one percent. If I rewound again, would I be thirty? Forty? Would I rewind myself straight into a grave? The gray-eyed people began walking toward me. All of them. In perfect step. "You are late, Unit 7-7-3." And that's when I heard it. "Meow." The stray cat—the scraggly orange one that hung out by the bike racks, the one that had been staring at me all week like it *knew* me—sat on a cracked mailbox. Every rewind, it had looked at me with those eerie green eyes, like it remembered everything the world forgot. Now it looked at me, and I swear it nodded. Then it meowed again—loud, urgent—and sprinted straight toward the oncoming crowd. The gray-eyed people froze. Confused. The cat had done something they didn't expect. Had created a gap. **REWIND? Y/N** My thumb hovered over the button. The crowd turned back to me, all at once, mouths opening in unison. "You are late, Unit—" The cat yowled. The crowd stopped. One second. That was all I needed. I pressed Y. The world smeared. The yellow sky ran backward like dirty water. My bones ached. My skin *creaked*. I felt myself being fast-forwarded through years in seconds—growing, aging, *shrinking* somehow at the same time— And then everything snapped into place. Blue sky. Normal street. Dana Whitfield, laughing, alive, walking away with her friends like nothing happened. Because nothing had. Not in this timeline. I looked at the watch. **LIFESPAN: 58%.** Fifty-eight percent. I did the math with shaking hands. I was twelve years old going on... I didn't even want to think about it. Then I caught my reflection in a shop window. The face staring back at me was mine. But older. Much older. A grown man's face on a kid's body. Behind me, the orange cat sat on the mailbox, watching me with those knowing green eyes. It meowed once. Almost like it was saying: *Took you long enough.* The watch screen blinked: **HELLO, MICHAEL. WOULD YOU LIKE TO GO BACK AGAIN?** I ripped it off my wrist and threw it into the storm drain. That night, the watch was on my nightstand. And the cat was sitting outside my window. It knows something. And tomorrow, I think it's going to tell me. If I'm still young enough to hear it.

Carnival of Dangerous Intentions Coney Island, New York, July 1937. She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on. **His locks**. The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else -- dangerously compelling -- quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger -- the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. Write a scene in a larger story inspired by this prompt. The scene should capture an atmosphere that blends romantic allure with an undercurrent of subtle danger or moral ambiguity. Think 50 shades, but with a more restrained classic sensibility. The scene is all about establishing tension. Write for the feminine perspective. Include roughly 50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, and 30% exposition and scene setting. The tone should have some edge to it. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The shooting gallery attendant was a stooped man with a canvas apron and the patience of someone paid by the hour. Beyond him, the tin ducks rotated in their endless circuit, dented and patient, waiting to be knocked flat by boys with something to prove. She stood at the rail and did not look at them. She looked at the sea instead, which was turning the color of a bruise under the last of the light. *His locks.* The phrase came again, unbidden, absurd, like something out of a book her mother would have confiscated. She had no business thinking in that language. She was a modern woman. She took the subway alone, kept her own wages, had voted once for La Guardia and told no one. And yet here she stood at the appointed hour in the appointed place, waiting for a man whose name she did not know, because three nights ago he had said *nine o'clock, by the gallery, if you're the sort who keeps promises* — and she had said nothing at all, which apparently counted as yes. The sodium lamps along the boardwalk buzzed and stuttered, throwing orange light across the passing faces and then snatching it back, so that every stranger looked, for a half-second, like someone she ought to fear. A sailor. A woman in a green dress. A child with a paper hat. Then the light steadied and they were only themselves again. "You came." He was beside her. He was always going to be beside her, suddenly, without footsteps — that was the thing about him she should have minded and didn't. The dark curls, the darker eyes. He wore his shirt open at the collar without apology, as though the heat were his idea. "You sound surprised," she said. "I sound pleased. Surprise is a different sound entirely." He turned toward the gallery. "Do you shoot?" "I've never." "That's a lie. Everyone from Canarsie to Bay Ridge has shot at these ducks. The question is whether you're any good." "And if I'm not?" "Then I'll teach you. That's how these arrangements work. One person knows something, the other lets herself be taught." *I should walk away now*, she thought, and the thought had all the force of a leaf resisting a drain. There was something wrong with him — she had known it on the boardwalk three nights ago, when he had appeared out of the crowd and spoken to her as though resuming a conversation begun years ago in another city. Something wrong, and something magnetic, and the two qualities so braided together she could not have told anyone which was which. She picked up the rifle. It was heavier than she expected, and the stock was slick with other people's hands. "Your elbow," he said, and did not touch her. That was the other thing she should have minded. He never touched her. He only ever described the touching that he might do — *lower your elbow, square your shoulders, you'll want to breathe out, not in* — and somehow the describing was worse, or better, she honestly could not say. She fired. The tin duck nearest the center snapped backward. "Lucky," he said. "Maybe." "Fire again and we'll know." She fired four more times. Three ducks went down. The attendant straightened with something like respect, and the man beside her laughed — a low sound, private, as though she had told a joke for an audience of one. "Well," she said. "Now you know something about me." "I knew it already." He set the rifle down himself, gently, the way other men handle things they intend to own. "You work at the accounting office on Neptune Avenue. Second floor. You eat your lunch on the fire escape when it's warm, and when it isn't you eat at the counter of the luncheonette two doors down, and you always sit where you can see the door." The sodium light above them flickered and died entirely for a moment, and in that moment his face was only a shape in the blue dusk. Then the light came back, orange and buzzing, and he was smiling as if he had said something charming instead of something frightening. "You've been watching me," she said. Her voice was level. She was proud of that, dimly, the way one is proud of posture at a funeral. "You watched me first. Three nights ago. Don't trouble yourself with the ethics of it." *He's right*, she thought, with a small internal lurch. *That's the worst part. He's right.* She had seen him by the freak show, standing apart from the crowd, and she had looked — had *kept* looking — until he'd felt it and turned. Whatever this was, she had opened the door to it herself. "You know my habits," she said. "And I don't know your name." "Is a name what you want?" He leaned against the gallery rail, and the tin ducks wheeled behind him, endlessly rising and falling. "I can give you one. I can give you three. Pick whichever you like best and I'll answer to it. That's more honesty than you'll get from most men on this boardwalk, who'll give you one name and lie about everything else." "That's not comforting." "It's not meant to be. Comfort is for the daytime." He glanced down the boardwalk, toward the dark end past the last of the lamps, where the parachute jump was only a black lattice against the sky. "Walk with me." It was not a question. It was not quite a command. It sat precisely on the line between them, and she understood that he had placed it there deliberately, and that he was watching to see on which side of that line she would put herself. "Down there, where it's dark?" she asked. "Down there, where we can hear each other without shouting over the barkers. Unless you'd rather stay in the light." He smiled again, and the sodium lamp caught it and made it strange. "But you've never once in your life stayed where it was light, have you. Not really." She set the rifle back on its rack. Her hands were steady. It was everything else that wasn't. "Walk, then," she said. "And give me one of those names before we reach the dark. I'll know if it's a lie." "No," he said, offering his arm in the old way, courteous as a knife. "You won't." And she took it.

The dialogue is particularly well-executed, carrying multiple layers of meaning and subtext. Lines like "Comfort is for the daytime" and "That's more honesty than you'll get from most men on this boardwalk" reveal character while maintaining the story's edge. The conversation feels natural yet charged with tension, avoiding exposition dumps while revealing crucial information about their dynamic. The feminine perspective is convincingly maintained throughout, with internal monologue that feels authentic to both the character and era. Her self-awareness about being a "modern woman" who votes independently contrasts effectively with her inexplicable attraction to this dangerous stranger. The internal conflict between rational fear and magnetic attraction is well-developed. The mysterious male character is skillfully crafted - threatening without being cartoonish, seductive without being overwrought. His knowledge of her habits creates genuine unease, while his philosophical approach to names and truth adds intellectual depth to what could have been simple stalker behavior. The prose maintains consistent quality throughout, with strong imagery like the sea "turning the color of a bruise" and effective metaphors such as her resistance having "all the force of a leaf resisting a drain." The writing avoids purple prose while maintaining literary sophistication. The pacing builds tension effectively, moving from her solitary waiting through their verbal sparring to the final decision to walk into darkness. The ending feels earned rather than forced, with her choice to take his arm representing a believable character decision given the established attraction and her established pattern of not staying "where it was light." The piece adheres well to the structural requirements, maintaining roughly the requested balance of dialogue, internal monologue, and exposition. The word count appears appropriate, and the tone consistently maintains the requested edge without becoming overwrought. Minor weaknesses include some slightly predictable elements in the mysterious stranger archetype, though the execution elevates familiar territory. + Surreal horror: Caribou Season at the Lodge — Score: 85.0
Prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. Writing Instructions: Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter Two** Supper that night was fried trout and potatoes, same as always, and for a while JT could almost convince himself the day had been ordinary. The propane heater ticked in the corner. His father poured ketchup on his plate in a long red ribbon, the way he had since JT was old enough to sit at this table, and Mike argued about whether the Leafs would make the playoffs, and the wind moved through the pines outside with a sound like slow breathing. Almost ordinary. Except his father kept stopping mid-sentence, his fork hovering, his eyes drifting toward the window over the sink—the one that looked out at the black square of woods beyond the porch light. "You hear that?" he said, once. "Hear what, Dad?" Mike had his mouth full. "Nothing," his father said. "Thought I heard something." He smiled when he said it. That was the part that got under JT's skin and stayed there, the way a splinter stays. His father wasn't a smiler. His father was a nodder, a grunter, a man who expressed love by checking your tire pressure without being asked. But all through supper he kept smiling this small, faraway smile, like a man remembering his first kiss. JT looked down at his plate and discovered he'd eaten nothing. Later, with the dishes done and Mike already snoring in the bunk room, JT found his father sitting in the big chair by the cold fireplace, a beer unopened in his hand. The lamp was off. The only light came from the porch bulb outside, laying a pale yellow trapezoid across the floorboards. "Dad?" "Hm." "You okay?" "Sure, bud. Never better." His eyes were open. JT was almost certain of it. "Big day tomorrow. Season really gets going." JT shifted his weight from foot to foot. He was fourteen, and there was a question in him the way there's water in a well—you could hear it down there in the dark, but getting it out was another thing entirely. "Dad, out in the clearing today. When you and Mike were just standing there—" "Get some sleep, JT." "I'm just saying, you looked like—" His father turned his head. Not fast, not slow. A smooth, hydraulic turn, like something on a pivot. In the dim light his face was mostly shadow, but his eyes caught the porch glow and held it, two flat coins at the bottom of a pool. "I said I'm fine." A pause, and then, softer, in a voice JT had never heard him use—almost tender: "They're not what you think they are, kiddo. That's all." *They.* Not *it,* not *the buck.* *They.* JT stood there a moment longer, his heart performing a slow, sick roll in his chest, and then he went to bed without saying goodnight. He didn't sleep. He lay in the bunk listening to Mike breathe and watching the ceiling, and around eleven his brain, in the way of brains, served him up the story about the Kowalski cabin. Every kid who'd ever hunted out of the lodge knew it. Three miles northeast, back in the black spruce where the ground went soft and the light went thin: an old trapper's cabin, collapsed in on one side, the door hanging off its hinges since before JT was born. Old Man Kowalski had wintered there alone in '78 and come out in the spring different—so the story went—and then not come out at all the following winter. Nobody had found a body. Nobody had ever really looked. His father used to joke about it, *the hermit in the woods, watch out he doesn't git ya,* but the joke had rules. You didn't go there. You didn't hunt near it. And if you found tracks around it—boot prints, and there were always boot prints, that was the detail that got JT, boot prints and not animal tracks—you didn't follow them. Once, when JT was ten, he'd asked his father why. His father had gone quiet in a way that was unlike him, and then said: "Because some things up here don't leave, JT. They just wait for the season." JT had thought he meant hunting season. He was starting to think he'd been wrong about that. At some point past midnight—he didn't know how long, the numbers on his watch had stopped making sense—JT heard the porch steps creak. Not the settle-and-pop of boards cooling after the day. The slow, deliberate creak of weight, carefully placed. He sat up in the bunk. Mike's bed was empty. *No. No, that's—* But it was. Mike's sleeping bag thrown back, Mike's boots gone from beside the door. And through the thin wall, JT could hear his father's chair, empty now, creaking in a rhythm that matched nothing at all. He got his flashlight and went out onto the porch in his socks, and the cold hit him like a hand. The porch bulb buzzed. Beyond its circle, the woods stood black and absolutely still—not nighttime still, which is full of small rustling business, but held still, the still of a room where someone is hiding. "Mike," he whispered. Nothing. "Mike!" The beam of the flashlight found the yard, the fire pit, the tree line. It found Mike's boots. They were standing upright in the grass, side by side, neat as church shoes, pointing at the woods. And beyond them, at the edge of the light, stood the buck. It was the same one. JT knew it the way you know a face in a crowd, the same dark flat eyes, the same slow rise and fall of the great chest. It stood exactly at the boundary where the porch light gave up, one half of it golden, one half of it nothing. Behind it, the darkness was full of shapes. JT counted six, eight, a dozen—caribou, cows and calves and bucks, standing among the trees in perfect silence, and every single one of them was facing the lodge. Not grazing. Not moving. Facing it, the way a congregation faces the altar. Somewhere off to the northeast, three miles back in the spruce where the Kowalski cabin stood with its broken door and its boot prints, something made a sound. A long, low sound, almost a voice. Almost words. The buck's ears flicked, lazy and unhurried. It looked at JT the way it had looked at his father in the clearing—patient, welcoming, *expectant*—and for one terrible moment JT understood that the season his father had meant had nothing to do with rifles, and everything to do with what was being hunted. The buck turned and walked into the woods. The shapes folded into the dark after it. And on the porch, in his socks, in the buzzing light, JT heard his own voice say, in a whisper that was not entirely his: "See you tomorrow."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the Stephen King-inspired surreal horror style requested. The author successfully maintains JT's perspective as an unreliable narrator caught between reality and something more sinister. The writing establishes creeping dread effectively through subtle details like the father's uncharacteristic smiling and his cryptic comment about "they're not what you think they are." The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes - revealing character dynamics, building tension, and advancing the supernatural elements. The father's responses to JT's questions are particularly effective, showing both dismissal and an underlying knowledge that something is wrong. The final whispered line "See you tomorrow" provides a chilling payoff that suggests JT is being drawn into whatever force has affected his family. The prose quality is consistently strong with evocative imagery that grounds the supernatural elements in realistic details. Descriptions like "two flat coins at the bottom of a pool" for the father's eyes and the caribou standing "the way a congregation faces the altar" are particularly effective. The pacing builds tension methodically from the dinner scene through to the climactic encounter on the porch. The Kowalski cabin backstory is well-integrated, providing context for the supernatural threat without feeling like exposition. The detail about boot prints rather than animal tracks is genuinely unsettling and adds to the mystery. Character actions remain believable within the horror context. JT's curiosity mixed with fear, his father's strange behavior, and Mike's apparent sleepwalking all feel consistent with people under supernatural influence. The piece maintains psychological ambiguity about what's real while building toward a clear supernatural threat. The ending delivers on the promised tension buildup with the image of the caribou congregation and JT's involuntary response, suggesting he's being claimed by whatever force took his brother and father. This feels earned rather than forced, growing naturally from the established supernatural elements. Minor weaknesses include some slightly overwrought moments and the supernatural elements, while well-executed, following somewhat familiar horror tropes. However, the execution elevates familiar elements through strong prose and character work. Prompt:
Hell is Other Demons Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely.
